terms.basis:
WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS, kept separate below.

WHAT THE CLAUSE SAYS. Section 7 does two distinct things. (1) It fixes the licence on article TEXT: contributors "agree to license it under" CC BY-SA 4.0 AND GFDL, and "Reusers may comply with either license or both." (2) It states the reuser's attribution duty in the "Re-use" clause: "When you reuse or redistribute a text page developed by the Wikimedia community, you agree to attribute the authors in any of the following fashions" — and the FIRST listed option is "Through hyperlink (where possible) or URL to the page or pages that you are reusing (since each page has a history page that lists all contributors, authors and editors)." Section 7 also imposes share-alike on derivative text ("you agree to license the modified or added content under CC BY-SA 4.0 or later"), a modification notice ("you agree to clearly indicate that the original work has been modified"), and a licence notice with "either a hyperlink or URL to the text of the license or a copy of the license itself."

THE TEXT-vs-FACTS DISTINCTION, WHICH THIS DOCUMENT ADDRESSES HEAD-ON. The ToU does not leave this to inference. It says: "Where you own Sui Generis Database Rights covered by CC BY-SA 4.0, you waive these rights. As an example, this means facts you contribute to the projects may be reused freely without attribution." That single sentence is the most load-bearing line on this page for Ball Knowledge. The CC BY-SA obligations in Section 7 attach to TEXT — the copyrightable expression on the page. They do not attach to the FACT the sentence conveys, because (i) facts are not subject to copyright in the first place, and (ii) the one right that could otherwise reach a compilation of facts, the EU sui generis database right, is expressly WAIVED by every contributor who holds it. So the licence hook that would normally drag a fact database into ShareAlike is severed at the source.

VERDICT (a) CITING ONE PAGE TO PROVE ONE FACT — permitted. Two independent grounds. First, the fact itself carries no licence condition at all ("facts ... may be reused freely without attribution"). Second, even if a card reproduced a snippet of the page's expression, the "Re-use" clause's first attribution option — hyperlink or URL to the page reused — is exactly what the project already does on every card. No further step is required for a fact-plus-link card.

VERDICT (b) EXTRACTING FACTS INTO OUR OWN DATABASE — permitted. Extracting the FACT (who won, what the score was, which year) and writing our own sentence around it copies nothing the licence governs. The waiver sentence covers this explicitly. The line NOT to cross is copying Wikipedia's SENTENCES into our records — a verbatim or lightly-reworded phrase is text, text is CC BY-SA 4.0 + GFDL, and then attribution, the modification notice and the licence notice all bite, and the ShareAlike clause quoted in row 10 starts asking what licence our own bank is under. Restated in our own words, this is a fact extraction and clean. Quoted, it is a text reuse with strings attached.

VERDICT (c) AGGREGATING AT SCALE — permitted, with one narrow condition and one operational limit. The condition: everything above must hold at scale too, i.e. the aggregate must be facts we have re-expressed, not a mirror of Wikipedia prose. There is no clause anywhere in this document limiting the VOLUME of facts a reuser may take, no anti-substitution clause, and no competing-service clause — the opposite: the preamble to Section 7 says the point is "to grow the commons of free knowledge," and Section 7 confirms "these licenses do allow commercial uses." The operational limit is not in Section 7 but in Section 4: automated uses that are "abusive or disruptive of the services" or that place "an undue burden on an API, Project Website or the networks or servers" are prohibited conduct. That is a rate-and-manner rule, not a rights rule, and Section 12 folds the User-Agent Policy, Robot Policy and API:Etiquette into the ToU by reference. Practically: the content is ours to take; hammering the live site to take it is not the sanctioned way to do it, and there is no need to, because of the dumps route below.

ONE HONEST CAVEAT ON (c). If we ever ship a bulk export of our own bank that includes substantial verbatim Wikipedia text, Section 7's ShareAlike clause and CC BY-SA 4.0 §3(b) would put the exported work under a BY-SA licence. Keeping the bank's prose original is what keeps our own licensing free, and that is a build discipline, not a legal grey area.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route:
YES — and it is the best-documented one of any holder in this run. Three tiers, all official.

1. FULL DATABASE DUMPS — https://dumps.wikimedia.org/ , licence page https://dumps.wikimedia.org/legal.html (fetched 2026-08-07, HTTP 200). Complete XML dumps of every project, free, no account, no key, refreshed twice monthly. Its licence page states verbatim: "Wikimedia's mission is to create educational content that is freely available to all people. In keeping with that goal, all information on Wikimedia projects may be freely shared, copied, remixed, and used for any purpose (including commercial purposes!) in perpetuity." And on text: "Except as discussed below, all original textual content is licensed under the GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL) and the Creative Commons Attribution-Share-Alike 4.0 License." It also flags its own subordination: "Where this information conflicts with specific information in the Wikimedia Foundation Terms of Use ... Those terms are controlling."

2. WIKIDATA IS CC0 — THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL FINDING HERE. Same legal page states: "Copyrights of structured data in the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespaces are waived using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) public domain dedication." CC0 means NO attribution obligation and NO share-alike, at any scale. For a basketball fact bank this is enormous: player birth dates, birthplaces, heights, teams-played-for, draft years, award wins, franchise histories and season links are all Wikidata structured statements, dumped at https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/ and queryable at https://query.wikidata.org/ (SPARQL). This is a clean, licence-free bulk pipeline for exactly the spine of the players table — and it sidesteps the whole text-vs-facts argument, because CC0 content has no strings of any kind.

3. THE APIs — MediaWiki Action API and REST API, blessed by ToU §12 ("We make available a set of APIs ... to enable users to build products that promote free knowledge"), conditioned on the User-Agent Policy, Robot Policy and API:Etiquette which §12 incorporates by reference. Free, needs a descriptive User-Agent with a contact. Right tool for targeted per-article pulls; wrong tool for a full sweep — use the dumps for that, which is precisely why the §4 "undue burden" clause is easy to stay clear of.

4. WIKIMEDIA ENTERPRISE — https://enterprise.wikimedia.com/ , the paid high-volume/SLA tier. Not needed at our scale; noted so nobody thinks bulk access requires payment. It does not.

PRACTICAL RECOMMENDATION: Wikidata dumps/SPARQL first (CC0, zero obligations), Wikipedia article dumps second (CC BY-SA 4.0 text, but we want the facts not the prose), live API only for one-off checks. Never a crawler against the live site.
terms.enforcement_history: NOT RESEARCHED IN THIS RUN — I read only the two named documents and dumps.wikimedia.org/legal.html, and I did not search for enforcement actions, so treat this field as unverified. What I can say from the documents themselves: neither the ToU nor the licence contains any clause aimed at reusers who take facts, and Section 7's stated purpose runs the other way ("To grow the commons of free knowledge and free culture"). The enforcement machinery the ToU does describe points INWARD at contributors and hosted content, not outward at reusers: Section 8 is DMCA takedown handling for infringing material hosted ON the Projects, and Section 13 is account termination. The only reuser-facing pressure the documents create is the trademark carve-out in Section 6 — "any use of our trade names, trademarks, service marks, logos, or domain names must be in compliance with these Terms of Use and in compliance with our Trademark Policy" — which is a real and separately enforced constraint. Concretely for us: freely reuse the facts, do NOT put a Wikipedia or Wikimedia logo, wordmark or puzzle-globe anywhere in the game or on a card, because the content licence grants nothing there and the trademark policy is the one thing WMF is known to defend. I have not checked whether any reuse enforcement action exists; if that matters to a decision, it needs its own search.

terms.basis:
THE VERSION, BECAUSE IT MATTERS. This is CC BY-SA 4.0 International, and it is the right one: WMF ToU Section 7 names "Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International License (\"CC BY-SA 4.0\")" as the licence contributors grant. Version matters for two reasons that bear directly on us. First, 3.0 and earlier had NO Section 4 — sui generis database rights were handled by exclusion, so the database question was murkier. 4.0 licenses SGDR expressly and then tells you exactly what happens when you build a database out of licensed content. Second, 4.0 introduced the 30-day cure period in Section 6(b) and relaxed attribution into "any reasonable manner ... For example, it may be reasonable to satisfy the conditions by providing a URI or hyperlink." Quoting a 3.0 analysis at a 4.0 licence would get the database answer wrong in the strict direction. Note also that older Wikipedia text carries CC BY-SA 3.0 in its history (the site relicensed to 4.0 in 2023) — but since the ToU offers current text under 4.0 and we are not redistributing prose, this does not change any verdict below.

A NOTE ON THE QUOTE'S SHAPE. The words are verbatim. The legal code is a deeply nested numbered list (a)(1)(A)(i); the rendering I extracted carries the sentences but not the letter/number markers, so I have preserved the indentation-as-paragraph-breaks and inserted the section labels ('Attribution.', 'ShareAlike.') exactly as they appear as run-in headings. No wording is altered, condensed or reordered. [...] marks where I skipped a definition not relevant here.

WHAT THE CLAUSE SAYS. Section 2(a)(1) is the grant: worldwide, royalty-free, irrevocable, to "reproduce and Share the Licensed Material, in whole or in part" and to "produce, reproduce, and Share Adapted Material." Section 3(a) is the price of Sharing: retain creator identification, copyright notice, licence notice, warranty disclaimer and "a URI or hyperlink to the Licensed Material to the extent reasonably practicable"; indicate modification; and state the licence with a link to it. Section 3(b) is the price of Sharing an ADAPTATION: your Adapter's License "must be a Creative Commons license with the same License Elements, this version or later, or a BY-SA Compatible License" — that is the viral clause, and it is the one that could in principle reach a fact bank. Section 4 is the database rule.

THE HINGE, AND IT IS ENTIRELY IN THE WORD 'Share'. Every condition in Section 3 is triggered by Sharing. 'Share' is defined as providing material to the public "by any means or process THAT REQUIRES PERMISSION UNDER THE LICENSED RIGHTS." If what you are distributing does not require the Licensor's permission, you have not Shared within the meaning of this licence and Section 3 never engages. That definition is doing all the work in the analysis below.

TEXT vs FACTS, ADDRESSED DIRECTLY. This licence governs "Copyright and Similar Rights" in the "Licensed Material." A Wikipedia article's TEXT is a literary work and is squarely inside that. The FACT the text reports is not: facts are not "material subject to Copyright and Similar Rights," so re-expressing a fact in our own words produces something that requires no permission, is therefore not Sharing the Licensed Material, and is therefore not Adapted Material either — Adapted Material requires modification "in a manner requiring permission." A card that says a player was drafted in a given year, written in our voice, is not a derivative of the Wikipedia sentence that told us so. A card that lifts Wikipedia's sentence IS. That is the whole line, and it is drawn by the definitions, not by volume.

VERDICT (a) CITING ONE PAGE TO PROVE ONE FACT — permitted, unconditionally. The fact is outside the licence's subject matter, so Section 3 is not reached. And in the belt-and-braces case where a card does carry a fragment of the page's expression, Section 3(a)(2) says the conditions may be satisfied "in any reasonable manner based on the medium, means, and context," giving the express example of "providing a URI or hyperlink to a resource that includes the required information" — the article URL, whose history page carries the author list. The project's existing per-card source link already satisfies the strictest reading available.

VERDICT (b) EXTRACTING FACTS INTO OUR OWN DATABASE — permitted. Section 4(a) removes any doubt even on the database-right theory: "for the avoidance of doubt, Section 2(a)(1) grants You the right to extract, reuse, reproduce, and Share all or a substantial portion of the contents of the database." The word 'extract' is in the licence. Extraction is granted expressly, and extraction of non-copyrightable facts needed no grant to begin with. Attribution under 3(a) attaches only when we Share licensed CONTENT — which, again, we do not, if the cards are written in our own words.

VERDICT (c) AGGREGATING AT SCALE — permitted, and this is the verdict most likely to be got wrong, so here is the reasoning in full. Section 4(b) is the trap people see: if you put a substantial portion of the database contents into a database in which YOU have Sui Generis Database Rights, then YOUR database "(but not its individual contents) is Adapted Material, including for purposes of Section 3(b)" — i.e. ShareAlike, i.e. our bank would have to be BY-SA. Two independent reasons that does not fire here. FIRST AND DECISIVE: WMF ToU Section 7 states that contributors "waive" their Sui Generis Database Rights — "Where you own Sui Generis Database Rights covered by CC BY-SA 4.0, you waive these rights. As an example, this means facts you contribute to the projects may be reused freely without attribution." Section 4 opens with the conditional "WHERE the Licensed Rights INCLUDE Sui Generis Database Rights that apply to Your use" — waived at source, they are not included, and Section 4 is inapplicable to Wikimedia content by its own terms. SECOND, INDEPENDENTLY: 4(b) is about copying database CONTENTS. A bank of questions we wrote, seeded by facts we read, does not contain Wikipedia's contents. Note also what 4(b) concedes even when it does apply — the individual contents are expressly NOT Adapted Material ("but not its individual contents"), so no per-fact viral effect exists under any reading. There is no scale threshold, no substitution test and no competing-database clause anywhere in this licence.

THE ONE REAL RISK, STATED PLAINLY. Everything above collapses if question or answer text is copied or close-paraphrased from Wikipedia prose. Then we are Sharing Adapted Material, 3(b) applies, and the Ball Knowledge bank would have to be published under CC BY-SA 4.0-or-later with the licence text or link attached. That is a writing-discipline requirement for the mine-questions pass — facts in, our sentences out — not a licensing negotiation. It is also worth noting Section 2(a)(4)'s carve-out that "simply making modifications authorized by this Section 2(a)(4) never produces Adapted Material," which covers reformatting but emphatically not rewriting.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route: The licence is not itself a distribution channel, but it is what makes the Wikimedia bulk routes usable, and it names its own compatibility escape hatch. (1) The BY-SA Compatible License list at https://creativecommons.org/compatiblelicenses is incorporated by Section 3(b)(1) — relevant only if we ever had to relicense a text-derived work, which the plan above avoids. (2) The full licence text for the notice obligation, if we ever Share licensed text and need to link the licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/legalcode.en (human-readable deed at https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/ — the deed is NOT the licence and should never be quoted as the operative terms, the same trap as the ToU summary box). (3) The actual bulk channels sit with the holder, not the licence, and are listed in the Wikimedia ToU row: dumps.wikimedia.org for article dumps under this licence, and — the far better route for a facts database — Wikidata's structured data under CC0, which is not under this licence at all and carries no attribution or share-alike condition whatsoever. Where a fact is available from both, take it from Wikidata: it is the same fact with zero licence surface.
terms.enforcement_history: NOT RESEARCHED IN THIS RUN — I read the legal code only and did not search for CC BY-SA litigation, so treat this as unverified. What the document itself provides on consequences, which is checkable: Section 6(a) states the licence terminates automatically upon breach of its conditions, and Section 6(b) provides that where the breach is cured within 30 days of discovery the licence reinstates automatically — a cure period that did not exist before 4.0 and that materially lowers the risk of an inadvertent attribution slip. Creative Commons is a licence steward and not a rightsholder here, so it has no standing to enforce; enforcement would lie with the individual Wikipedia contributors who authored the text, which is a large part of why reuser enforcement is rare in practice. I have not verified that last observation against any case and it should not be relied on as a finding. The practical takeaway is unaffected either way: keep our prose original, keep the per-card source link, and no enforcement question arises because no licensed material is being Shared.

[Wikidata:Data access — BULK ROUTES:]
Wikidata dumps are complete exports of all the Entities in Wikidata: https://dumps.wikimedia.org
Use a dump when your result set is likely to be very large. You'll also find a dump important when setting up your own query service.
Don't use a dump if you need current data: the dumps take a very long time to export and even longer to sync to your own query service.
You can query the data in Wikidata through our SPARQL endpoint, the Wikidata Query Service. The service can be used both as an interactive web interface, or programmatically by submitting GET or POST requests to https://query.wikidata.org/sparql.
WDQS is also not suitable when your desired data is likely to be large, a substantial percentage of all Wikidata's data. (Consider using a dump in such cases.)
If you get a 429 Too Many Requests response, stop sending further requests for a while (see the Retry-After response header). Please also refer to the global rate limits set for all Wikimedia APIs.
terms.basis:
ALL THREE VERDICTS REST ON ONE CLAUSE: "All structured data in the main, property and lexeme namespaces is made available under the Creative Commons CC0 License (Public domain)", reinforced by "All data in Wikidata has a CC0 license." CC0 is a public-domain dedication, so it draws no distinction between citing one fact, extracting many, and re-hosting the whole thing. (c) — the activity every other rightsholder restricts — is explicitly the intended use here: Wikidata:Data access tells you to take a dump when your result set is large, and to stand up your own query service. There is no volume ceiling, no non-commercial limit, no share-alike, no anti-substitution clause anywhere on these pages.

ATTRIBUTION — THE SPECIFIC QUESTION ASKED. Two findings, and the first one is a negative that must not be papered over: **the Wikidata:Licensing page never uses the word "attribution" about CC0 at all.** It mentions attribution only to say what CC0 is NOT — that CC-BY ("Creative Commons Attribution, the very permissive license accepted on other Wikimedia projects") is among the licences Wikidata contributors avoid uploading data under, and that non-structured namespace TEXT is CC-BY-SA 4.0. So the "requested but not required" formulation is NOT on the named document. It is on Wikidata:Data access, quoted verbatim above: "We offer the data in Wikidata freely and with no requirement for attribution under CC-0. In return, we would greatly appreciate it if, in your project, you mention Wikidata as the origin of your data." That is the answer in the project's own words: **no attribution obligation; attribution requested, appreciated, and unenforceable.** The CC0 1.0 deed (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/, fetched 2026-08-07, HTTP 200) is consistent — it carries the standard no-warranty language and imposes no conditions. Practical read for Ball Knowledge: a "Data from Wikidata" line is free goodwill, not a legal requirement, and the page even supplies the wording to use.

WHAT IS **NOT** CC0 — THE CARVE-OUTS, IN THE PAGE'S OWN LANGUAGE, AND WHERE THE PAGE GOES SILENT. This is where getting it wrong in the generous direction bites, so I am separating what is quoted from what is absent.
1. NAMESPACE CARVE-OUT, QUOTED: "text in other namespaces is made available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 License." CC0 covers item/property/lexeme statements — labels, descriptions, aliases, claims, qualifiers, references. It does NOT cover Talk pages, project pages, Help pages, or Wikidata: pages. The prose of Wikidata:Licensing itself is CC-BY-SA, not CC0.
2. THE TWO NAMESPACE LISTS DISAGREE, AND THE BODY TEXT IS THE STALER ONE. The body says "main, property and lexeme". The site footer — and the whole of Wikidata:Copyright, which the body names as the authoritative policy statement — says "main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema". Four namespaces, not three. Take the footer/Copyright version; the body sentence predates the EntitySchema namespace. Irrelevant to this project (we would touch main only) but worth recording so nobody "fixes" it the wrong way later.
3. MEDIA — AND I WILL NOT INVENT LANGUAGE HERE. **Wikidata:Licensing says nothing whatsoever about media, images, or files.** The word does not appear in a licensing sense anywhere on the page. That silence is itself the important finding: images shown on Wikidata items are not hosted by Wikidata, they live on Wikimedia Commons under their own per-file licences (CC-BY-SA, CC-BY, PD, fair-use-equivalents), and the CC0 dedication quoted above reaches only the STRUCTURED DATA — including the P18 statement that says "this item's image is File:X.jpg", but NOT the pixels of File:X.jpg. Do not read the CC0 grant onto any player photo, logo, or scan reached through Wikidata. Each file must be cleared on its own Commons page. I have not fetched the Commons licensing policy in this pass, so treat that sentence as the project's standing understanding rather than as something I quoted today.
4. WHAT CC0 DOES NOT CLEAR AT ALL: publicity/personality rights, trademarks (every NBA team mark reachable via Wikidata is still a trademark), and third-party rights generally. CC0 is a copyright waiver by the contributor; it cannot waive rights the contributor never held. The page half-admits this by noting that a contributor "applies a CC0 license to their contribution ... irrespective of whether the user has any claim of ownership to the data they contribute" — i.e. Wikidata's CC0 is only as good as the upstream chain, and the page openly acknowledges the community sometimes takes data whose copyright status is contested.
5. ACCURACY IS A SEPARATE PROBLEM FROM LICENSING. CC0 licences the data; it warrants nothing about it. For a quiz game where a wrong card is the product defect, Wikidata is a legally free INDEX, not a citable authority — its own statements carry references to third-party sources, and those references are what a card should be verified against under DEEPRESEARCH_KNOWLEDGE.md's source tiers.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route:
YES — the strongest one in the whole survey, and it is unconditional. Three official tiers, all quoted above from https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Data_access:
(1) FULL DUMPS — "Wikidata dumps are complete exports of all the Entities in Wikidata: https://dumps.wikimedia.org" (Wikidata specifics at https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Database_download). Complete entity exports, JSON/RDF, no key, no registration, no terms beyond CC0. The page actively directs large consumers here: "Use a dump when your result set is likely to be very large."
(2) SPARQL — the Wikidata Query Service, https://query.wikidata.org/sparql, GET or POST, programmatic use explicitly sanctioned. Caveats are capacity, not permission: "WDQS is also not suitable when your desired data is likely to be large, a substantial percentage of all Wikidata's data. (Consider using a dump in such cases.)" Note also the graph split — scholarly-article items now live at query-scholarly.wikidata.org.
(3) PER-ENTITY REST/Linked Data — Special:EntityData/Q42.ttl etc., with ?flavor=dump to trim referenced-entity descriptions. Same guidance: "Don't use the API when your result set is likely to be large."
The only operational limits are courtesy rate limits, not licence limits: "If you get a 429 Too Many Requests response, stop sending further requests for a while (see the Retry-After response header)." And the page invites self-hosting to escape even those: "you can host your own instance of the Wikidata Query Service and query it as much as you like, out of contention with any others."
WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE PLAN: this is the openly-licensed backbone. A Wikidata dump or a set of SPARQL pulls can legally supply the SKELETON of players.json — canonical names, birth dates, heights, positions, teams-played-for with start/end dates, draft year, hall-of-fame membership, external ids (NBA.com id, Basketball-Reference id, sports-reference slug) — redistributable by us with no attribution obligation and no volume cap. It cannot supply the stat lines a quiz card turns on, and it should never be trusted unverified. Correct division of labour: Wikidata for the spine and the ID crosswalk (its external-id properties are the cheapest way to join our records to every restricted source without scraping them), restricted sources cited one-at-a-time for the facts a card asserts.
terms.enforcement_history: Not applicable in the usual sense, and I did not go looking for takedown records — there is nothing here to enforce. CC0 is a waiver, so there is no licensor with standing to object to bulk reuse of Wikidata's structured data; the project's stated posture is the opposite of enforcement ("We offer the data in Wikidata freely and with no requirement for attribution", plus an invitation to run your own query service). What the Licensing page DOES record is Wikidata as the party on the receiving end of other people's claims: "Wikidata contributors sometimes avoid uploading data when someone has made any of the following kinds of copyright claims on the data", listing traditional copyright, any non-CC0 Creative Commons licence, and "any specialized license with restrictions" — and it notes the community's caution "does not constitute recognition or confirmation ... of the given copyright claim's validity." The page cites Feist v. Rural (1991) as the community's touchstone that "a company that compiles a set of phone numbers cannot copyright them", offered as "supporting evidence that collecting identifying information from compilations of data is permissible, since this sort of information is not eligible for copyright." That is the community's legal theory, not a court holding about sports data, and it should not be relayed to Aaron as settled law covering our other sources. The realistic risk vector on Wikidata is operational (a 429 / IP block for hammering WDQS instead of taking a dump), never licensing.

terms.document: English Wikipedia robots.txt (item 12)
terms.quote:
# robots.txt for http://www.wikipedia.org/ and friends
#
# Please note: There are a lot of pages on this site, and there are
# some misbehaved spiders out there that go _way_ too fast. If you're
# irresponsible, your access to the site may be blocked.
#

# Observed spamming large amounts of https://en.wikipedia.org/?curid=NNNNNN
# and ignoring 429 ratelimit responses, claims to respect robots:
# http://mj12bot.com/
User-agent: MJ12bot
Disallow: /

[...]

# Some bots are known to be trouble, particularly those designed to copy
# entire sites. Please obey robots.txt.
User-agent: sitecheck.internetseer.com
Disallow: /
[...]
User-agent: HTTrack
Disallow: /
[...]
# Sorry, wget in its recursive mode is a frequent problem.
# Please read the man page and use it properly; there is a
# --wait option you can use to set the delay between hits,
# for instance.
User-agent: wget
Disallow: /

# The 'grub' distributed client has been *very* poorly behaved.
User-agent: grub-client
Disallow: /
[...]
# A capture bot, downloads gazillions of pages with no public benefit
# http://www.webreaper.net/
User-agent: WebReaper
Disallow: /

# Per their statement, semrushbot respects crawl-delay directives
# We want them to overall stay within reasonable request rates to
# the backend (20 rps); keeping in mind that the crawl-delay will
# be applied by site and not globally by the bot, 5 seconds seem
# like a reasonable approximation
User-agent: SemrushBot
Crawl-delay: 5

#
# Friendly, low-speed bots are welcome viewing article pages, but not
# dynamically-generated pages please.
#
# Inktomi's "Slurp" can read a minimum delay between hits; if your
# bot supports such a thing using the 'Crawl-delay' or another
# instruction, please let us know.
#
# There is a special exception for API mobileview to allow dynamic
# mobile web & app views to load section content.
# These views aren't HTTP-cached but use parser cache aggressively
# and don't expose Special-pages and other uncached content.
#
# Another exception is for REST API documentation, located at
# /api/rest_v1/?doc.
#
User-agent: *
Allow: /w/api.php?action=mobileview&
Allow: /w/load.php?
Allow: /api/rest_v1/?doc
Allow: /w/rest.php/site/v1/sitemap
Disallow: /w/
Disallow: /api/
Disallow: /trap/
Disallow: /wiki/Special:
[...]
Sitemap: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/rest.php/site/v1/sitemap/0
terms.basis: Quoted from the raw 28,275-byte file (HTTP 200, saved to disk); the [...] marks are my elisions of the long per-bot and per-namespace blocks, everything between them is character-for-character including the leading '#'. (a) CITE: the default group 'User-agent: *' disallows /w/, /api/, /trap/ and the Special: namespaces but NOT /wiki/<Article>. Fetching an article page to prove one fact is explicitly contemplated: 'Friendly, low-speed bots are welcome viewing article pages, but not dynamically-generated pages please.' (b) EXTRACT: same clause permits it, but two conditions ride on it — 'low-speed', and 'not dynamically-generated pages', which is what 'Disallow: /w/' and 'Disallow: /api/' enforce in machine-readable form. So an extraction pass that walks /wiki/ article URLs is inside the file; one that walks api.php or index.php query URLs is outside it for a generic crawler. Restricted, not prohibited. (c) AGGREGATE: this file does not forbid building a database — it says nothing about what you do with what you read. What it restricts is the MANNER, and it restricts it by name: 'Some bots are known to be trouble, particularly those designed to copy entire sites', followed by HTTrack, WebZIP, WebCopier, WebStripper, Teleport, Offline Explorer and recursive wget all set to 'Disallow: /'. The header states the sanction directly: 'If you're irresponsible, your access to the site may be blocked.' Restricted on manner. NOTE THE COLLISION WITH THE PROJECT'S OWN TOOLING: 'User-agent: libwww / Disallow: /' and 'User-agent: wget / Disallow: /' — a curl/wget-based fetch loop is arguably named here, and separately the Wikimedia User-Agent policy (row 14) says a generic or browser-copied UA will be blocked. The one Crawl-delay in the file, 5 seconds for SemrushBot, is the only explicit pace number and the comment behind it names 20 rps as the backend-wide ceiling they are budgeting against.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route: None in this document. The only bulk-shaped thing it publishes is the sitemap endpoint: 'Sitemap: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/rest.php/site/v1/sitemap/0' (and the matching 'Allow: /w/rest.php/site/v1/sitemap'), which lists titles, not content. The real sanctioned bulk route is dumps.wikimedia.org — see row 13.
terms.enforcement_history: The file is itself an enforcement log, which is unusual and worth reading as evidence. It names bots that were caught and the behaviour that caught them: MJ12bot — 'Observed spamming large amounts of https://en.wikipedia.org/?curid=NNNNNN and ignoring 429 ratelimit responses, claims to respect robots'; NPBot — 'Hits many times per second, not acceptable'; WebReaper — 'A capture bot, downloads gazillions of pages with no public benefit'; grub-client — 'The grub distributed client has been *very* poorly behaved'; 'User-agent: fast' — 'Misbehaving, requests much too fast'. Each is answered with a blanket 'Disallow: /'. The stated consequence for the general case is a block ('your access to the site may be blocked'). No litigation; this holder enforces at the network layer, not in court.

terms.document: Wikimedia bulk-download route: dumps.wikimedia.org index + dumps licensing page + Wikidata:Database download + wikitech Robot policy (item 13)
terms.quote:
[dumps.wikimedia.org/legal.html] "Wikimedia's mission is to create educational content that is freely available to all people. In keeping with that goal, all information on Wikimedia projects may be freely shared, copied, remixed, and used for any purpose (including commercial purposes!) in perpetuity. To help guide users of dumps.wikimedia.org, this page contains more detailed information about Wikimedia's licensing and licensing policies as they may apply to our dumps." / "This is a high-level guide only. Where this information conflicts with specific information in the Wikimedia Foundation Terms of Use, or with other information contained inside the dumps themselves, this description should be ignored. Those terms are controlling." / "Except as discussed below, all original textual content is licensed under the GNU Free Documentation License (GFDL) and the Creative Commons Attribution-Share-Alike 4.0 License." / "Wikidata: Copyrights of structured data in the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespaces are waived using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) public domain dedication. All unstructured content in other namespaces is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution-Share-Alike 4.0 License." / "Analytics Datasets: All Analytics datasets are available under the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) public domain dedication, unless otherwise specified." / "Wikimedians diligently remove copyright infringements, but because that removal is an ongoing process, these dumps may contain some copyright infringements which have not yet been noticed and removed. Your use of this material is AT YOUR OWN RISK."

[dumps.wikimedia.org index] "If you are reading this on Wikimedia servers, please note that we are now enforcing the Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy for dumps downloads. Downloads are also rate limited and capped at 3 connections per-IP. These controls will help to ensure that everyone can access the files with reasonable download times. Clients that do not respect the user-agent policy or who try to evade these limits may be blocked." / "MediaWiki Content File Exports — A complete copy of all public Wikimedia wikis, in the form of wikitext source and metadata embedded in XML - the editable source of each page." / "Database backup dumps — A complete copy of all public Wikimedia wikis, in the form of wikitext source and metadata embedded in XML (Note: These XML dumps are deprecated, please use MediaWiki Content File Exports instead). A number of raw database tables in SQL form are also available. These snapshots are provided monthly."

[Wikidata:Database download, section 'License'] "These databases can be used for personal or commercial use, backups or offline use. All structured data from the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespace is available under the Creative Commons CC0 License. Text in the other namespaces is available under the Creative Commons Attribution/Share-Alike License; additional terms may apply." / "JSON dumps containing all Wikidata entities in a single JSON array can be found under https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/. [...] The dumps are being created on a weekly basis. This is the recommended dump format."

[wikitech Robot policy, first generally-applicable rule] "Consider if dumps are more efficient than live requests. Check if you can use Wikimedia Dumps or other forms of offline collection of our data instead of making live requests. If dumps are a viable option for your use case it will reduce the strain on our very limited resources and make your life easier."

[Wikimedia Foundation Terms of Use §7, the sui generis clause] "Please note that these licenses do allow commercial uses of your contributions, as long as such uses are compliant with the terms of the respective licenses. Where you own Sui Generis Database Rights covered by CC BY-SA 4.0, you waive these rights. As an example, this means facts you contribute to the projects may be reused freely without attribution."
terms.basis: All four pages fetched today, HTTP 200. Verbatim with one mechanical caveat: I extracted from HTML, so inline hyperlink markup was flattened — the words and their order are the document's, and single spaces stand where an <a> tag was. The robots.txt row above is raw text and needs no such caveat. (a) CITE: covered a fortiori by the licence — content 'may be freely shared, copied, remixed, and used for any purpose (including commercial purposes!) in perpetuity', subject to CC BY-SA attribution. (b) EXTRACT: permitted, and this is the strongest 'yes' in the whole survey, because of the sui generis waiver in ToU §7 — 'Where you own Sui Generis Database Rights covered by CC BY-SA 4.0, you waive these rights. As an example, this means facts you contribute to the projects may be reused freely without attribution.' That sentence disposes of the database-right theory that every other holder in this survey relies on. Individual FACTS extracted from Wikimedia projects carry no database right against us. Note what it does NOT do: the CC BY-SA licence on the prose still binds if you copy the SENTENCES. Facts free, wording licensed. And Wikidata structured data is CC0 outright — no attribution obligation at all, per both legal.html and the Wikidata licence section. (c) AGGREGATE AT SCALE: permitted, explicitly and by design. 'A complete copy of all public Wikimedia wikis' is the product being offered. There is no substitution clause anywhere on these pages — no 'you may not build a competing service', no volume cap on the DATA. The only limits attach to the TRANSPORT (3 connections per IP, UA policy) and they are stated as fairness controls, not as restrictions on use. Two conditions to carry forward: legal.html says the ToU control where they conflict, and the dumps ship with a warranty disclaimer — 'Your use of this material is AT YOUR OWN RISK' regarding not-yet-removed copyright infringements inside the dump.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route: YES — and it is the most permissive route found anywhere in this survey. (1) https://dumps.wikimedia.org/ — 'MediaWiki Content File Exports: A complete copy of all public Wikimedia wikis' (the current recommended form; the older XML 'Database backup dumps' are marked deprecated in favour of it), monthly, plus 'A number of raw database tables in SQL form'. Free, no account, no contract. Mirrors listed on-site. Announce list: xmldatadumps-l. (2) https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/ — Wikidata JSON dumps, ALL entities, weekly, CC0, described on the Wikidata page as 'the recommended dump format'; canonical RDF (Turtle/NTriples) and smaller 'truthy' RDF dumps at the same location; incremental 24-hour add/change dumps at https://dumps.wikimedia.org/other/incr/wikidatawiki/. (3) Analytics datasets (pageviews etc.), CC0. (4) 'Other files' — Structured Data from Commons, CirrusSearch search indexes, daily page and media titles. Terms on all of it: CC BY-SA 4.0 / GFDL for text, CC0 for Wikidata structured data and Analytics. Access conditions: compliant descriptive User-Agent, max 3 connections per IP, respect the download rate limit. AND WIKIMEDIA THEMSELVES SAY TO PREFER THIS OVER CRAWLING — the Robot policy's first rule is literally 'Consider if dumps are more efficient than live requests.' For Ball Knowledge, the Wikidata JSON/RDF dump is the object of interest: CC0 structured facts about players, teams, seasons and awards, with stable Q-ids to join on, no attribution obligation, and no rate limit once downloaded.
terms.enforcement_history: Transport-layer only, and recent: 'we are NOW enforcing the Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy for dumps downloads. Downloads are also rate limited and capped at 3 connections per-IP. [...] Clients that do not respect the user-agent policy or who try to evade these limits may be blocked.' The word 'now' dates this to a tightening already in force. No enforcement of any kind against USE of the downloaded data — there is no clause to enforce, because the licence grants the use. Contact for licensing questions is legal@wikimedia.org.

terms.document: Wikimedia API terms and rate limits: Policy:API usage guidelines + Wikimedia APIs/Rate limits + Wikimedia APIs/Access policy + Policy:Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy + wikitech Robot policy + Wikimedia Enterprise pricing and API License Agreement (item 14)
terms.quote:
[Policy:API usage guidelines, Version 1.0, Date: August 26, 2024] "When using Wikimedia APIs, an operator must: Follow the User-Agent policy and otherwise correctly label user agents; Follow rate limiting requests (e.g., throttling notification) you may receive; Follow the requirements of the content licenses when republishing downloaded or cached data; and Follow the robot policy if your software is automatically consuming content at a large scale." / "When using Wikimedia APIs, an operator must not: Send traffic via concurrent connections to Wikimedia APIs resulting in a degradation of service to others or endangering the stability of the site; Request data at a high rate, far beyond common use cases, such as in spikes or in a manner intentionally meant to circumvent this policy; Spread Wikimedia API requests over multiple user agents to hide excessive use by a single operator; or Send high traffic originating from a single source or targeting a specific wiki/resource that ends up blocking others from using or accessing that resource." / "For the avoidance of doubt, the existence of this policy does not require members of the Wikimedia community to get prior permission from the Wikimedia Foundation before using the APIs in a manner consistent with this policy." / "The Foundation reserves the right to enforce this policy through blocking API access, disabling a program, or any similar action." / "Sub-licensing. Operators (or those acting on their behalf) may not sublicense, lease, assign, or guarantee the availability or functionality of a Wikimedia Foundation-managed API to any third party. [...] For the avoidance of doubt, this term does nothing to limit the use and republication of Wikimedia content in accordance with the free licenses that content is licensed under."

[Wikimedia APIs/Rate limits] "Requests to Wikimedia APIs are subject to rate limiting to protect Wikimedia infrastructure from overloading and to ensure fair access to resources for all clients. Rate limits apply across all sites and platforms, including requests to the Action API and REST APIs, and are enforced per user." / "The rate limits described on this page are new in 2026 and are subject to experimentation and change." / "API rate limits are being deployed in 2026 to ensure fair and sustainable access to Wikimedia resources. The goal is to reduce the amount of unauthenticated, automated API requests (about 33% at the end of 2025) and to prevent high-volume commercial consumers from putting undue load on our infrastructure." / Limits table, req/min: "Unidentified — Requests with no identifying characteristics other than IP address — 10"; "User-Agent only — Unauthenticated bot requests with a compliant User-Agent header — 200"; "Authenticated requests from users who are new or have few edits — 200"; "Authenticated requests from users who are established editors — 2000"; "Authenticated requests from bots accounts with a bot flag on any wiki — Exempt"; "Wikimedia Cloud Services (WMCS) — Server-side requests from WMCS with a compliant User-Agent — Exempt". / "limit the number of concurrent requests to 3 or fewer." / "respect the Retry-After header provided with a 429 Too Many Requests status code." / "If you require high-volume, commercial access: Wikimedia Enterprise APIs are available with free access for all users up to certain speed and volume limits. commercial rates are offered for those who require higher speed, volumes or SLA requirements."

[wikitech Robot policy] "REST API rules [...] If unauthenticated, keep the concurrency of your requests to 3 at a time, and below 5 requests per second overall. If authenticated, you can raise the number of requests per second to 10." / "Action API rules [...] If unauthenticated, keep the concurrency of your requests to 1 at a time, and below 5 requests per second overall. If authenticated, you can raise the concurrency to 3 overall, and the number of requests per second to 10. Avoid using expensive API endpoints: if your request takes more than 1 second to serve, please wait 5 seconds before making another request." / "Website rules [...] Always crawl the website via the /wiki/Article_name URLs, with no query parameters. [...] still ensure that the maximum concurrent number of requests is fewer than 10 overall, and keep the average requests per second below 20." / "If you are an external entity and you need a higher volume of requests, you should use Wikimedia Enterprise APIs instead. This is the preferred choice for commercial, high-volume users of the APIs."

[Policy:Wikimedia Foundation User-Agent Policy] "Scripts should use an informative User-Agent string with contact information, or they may be blocked without notice." / "User-Agent: CoolBot/0.0 (https://example.org/coolbot/; coolbot@example.org) generic-library/0.0" / "Do not copy a browser's user agent for your bot, as bot-like behavior with a browser's user agent will be assumed malicious. Do not use generic agents such as 'curl', 'lwp', 'Python-urllib', and so on." / "On Wikimedia wikis, if you don't supply a User-Agent header, or you supply an empty or generic one, your request will fail with an HTTP 403 error."

[Wikimedia APIs/Access policy] "By using the API, you agree to Wikimedia's terms of use and privacy policy." / "Most content and data provided via Wikimedia APIs can also be downloaded in bulk via dumps.wikimedia.org."

[Wikimedia Enterprise pricing] "Free account — Snapshot API: Updates: Monthly; Requests: up to 30/mo; Snapshot Chunks: up to 1,500/mo; Structured Contents beta. On-demand API: Requests: up to 50,000/mo; Structured Contents beta." / "Sign up for a free account and start building right away, with no credit card required." / "Over 99.9% of data available through Wikimedia Enterprise services is under a Creative Commons license, allowing you to put that data to work in the best way for your business. Every request has metadata clearly explaining the attached license."

[Wikimedia Enterprise API License Agreement, §3] "3.2 Content. Any Content shall be subject to the applicable Free Culture Licenses and Open Source Licenses that apply to such Content. For the avoidance of doubt, except as explicitly stated herein, the terms of this Agreement shall not apply to any Content." / "3.4 License Restrictions. [...] Customer shall not (or attempt to): [...] (c) create a substitute or similar service or product as that of the Enterprise APIs; [...] (h) aggregate Content with third party data in such a way that an end user cannot attribute the Content under the applicable Free Culture Licenses; (i) knowingly create an application that violates the terms of service or privacy policies of the Content Sources"
terms.basis: Seven pages, all HTTP 200 today. Verbatim with the same mechanical caveat as row 13: extracted from HTML, so inline link markup is flattened to single spaces; wording and order are the documents'. Rate-limit numbers are transcribed from the table rows. THE CENTRAL DISTINCTION ON THIS ROW, and it is easy to get wrong: these documents restrict the ACCESS CHANNEL, not the USE of the content. Access policy §'Data and content licensing' and Enterprise ALA §3.2 both push the content question back to the free licences, and the API usage guidelines say the sub-licensing clause 'does nothing to limit the use and republication of Wikimedia content in accordance with the free licenses'. So the (b) and (c) verdicts below are about HOW YOU PULL, and the answer to WHAT YOU MAY BUILD stays the row-13 answer: permitted. (a) CITE one fact: permitted — no clause anywhere restricts a low-volume read, and the guidelines say no prior permission is needed 'before using the APIs in a manner consistent with this policy'. (b) EXTRACT via API: restricted, with numbers rather than a prohibition. The binding clauses are the Rate limits table (unidentified 10 req/min; compliant-UA unauthenticated bot 200 req/min; established authenticated editor 2000; bot-flagged account exempt), the concurrency rules in the Robot policy (Action API unauthenticated: concurrency 1, under 5 req/s; REST unauthenticated: concurrency 3, under 5 req/s), and the User-Agent policy, which is the one most likely to bite us: 'Do not use generic agents such as curl, lwp, Python-urllib' and 'Do not copy a browser's user agent for your bot' — the exact Chrome UA string this run is fetching with is, on their own wording, the wrong thing to send from an automated job. Any Ball Knowledge fetcher needs a real UA of the form 'BallKnowledge/1.0 (https://<site>; <email>)'. (c) AGGREGATE at scale via API: restricted and explicitly routed elsewhere. 'Request data at a high rate, far beyond common use cases' is a must-not; the Robot policy says an external entity needing high volume 'should use Wikimedia Enterprise APIs instead'; the Rate limits page states the 2026 deployment is aimed 'to prevent high-volume commercial consumers from putting undue load on our infrastructure'. There is NO clause prohibiting the resulting database — the substitution-style clause that does exist, Enterprise ALA §3.4(c), forbids creating a substitute for the ENTERPRISE API SERVICE, not for Wikipedia's content. Two Enterprise clauses do bind a downstream product if we take that route: §3.4(h) bars aggregating Content with third-party data 'in such a way that an end user cannot attribute the Content under the applicable Free Culture Licenses' — i.e. a card built from a Wikimedia fact must remain attributable — and §3.4(i) bars building an app that violates the Content Sources' own terms. Note also §3.1 grants the licence 'on a trial basis' and §3.3 lets Wikimedia 'restrict Customer's access to and use of the Enterprise APIs at any time in Wikimedia's sole discretion'.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route: YES, a second one, and it is free at a useful size. WIKIMEDIA ENTERPRISE (https://enterprise.wikimedia.com/, a Wikimedia Foundation company, Wikimedia LLC). Free account, no credit card: On-demand API up to 50,000 requests/month; Snapshot API 30 requests/month with up to 1,500 snapshot chunks/month, monthly refresh; Structured Contents endpoints included. Paid tier adds daily/realtime refresh, unlimited requests, up to 99% SLA, bespoke egress pricing. Covers Wikipedia, Wikidata, Wiktionary, Wikibooks, Wikiquote, Wikisource, Wikiversity, Wikivoyage, Wikinews. Terms: the API License Agreement at https://enterprise.wikimedia.com/terms/ governs the SERVICE; the CONTENT stays under its own free licences per §3.2, and Enterprise's own marketing states 'Over 99.9% of data available through Wikimedia Enterprise services is under a Creative Commons license'. Every response carries machine-readable licence metadata, which is exactly the field a per-card provenance system wants. Also named as a sanctioned escalation path: run in Wikimedia Cloud Services / Toolforge (rate-limit exempt), or get a bot flag from a local wiki community (also exempt). Human escalation contact for bot operators: bot-traffic@wikimedia.org; policy exceptions: legal@wikimedia.org. FOR BALL KNOWLEDGE THE PRACTICAL ORDER IS: Wikidata CC0 dump (row 13) first, Enterprise free tier for freshness, the public Action/REST API only for one-off verification reads with a proper User-Agent.
terms.enforcement_history: Stated, graduated and technical — no litigation. Guidelines: 'The Foundation reserves the right to enforce this policy through blocking API access, disabling a program, or any similar action. Any choice to take or not take an enforcement action in a given situation will not be a waiver of any future action.' Lifting is discretionary and conditioned on remediation — reducing request rate, implementing exponential backoff, or following the UA naming conventions. UA policy: requests with a missing, empty or generic User-Agent 'will fail with an HTTP 403 error', and scripts without contact information 'may be blocked without notice'. Robot policy: 'Bots that repeatedly try to get around these guidelines or rate limits, and/or threaten the stability of the sites may be blocked.' The 2026 rate-limit rollout is enforcement made structural rather than case-by-case, with a stated target of cutting the ~33% of API traffic that was unauthenticated automation at end-2025. Runtime signals are 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After, and 503 when a backend is overloaded. Enterprise ALA §3.3 reserves suspension at sole discretion. Crucially, the policy notes that being contactable is what buys you a conversation instead of a block: the Foundation 'may contact the operator to discuss [...] This is only possible if the operator's scripts adhere to the User-Agent policy and include up-to-date contact information.'

(a) CITING one fact rests on 'copyright law is clear that facts cannot be copyrighted, so you are free to reuse facts found on this site in accordance with copyright laws' — and, on the companion sharing page, 'You are free to use this data anywhere, we would just ask that you include the citation at the bottom of the table as a courtesy to us for providing this service' (https://www.sports-reference.com/sharing.html, read 2026-08-07). (b) EXTRACTING into an own database is restricted, not banned, and the restriction is narrower than it first reads: the automation clause bars automated access only 'in a manner that adversely impacts site performance or access', and the facts sentence expressly frees the facts themselves. Cutting the other way is the plain-English gloss 'you should not create websites or tools based on data you scrape from Sports Reference or any of our sites', plus the admission that for some datasets 'our licenses completely preclude any redistribution' and 'we cannot even give you explicit permission to reuse en masse what you find on the site' — i.e. SR itself cannot grant what a bulk reuser would need. (c) AGGREGATING at scale rests on the competing-database clause, which prohibits using any statistics or data '(i) to create any database, archive, or other data store that competes with or constitutes a material substitute for the services or data stores offered on the Site or by the Site's Data Providers'. SEPARATELY AND IMPORTANT FOR THIS PROJECT: the AI clause bars using Content 'for purposes of training, fine-tuning, PROMPTING, or instructing artificial intelligence models'. 'Prompting' is the operative word — on its face that covers pasting an SR page into a model to have it write a question card, which is a thing an AI-built quiz bank does by default. That is a distinct exposure from the database clause and does not depend on scale.

You are free to use this data anywhere, we would just ask that you include the citation at the bottom of the table as a courtesy to us for providing this service.' terms.quote: FBref & Stathead Data Update  Posted by sean on January 20, 2026  At Sports Reference we have taken great pride in the role FBref has played over the last seven years as an expansive source for soccer fans all over the world. Their demand came unexpectedly despite our long-standing and good-faith operation of FBref and Stathead. We have operated the sites in a consistent manner from their creation (well before the signing of this agreement) through today, and we have always welcomed open and frank discussions about how the sites operate.  Any effort to retain access to this advanced data would have been costly and uncertain. Under the circumstances, we have decided to comply with the termination notice. terms.basis: Enforcement row — no verdicts claimed, per instruction. Text from the HTML downloaded today, whitespace normalised. 'sean' is Sean Forman, SR's founder and president. This is the single best-evidenced enforcement event in the whole run and it runs the OPPOSITE direction from what the brief anticipated: Sports Reference is the RECIPIENT, not the sender. The reason it matters to Ball Knowledge is causal, not analogical. SR's bot-traffic page explains the absence of an API by saying 'our licenses completely preclude any redistribution' and 'we can not provide the data available as a download'. This post is that clause being exercised in public, at one week's notice, destroying seven years of a product. It shows the real threat model in sports data is not copyright litigation over facts — it is a licence termination one layer upstream of whoever you are reading. A downstream reuser has no standing in that fight and no warning of it.
terms.sanctioned_bulk_route: Negative finding, and a sharp one: the sanctioned route can be revoked without notice. 'Please do not send requests for data or access to a product that no longer exists. The advanced data has been deleted and cannot be provided.'
terms.enforcement_history: WHAT I FOUND, SPORTS REFERENCE, WITH DATES. (1) 26 Oct 2022 — SR publishes its bot-traffic page and begins automated rate limiting. (2) 29 May 2024 — page updated; FBref/Stathead cut to 10 req/min, other sites 20 req/min, ban 'up to a day'. (3) ~13 Jan 2026 — SR's advanced soccer data provider serves a letter terminating the feed and demanding immediate deletion; SR complies. Announced 20 Jan 2026 by Sean Forman at the URL above. (4) May 2025 — a related, smaller retrenchment, 'Removing FBref Translations' (https://www.sports-reference.com/blog/2025/05/removing-fbref-translations/), surfaced in search but not fetched. WHAT I DID NOT FIND, WHICH IS THE MORE USEFUL HALF. Four separate searches for a cease and desist, lawsuit, DMCA notice, PyPI removal, or GitHub takedown by Sports Reference LLC against any scraper, dataset or reuser returned NOTHING — no case, no docket, no news item, no blog post, no Lumen entry. Against that, the scrapers are numerous, public, named after the site, and unmolested: jaebradley/basketball_reference_web_scraper, 552 stars, MIT, not archived, publicly active since ~2016, whose README says in as many words 'Basketball Reference is a great site (especially for a basketball stats nut like me), and hopefully they don't get too pissed off at me for creating this'; vishaalagartha/basketball_reference_scraper, 289 stars, not archived, whose README documents the countermeasure rather than fearing it — 'Sports Reference recently instituted a rate limiter preventing users from making an excess of 20 requests/minute. This package abstracts the waiting logic to ensure you never hit this threshold.' basketball-reference-web-scraper drew 4,492 PyPI downloads in the last 30 days (pypistats.org, measured 2026-08-07). Kaggle carries datasets whose URL slug is literally the provenance — kaggle.com/datasets/patrickhallila1994/nba-data-from-basketball-reference, kaggle.com/datasets/theronwolcott/basketballreference, and sumitrodatta/nba-aba-baa-stats ('NBA Stats (1947-present)') — all live today. Kaggle does honour copyright complaints when it gets them (Retraction Watch, 29 July 2026, documents Kaggle pulling a dataset for infringement), so the mechanism exists and has simply not been pointed at these. CONCLUSION I WILL STAND BEHIND: Sports Reference enforces at the network layer, in minutes and hours, against request rate — and has no public record of ever enforcing in a courtroom against anyone reusing its facts. The exposure is losing access, not being sued.

terms.quote: V. The Lawsuit  128. By the end of January 1996, NBA presented Motorola a letter demanding that it "cease and desist from further advertisement, distribution and sale of the NBA SportsTrax Device." (Ex. 85.)  129. In a letter dated February 2, 1996, NBA presented AOL with an analogous cease and desist letter. ...  139. Although the record does not reveal precisely when NBA and Motorola stopped negotiating, it does reveal that their negotiations continued at least until early 1995 and that Motorola never communicated to NBA its decision to proceed with SportsTrax with or without NBA's involvement. Further, NBA was involved in negotiations with Stats until January 1996; SportsTrax did not begin selling in the retail market until January 1996; Stats made the real-time enhancements to its AOL site in January 1996; NBA mailed Motorola a cease and desist letter in January 1996 and mailed AOL such a letter on February 2, 1996; and NBA filed this action, requesting expedited relief, on March 5, 1996. ...  I find that through the SportsTrax product and Stats' AOL site, defendants disseminated to NBA fans game information on a real-time basis. In so doing, they have misappropriated the essence of NBA's most valuable property--the excitement of an NBA game in progress.
terms.basis: Enforcement row — no verdicts claimed. Full text of the district court opinion, NBA v. Sports Team Analysis and Tracking Systems (Stats, Inc.) and Motorola, 939 F. Supp. 1071 (S.D.N.Y. 1996) (Preska, J.), hosted by CPTech; whitespace normalised. I am reporting this as the EVENT — the only documented instance of the NBA sending cease and desist letters over reuse of its game data — not as the law. The appellate outcome belongs to whichever agent is reading the opinions; I note only that the Second Circuit reversed on 30 January 1997 (105 F.3d 841) and vacated the injunction. The load-bearing detail for Ball Knowledge is WHAT the NBA went after: real-time, in-progress game information, 'the excitement of an NBA game in progress'. Every fact in this project is historical and settled. The one enforcement action the NBA has ever brought over its data is aimed at precisely the category this project does not touch.

terms.enforcement_history: NBA, DATED. End of January 1996 — cease and desist letter to Motorola over SportsTrax. 2 February 1996 — analogous cease and desist letter to America Online over the Stats AOL site. 5 March 1996 — suit filed, S.D.N.Y., No. 96 Civ. 1615 (LAP), pleading copyright infringement, NY common-law commercial misappropriation, Lanham Act s.43(a) and Communications Act s.605. 7 August 1996 — judgment for permanent injunction signed; the same day AOL filed a declaratory action in E.D. Va. 14 August 1996 — NBA moved to broaden the injunction beyond SportsTrax; granted. 30 January 1997 — Second Circuit reverses the misappropriation holding and vacates the injunction (105 F.3d 841). NEGATIVE FINDING, THIRTY YEARS ON: I searched specifically for any NBA cease and desist, DMCA notice or suit against a scraper, dataset publisher or GitHub project reusing stats.nba.com data and found NONE. Not one. swar/nba_api — 3.7k stars, 722 forks, public since 2018, 236,010 PyPI downloads in the last 30 days (pypistats.org, measured 2026-08-07) — exists in the open, is named after the league, and has never been touched. Its README does not even reproduce a restriction; it says only that 'NBA.com has a Terms of Use regarding the use of the NBA's digital platforms' and links out. Kaggle's wyattowalsh/basketball ('NBA Database'), built on those same endpoints, is live. The NBA's answer to unofficial clients is engineering, not lawyers — see the next row.

(1) cdn.nba.com live endpoints (scoreboard, box scores, play-by-play) reportedly sit outside the bot protection and answer from anywhere — community observation, unverified by me, and offering live data this project does not need. (2) The undocumented stats.nba.com/stats/ endpoints themselves, which nba_api wraps. The NBA publishes no developer tier, no key, no pricing and no documentation; nba_api's own README notes 'NBA.com does not provide information regarding new, changed, or removed endpoints', which is the tell — there is no contract to breach because there is no programme to join. terms.enforcement_history: NBA TECHNICAL ENFORCEMENT, WHAT IS DATED AND WHAT IS NOT. Datacenter-IP blocking is the long-running one: bttmly/nba's README documents AWS-block symptoms and ships scripts/proxy as the workaround; swar/nba_api issue #320 'NBA API: timeout for /stats endpoints', opened 28 December 2022 and STILL OPEN, reports /stats failing on Heroku while /live works and the reporter already takes the cause as read — 'the NBA block their API for Heroku instances'. Issue #498 '[Bug]: Connection issues with nba-api on AWS EC2 (Error 10054 / Timeout)', 14 January 2025, is the same failure on EC2, works locally, and was triaged as a third-party-endpoint problem. Layered on top, per community reporting I could not verify at source: Akamai bot protection rejecting requests by TLS fingerprint, which kills Node's and Bun's built-in fetch outright and forces curl-impersonate or similar. Header/UA churn is the recurring maintenance tax: issue #155 'Is the API still working? Are there new headers?' (20 July 2020) is the archetype, and PR #636 'Updating headers' merged 21 February 2026 was the same fix ten years on. Two live 2026 breakages: issue #633 'Issue with multiple requests' (19 February 2026, open) — code working on 12 February 2026 began timing out on the second and third sequential call; and issue #678 '[Bug]: nba_api.live silently swallows 403s and raises a misleading JSONDecodeError' (27 May 2026, open), which confirms 403s are being served today. THE COMMUNITY RESPONSE, EVERY TIME, IS ROUTING AROUND: pass-through proxies on non-cloud IPs, VPS relays, paid proxy services, TLS-handshake spoofing, header rotation. NOT ONCE, across the issues I read, does anyone report a letter, a takedown, a suspended account or any contact from the NBA. The enforcement is entirely at the network edge and entirely impersonal.

law.topic: Feist — holding that facts are not copyrightable (fact/expression dichotomy)
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991) (O'Connor, J.), Part II-A of the opinion
law.quote: It is this bedrock principle of copyright that mandates the law's seemingly disparate treatment of facts and factual compilations. "No one may claim originality as to facts." Id., § 2.11[A], p. 2-157. This is because facts do not owe their origin to an act of authorship. The distinction is one between creation and discovery: The first person to find and report a particular fact has not created the fact; he or she has merely discovered its existence. To borrow from Burrow-Giles, one who discovers a fact is not its "maker" or "originator." 111 U.S., at 58, 4 S.Ct., at 281. "The discoverer merely finds and records." Nimmer § 2.03[E]. Census takers, for example, do not "create" the population figures that emerge from their efforts; in a sense, they copy these figures from the world around them. ... Census data therefore do not trigger copyright because these data are not "original" in the constitutional sense. Nimmer § 2.03[E]. The same is true of all facts—scientific, historical, biographical, and news of the day. "[T]hey may not be copyrighted and are part of the public domain available to every person." Miller, supra, at 1369.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS (the clause each verdict rests on): 'facts do not owe their origin to an act of authorship'; 'The same is true of all facts—scientific, historical, biographical, and news of the day'; 'they may not be copyrighted and are part of the public domain available to every person.' VERDICTS ON THE THREE ACTIVITIES, as a matter of COPYRIGHT ONLY: (a) citing one page to prove one fact — PERMITTED; the fact itself is public domain and copyright never attached to it. (b) extracting individual facts into an own database and citing the source — PERMITTED; extraction of facts is extraction of uncopyrightable matter. (c) aggregating at scale into a substituting database — PERMITTED AS TO THE FACTS THEMSELVES; Feist places no ceiling on how MANY uncopyrightable facts you may take. Scale is not a copyright variable here. IMPORTANT LIMIT ON THIS ROW, kept separate from the quote: Feist is a copyright case and nothing else. It does not speak to contract (a site's terms of use), to the CFAA, to trespass-to-chattels, to database sui generis rights outside the US, or to hot-news misappropriation — the opinion itself gestures at the alternative in its 'may in certain circumstances be available under a theory of unfair competition' aside. A Feist verdict of 'permitted' means 'not a copyright infringement', never 'no legal exposure'. NOTE ON SOURCING: supreme.justia.com returned HTTP 403 to both WebFetch and curl today; law.cornell.edu returned HTTP 200 and is the text quoted throughout. Cornell's transcription carries occasional whitespace artifacts (e.g. 'sufficientef fort' elsewhere in the opinion); every sentence quoted in these rows was string-matched against the fetched file and is clean, with ellipses marking omitted citation matter.

law.topic: Feist — the originality standard, and its application to compilations
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991), Parts II-A and III (statutory construction of 17 U.S.C. § 101 'compilation')
law.quote: The sine qua non of copyright is originality. To qualify for copyright protection, a work must be original to the author. ... Original, as the term is used in copyright, means only that the work was independently created by the author (as opposed to copied from other works), and that it possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity. ... To be sure, the requisite level of creativity is extremely low; even a slight amount will suffice. The vast majority of works make the grade quite easily, as they possess some creative spark, "no matter how crude, humble or obvious" it might be. ... Factual compilations, on the other hand, may possess the requisite originality. The compilation author typically chooses which facts to include, in what order to place them, and how to arrange the collected data so that they may be used effectively by readers. These choices as to selection and arrangement, so long as they are made independently by the compiler and entail a minimal degree of creativity, are sufficiently original that Congress may protect such compilations through the copyright laws. ... Originality requires only that the author make the selection or arrangement independently (i.e., without copying that selection or arrangement from another work), and that it display some minimal level of creativity. Presumably, the vast majority of compilations will pass this test, but not all will. There remains a narrow category of works in which the creative spark is utterly lacking or so trivial as to be virtually nonexistent. ... Such works are incapable of sustaining a valid copyright.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'independently created by the author ... and that it possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity'; 'These choices as to selection and arrangement ... are sufficiently original'; 'a narrow category of works in which the creative spark is utterly lacking'. THIS PROJECT'S OWN COMPILATION — the direction that usually gets skipped. The selection criterion here is 'facts a trivia game can use', which is a curatorial judgement, not a mechanical rule. That is materially unlike Rural's white pages, where selection was 'everyone who applies for telephone service' and arrangement was alphabetical. On Feist's own terms — 'the requisite level of creativity is extremely low' — a question bank whose contents were chosen for playability, difficulty spread, era balance and surprise almost certainly clears the bar, so the bank's SELECTION AND ARRANGEMENT are protectable. Practical consequences, stated plainly: (1) the protection covers the shape of the bank, not its contents — anyone may lift the underlying facts from it and owe nothing; (2) the protection is against someone copying the SET AND ORDER, which is exactly the realistic theft (a scrape of the whole questions.js), so it is not worthless; (3) it strengthens as the curation gets more visibly deliberate — a documented selection rationale is evidence of the 'creative spark', which is a small argument for keeping the pack-design reasoning written down rather than tacit; (4) the QUESTION TEXT is separately protectable as written expression under the same opinion ('if the compilation author clothes facts with an original collocation of words'), and that is the strongest single protection this project has, which argues for writing questions in our own voice rather than lifting a source's sentence. CAUTION AGAINST OVERREADING: 'protectable' does not mean 'defensible cheaply', and a thin copyright in selection loses the moment a copier reshuffles.

law.topic: Feist — rejection of 'sweat of the brow' / 'industrious collection'
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991), Part II-B-1 (discussing and repudiating Jeweler's Circular Publishing Co. v. Keystone Publishing Co., 281 F. 83 (2d Cir. 1922))
law.quote: Making matters worse, these courts developed a new theory to justify the protection of factual compilations. Known alternatively as "sweat of the brow" or "industrious collection," the underlying notion was that copyright was a reward for the hard work that went into compiling facts. ... The "sweat of the brow" doctrine had numerous flaws, the most glaring being that it extended copyright protection in a compilation beyond selection and arrangement—the compiler's original contributions—to the facts themselves. Under the doctrine, the only defense to infringement was independent creation. A subsequent compiler was "not entitled to take one word of information previously published," but rather had to "independently wor[k] out the matter for himself, so as to arrive at the same result from the same common sources of information." Id., at 88-89 (internal quotations omitted). "Sweat of the brow" courts thereby eschewed the most fundamental axiom of copyright law—that no one may copyright facts or ideas. ... Without a doubt, the "sweat of the brow" doctrine flouted basic copyright principles. ... But "sweat of the brow" courts took a contrary view; they handed out proprietary interests in facts and declared that authors are absolutely precluded from saving time and effort by relying upon the facts contained in prior works. In truth, "[i]t is just such wasted effort that the proscription against the copyright of ideas and facts . . . [is] designed to prevent."
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'they handed out proprietary interests in facts and declared that authors are absolutely precluded from saving time and effort by relying upon the facts contained in prior works'; 'It is just such wasted effort that the proscription against the copyright of ideas and facts is designed to prevent.' WHY THIS IS THE OPERATIVE ROW FOR ACTIVITY (b). The intuition that a site which spent decades compiling box scores has earned a property right in them is precisely the doctrine Feist killed. Under US copyright, effort expended in collection generates no rights in what was collected. That disposes of the most common in-house worry — 'they did the work, we are free-riding' — as a COPYRIGHT matter. It also cuts the other way and should be said out loud: this project's own scraping effort, verification passes and dateChecked discipline earn it no rights in ITS facts either. Nobody owes us anything for reusing a stat we verified. Also note the direction the Court points instead: it quotes Nimmer that 'Protection for the fruits of such research ... may in certain circumstances be available under a theory of unfair competition' — the fallback lives in unfair competition and contract, not copyright, and that is where any real risk to activity (c) will come from.
