law.topic: Feist — 'thin' copyright: facts may be copied at will, even for a competing work
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991), Parts II-A and III (construing 17 U.S.C. § 103(b))
law.quote: This inevitably means that the copyright in a factual compilation is thin. Notwithstanding a valid copyright, a subsequent compiler remains free to use the facts contained in another's publication to aid in preparing a competing work, so long as the competing work does not feature the same selection and arrangement. ... As applied to a factual compilation, assuming the absence of original written expression, only the compiler's selection and arrangement may be protected; the raw facts may be copied at will. This result is neither unfair nor unfortunate. It is the means by which copyright advances the progress of science and art. ... Thus, if the compilation author clothes facts with an original collocation of words, he or she may be able to claim a copyright in this written expression. Others may copy the underlying facts from the publication, but not the precise words used to present them. ... No matter how original the format, however, the facts themselves do not become original through association. ... Rather, the facts contained in existing works may be freely copied because copyright protects only the elements that owe their origin to the compiler—the selection, coordination, and arrangement of facts.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'a subsequent compiler remains free to use the facts contained in another's publication to aid in preparing a competing work, so long as the competing work does not feature the same selection and arrangement'; 'the raw facts may be copied at will'; 'Others may copy the underlying facts from the publication, but not the precise words used to present them.' THIS IS THE CLAUSE THAT DRAWS THE OPERATIONAL LINE, and it is a line about FORM, not about volume. Copy the fact: safe. Copy the sentence: not safe. Copy the set-and-order: not safe. Three rules that fall directly out of the quoted text and can be enforced in tooling: (1) NEVER STORE OR SHIP A SOURCE'S SENTENCE — 'not the precise words used to present them' is the one bright prohibition in this opinion, and it is the one a scraper trips over by default because verbatim capture is the easy implementation. Store the datum, write our own prose. (2) VOLUME IS NOT THE COPYRIGHT RISK; STRUCTURE IS. Taking 10,000 facts from a source is no worse under Feist than taking 10, but reproducing that source's own ordering, groupings, tiers or leaderboard cuts imports their protectable selection. Normalise into this project's own schema and the exposure drops. (3) 'IN PREPARING A COMPETING WORK' IS EXPRESSLY BLESSED — the Court says so in terms, so 'but we'd be competing with them' is not by itself a copyright objection to activity (c). The remaining exposure at scale is contractual and technical (terms of use, rate limits, access controls), which Feist does not reach at all.

law.topic: Feist — application: why Rural's white pages failed, and what makes a selection uncreative
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991), Part III-B
law.quote: Rural's selection of listings could not be more obvious: It publishes the most basic information—name, town, and telephone number—about each person who applies to it for telephone service. This is "selection" of a sort, but it lacks the modicum of creativity necessary to transform mere selection into copyrightable expression. ... Nor can Rural claim originality in its coordination and arrangement of facts. The white pages do nothing more than list Rural's subscribers in alphabetical order. This arrangement may, technically speaking, owe its origin to Rural; no one disputes that Rural undertook the task of alphabetizing the names itself. But there is nothing remotely creative about arranging names alphabetically in a white pages directory. It is an age-old practice, firmly rooted in tradition and so commonplace that it has come to be expected as a matter of course. ... It is not only unoriginal, it is practically inevitable. This time-honored tradition does not possess the minimal creative spark required by the Copyright Act and the Constitution.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'lacks the modicum of creativity necessary to transform mere selection into copyrightable expression'; 'It is not only unoriginal, it is practically inevitable.' READ THIS ROW IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, because it is the row that tells you which SOURCES are thinly protected and which parts of OUR OWN bank are. AGAINST SOURCES: the parts of a sports reference site that most resemble Rural's white pages — the complete, exhaustive, chronologically or alphabetically ordered tables (every game in a season, every player alphabetically, a career log in date order) — are the parts with the weakest claim, because completeness is the opposite of selection and chronology is the 'practically inevitable' arrangement. Those are, conveniently, exactly the pages this project reads. By contrast a source's HAND-BUILT lists — a top-100 ranking, an editorially chosen 'greatest games', an awards shortlist with idiosyncratic criteria — are curated selections and are the ones to normalise away from rather than mirror. FOR OUR OWN BANK: the mirror-image warning is that any part of our compilation that is merely exhaustive inherits Rural's weakness. A players.json that simply lists every player is close to a white pages. The protectable creativity sits in the question bank's curation and wording, not in the roster tables underneath it. Worth being honest about that split rather than claiming protection over the whole repo.

law.topic: Feist — sanctioned bulk route: none exists in this document (explicitly recorded as a negative finding)
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991) — read in full for any licensing, dump, API or bulk-access provision
law.quote: The primary objective of copyright is not to reward the labor of authors, but "[t]o promote the Progress of Science and useful Arts." Art. I, § 8, cl. 8. ... To this end, copyright assures authors the right to their original expression, but encourages others to build freely upon the ideas and information conveyed by a work. ... This principle, known as the idea/expression or fact/expression dichotomy, applies to all works of authorship.
law.what_it_means_here: NEGATIVE FINDING, recorded so a later session does not re-search for it: Feist is a judicial opinion, not a rightsholder's terms, so it publishes no dump, no data download and no official API tier. There is nothing to name here. The reason this row exists at all is that Feist changes the value of the bulk-route question rather than answering it: because the facts themselves are free ('encourages others to build freely upon the ideas and information conveyed by a work'), a paid or sanctioned bulk feed from a sports data holder is being bought for ACCESS, RELIABILITY, SCHEMA AND INDEMNITY — not for permission to use the facts, which no one needs. That should reframe any future negotiation: we are not licensing the numbers, we are buying delivery and a contractual safe harbour. Where a sanctioned route genuinely matters is the layer Feist does not touch — a terms-of-use covenant against scraping is enforceable as CONTRACT whatever copyright says, and an official feed is the clean way around it. law.topic: NBA v. Motorola — the holding: a NARROW hot-news exception survives Copyright Act preemption
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. Jan. 30, 1997), slip op. ¶¶ 2, 68 (public.resource.org full text)
law.quote: The crux of the dispute concerns the extent to which a state law "hot-news" misappropriation claim based on International News Service v. Associated Press, 248 U.S. 215, 39 S.Ct. 68, 63 L.Ed. 211 (1918) ("INS "), survives preemption by the federal Copyright Act and whether the NBA's claim fits within the surviving INS-type claims. We hold that a narrow "hot-news" exception does survive preemption. However, we also hold that appellants' transmission of "real-time" NBA game scores and information tabulated from television and radio broadcasts of games in progress does not constitute a misappropriation of "hot news" that is the property of the NBA. … Our conclusion, therefore, is that only a narrow "hot-news" misappropriation claim survives preemption for actions concerning material within the realm of copyright.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the two quoted holding sentences ("a narrow 'hot-news' exception does survive preemption" / "only a narrow 'hot-news' misappropriation claim survives preemption"). This is the doctrinal ceiling for any misappropriation theory a stats holder might raise against Ball Knowledge. What survives is narrow and INS-shaped, and the court applied it to REJECT the NBA's claim against a party transmitting real-time scores. VERDICTS under this clause — (a) citing one page to prove one fact: PERMITTED; nothing in the surviving claim touches a single sourced citation. (b) extracting individual facts into our own DB and citing the source: PERMITTED; the claim that survives is about hot news, not about fact extraction. (c) aggregating at scale into a substitute DB: RESTRICTED, not by this clause but by the five elements in the next row — this clause only tells you the door is narrow, not where the line falls. The ellipsis marks a jump from ¶2 to ¶68; both fragments are verbatim, nothing inside either is elided. Source renders em dashes as '--' and uses straight quotes.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit (NY, CT, VT), construing New York state misappropriation law against 17 U.S.C. § 301 preemption. Persuasive elsewhere; not binding outside the 2d Cir.

law.topic: THE FIVE-ELEMENT TEST — the operative statement (¶ 69, 'elements central to an INS claim')
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶ 69
law.quote: In our view, the elements central to an INS claim are: (i) the plaintiff generates or collects information at some cost or expense, see FII, 808 F.2d at 206; INS, 248 U.S. at 240, 39 S.Ct. at 72-73; (ii) the value of the information is highly time-sensitive, see FII, 808 F.2d at 209; INS, 248 U.S. at 231, 39 S.Ct. at 69-70; Restatement (Third) Unfair Competition, § 38 cmt. c.; (iii) the defendant's use of the information constitutes free-riding on the plaintiff's costly efforts to generate or collect it, see FII, 808 F.2d at 207; INS, 248 U.S. at 239-40, 39 S.Ct. at 72-73; Restatement § 38 at cmt. c.; McCarthy, § 10:73 at 10-139; (iv) the defendant's use of the information is in direct competition with a product or service offered by the plaintiff, FII, 808 F.2d at 209, INS, 248 U.S. at 240, 39 S.Ct. at 72-73; (v) the ability of other parties to free-ride on the efforts of the plaintiff would so reduce the incentive to produce the product or service that its existence or quality would be substantially threatened, FII, 808 F.2d at 209; Restatement, § 38 at cmt. c.; INS, 248 U.S. at 241, 39 S.Ct. at 73 ("[INS's conduct] would render [AP's] publication profitless, or so little profitable as in effect to cut off the service by rendering the cost prohibitive in comparison with the return.")
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: element (ii), "the value of the information is highly time-sensitive", and element (iv), "in direct competition with a product or service offered by the plaintiff". This is the test itself, quoted whole including the internal citations. Applying it to the project: element (ii) FAILS for everything Ball Knowledge does — who led the 1986-87 NBA in rebounds has no time-sensitive value; element (iv) FAILS because a trivia game is not in direct competition with a reference site's product; element (v) FAILS because a trivia bank does not threaten the existence of Basketball-Reference. VERDICTS: (a) citing one page to prove one fact — PERMITTED, fails (ii)/(iv)/(v) three times over. (b) extracting facts into our DB and citing the source — PERMITTED on the same three failures. (c) aggregating at scale into a substitute DB — this is the ONLY activity where the test bites, and it bites through (iii)+(iv)+(v), not (ii): a wholesale mirror of a stats site is a directly competing product built by free-riding. But note that even (c) still has to clear element (ii), and historical stats are not time-sensitive, so hot-news is a WEAK theory against (c). The real exposure for (c) is contract/ToS and database-scraping law, not this case. Verdict for (c) under THIS authority: UNCLEAR-to-permitted, and any prohibition on (c) must be sourced elsewhere. NOTE: the Caselaw Access Project scan of this same paragraph OCRs '(iii)' as '(in)' and 'cmt. c.' as 'cmt. e.'; the text quoted here is the clean public.resource.org rendering, which I verified word-for-word against the CAP scan.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit; New York misappropriation law as narrowed by § 301 preemption.

law.topic: THE FIVE-ELEMENT TEST — the holding-summary formulation (¶ 14), which is the version most often quoted by later courts
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶ 14
law.quote: We hold that the surviving "hot-news" INS-like claim is limited to cases where: (i) a plaintiff generates or gathers information at a cost; (ii) the information is time-sensitive; (iii) a defendant's use of the information constitutes free riding on the plaintiff's efforts; (iv) the defendant is in direct competition with a product or service offered by the plaintiffs; and (v) the ability of other parties to free-ride on the efforts of the plaintiff or others would so reduce the incentive to produce the product or service that its existence or quality would be substantially threatened. We conclude that SportsTrax does not meet that test.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the framing words "is limited to cases where" plus element (ii) "the information is time-sensitive". This is the same test as ¶ 69 but stated as a limitation — the claim is LIMITED TO cases meeting all five. That framing matters: it is a conjunctive gate, so failing any one element defeats the claim, and historical stats fail (ii) on their face. VERDICTS: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) not reached by this clause for non-time-sensitive data — the gate closes at element (ii) before competition is even considered. Also worth recording for the project's own defensive posture: the court concluded the defendant transmitting live NBA scores "does not meet that test", which is a far more aggressive activity than anything Ball Knowledge does.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit.

law.topic: The three 'extra elements' that let a hot-news claim escape § 301 preemption
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶ 71
law.quote: We therefore find the extra elements--those in addition to the elements of copyright infringement--that allow a "hotnews" claim to survive preemption are: (i) the time-sensitive value of factual information, (ii) the free-riding by a defendant, and (iii) the threat to the very existence of the product or service provided by the plaintiff.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: extra element (i), "the time-sensitive value of factual information". This is the preemption-side companion to the five-element test and it is the single most useful sentence in the opinion for this project. Time-sensitivity is not merely one of five factors — it is one of only three things that make the state claim NON-EQUIVALENT to copyright and therefore survivable at all. Strip time-sensitivity out and the state claim collapses back into a copyright claim, which then fails outright because facts are not copyrightable (see the Feist row below). So for historical basketball facts the plaintiff is caught in a pincer: no hot-news claim (not time-sensitive) and no copyright claim (facts). VERDICTS: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) PERMITTED as against a hot-news theory specifically — a bulk historical aggregator cannot be reached by hot-news at all, though it remains exposed on contract/ToS grounds this case says nothing about. Source spells it 'hotnews' (unhyphenated) here and renders the em dashes as '--'; both are the source's own rendering, reproduced exactly.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit; 17 U.S.C. § 301 preemption analysis.

law.topic: How the court APPLIED time-sensitivity — the decisive passage for the historical-facts question
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶ 72
law.quote: We conclude that Motorola and STATS have not engaged in unlawful misappropriation under the "hot-news" test set out above. To be sure, some of the elements of a "hot-news" INS claim are met. The information transmitted to SportsTrax is not precisely contemporaneous, but it is nevertheless time-sensitive.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "not precisely contemporaneous, but it is nevertheless time-sensitive." This shows where the court drew the time-sensitivity line, and it is the sentence that answers the reaches-historical-facts question from the text rather than from reasoning. The court found data delayed by two-to-three minutes from a live game still time-sensitive — so the concept has some slack in it. But the slack is measured in MINUTES OFF A GAME IN PROGRESS. The entire market the court had in view was live-score pagers. Nothing in the opinion extends 'time-sensitive' to a completed game, a completed season, or a career total. Ball Knowledge's bank is made of settled historical facts — final results, career totals, award winners — which are the opposite pole from the data in this case. VERDICTS for all three activities where the data is historical: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) not reachable by hot-news. CAVEAT worth filing: if the project ever ships LIVE or same-day content — a scores ticker, a daily card built off a game finishing that night, in-progress standings — that content moves toward the pole the court WAS talking about, and elements (ii) and (iv) start to matter. The doctrine is dormant for the current bank, not absent from the project's future.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit.

law.topic: Free-riding is INDISPENSABLE — bearing your own collection costs defeats the claim
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶¶ 76, 78
law.quote: An indispensable element of an INS "hot-news" claim is free riding by a defendant on a plaintiff's product, enabling the defendant to produce a directly competitive product for less money because it has lower costs. … However, that is not the case in the instant matter. SportsTrax and Gamestats are each bearing their own costs of collecting factual information on NBA games, and, if one produces a product that is cheaper or otherwise superior to the other, that producer will prevail in the marketplace. This is obviously not the situation against which INS was intended to prevent: the potential lack of any such product or service because of the anticipation of free-riding.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "An indispensable element … is free riding … enabling the defendant to produce a directly competitive product for less money because it has lower costs." This is the element most likely to be argued against a project that reads facts off someone else's stats page, so it deserves an honest reading rather than a comfortable one. HONEST NOTE: activity (c) — bulk aggregation — is the one place where Ball Knowledge WOULD arguably be lowering its costs by taking another party's collection work, which is exactly the shape of free-riding the court describes. What saves it is not this element but element (ii): no time-sensitivity, no claim, however much free-riding there is. VERDICTS: (a) PERMITTED — one cited page is not a competing product. (b) PERMITTED — hand-extraction with citation still leaves the project bearing the writing and verification cost, and produces a trivia game, not a competitor. (c) RESTRICTED — this clause is the one that would be quoted against a bulk pull, and the project should not rely on hot-news failing here; it should rely on it failing at (ii) and on staying clear of ToS. The ellipsis jumps ¶76 to ¶78; both fragments verbatim, nothing elided inside either.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit.

law.topic: Direct competition must be in the plaintiff's PRIMARY market (footnote 8), and the NFL lottery case
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), n.8, quoting Restatement (Third) of Unfair Competition § 38 cmt. c and NFL v. Governor of Delaware, 435 F. Supp. 1372 (D. Del. 1977)
law.quote: Some authorities have labeled this element as requiring direct competition between the defendant and the plaintiff in a primary market. "[I]n most of the small number of cases in which the misappropriation doctrine has been determinative, the defendant's appropriation, like that in INS, resulted in direct competition in the plaintiffs' primary market ... Appeals to the misappropriation doctrine are almost always rejected when the appropriation does not intrude upon the plaintiff's primary market.", Restatement (Third) of Unfair Competition, § 38 cmt. c, at 412-13; see also National Football League v. Governor of State of Delaware, 435 F.Supp. 1372 (D.Del.1977). In that case, the NFL sued Delaware over the state's lottery game which was based on NFL games. In dismissing the wrongful misappropriation claims, the court stated: While courts have recognized that one has a right to one's own harvest, this proposition has not been construed to preclude others from profiting from demands for collateral services generated by the success of one's business venture.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "Appeals to the misappropriation doctrine are almost always rejected when the appropriation does not intrude upon the plaintiff's primary market", and the NFL-lottery quote about "collateral services generated by the success of one's business venture." This is the closest analogue in the opinion to what Ball Knowledge actually is: a GAME built on the back of someone else's sport and someone else's stats, sold into a market the rights-holder is not in. The NFL lost that claim. A trivia game is a collateral service, not an intrusion into the NBA's primary market (tickets, broadcasts) or Basketball-Reference's primary market (reference lookup). VERDICTS: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) still RESTRICTED — a full mirror of a stats site WOULD intrude on that site's primary market, which is precisely the distinction this footnote draws. The footnote is the cleanest available authority for the proposition that a trivia product occupies a different market from a stats product; it is the sentence to reach for if anyone ever asks the project to justify itself.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit (footnote, persuasive within the opinion's reasoning); Restatement; D. Del.

law.topic: Athletic events are NOT copyrightable — the underlying games are not works of authorship
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶¶ 18-19
law.quote: In our view, the underlying basketball games do not fall within the subject matter of federal copyright protection because they do not constitute "original works of authorship" under 17 U.S.C. § 102(a). Section 102(a) lists eight categories of "works of authorship" covered by the act, including such categories as "literary works," "musical works," and "dramatic works." The list does not include athletic events, and, although the list is concededly non-exclusive, such events are neither similar nor analogous to any of the listed categories. Sports events are not "authored" in any common sense of the word.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "The list does not include athletic events" and "Sports events are not 'authored' in any common sense of the word." The events themselves — what happened in the 1998 Finals, who scored what — are outside copyright entirely. This is the foundation under everything the project does: the raw material of the question bank is not anyone's copyrighted work. VERDICTS on a COPYRIGHT theory: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) PERMITTED as to the underlying events. Note carefully what this does NOT decide: it says nothing about the copyright in a particular WRITTEN presentation of those facts (a Basketball-Reference page's prose, its selection and arrangement, its site design), and nothing about contract/ToS restrictions, which bind regardless of copyright. Footnote 3 in the source is dropped from the quote at the point after "dramatic works."; nothing else is elided.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit, 17 U.S.C. § 102(a).

law.topic: Reproducing FACTS from a copyrighted broadcast is not infringement — the fact/expression dichotomy applied to basketball data
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶¶ 32-33, applying Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991)
law.quote: Although the broadcasts are protected under copyright law, the district court correctly held that Motorola and STATS did not infringe NBA's copyright because they reproduced only facts from the broadcasts, not the expression or description of the game that constitutes the broadcast. The "fact/expression dichotomy" is a bedrock principle of copyright law that "limits severely the scope of protection in fact-based works." Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Tel. Service Co., 499 U.S. 340, 350, 111 S.Ct. 1282, 1290, 113 L.Ed.2d 358 (1991). " 'No author may copyright facts or ideas. The copyright is limited to those aspects of the work--termed 'expression'--that display the stamp of the author's originality.' " Id. (quoting Harper & Row, Publishers, Inc. v. Nation Enter., 471 U.S. 539, 547, 105 S.Ct. 2218, 2224, 85 L.Ed.2d 588 (1985)). We agree with the district court that the "[d]efendants provide purely factual information which any patron of an NBA game could acquire from the arena without any involvement from the director, cameramen, or others who contribute to the originality of a broadcast." 939 F.Supp. at 1094. Because the SportsTrax device and AOL site reproduce only factual information culled from the broadcasts and none of the copyrightable expression of the games, appellants did not infringe the copyright of the broadcasts.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "they reproduced only facts from the broadcasts, not the expression" and "No author may copyright facts or ideas." This is the single most directly on-point holding for Ball Knowledge in the whole search: a party that pulled BASKETBALL FACTS out of someone else's copyrighted product and resold them commercially did not infringe, because it took only facts. That is structurally identical to reading a stat off a page and writing a question around it. VERDICTS on the copyright theory: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED — extracting individual facts into an own database is exactly what STATS did and it was held non-infringing, (c) PERMITTED AS TO THE FACTS THEMSELVES but with a real caveat: taking a page's SELECTION AND ARRANGEMENT wholesale is a different question this holding does not answer, and Feist's originality floor cuts both ways — thin protection can still be protection for a creatively arranged compilation. The project's practice of writing its own question text around a sourced fact, rather than copying prose, sits comfortably inside the quoted rule. NOTE: this holding is about COPYRIGHT ONLY. It does not license breaching a site's terms of use, and the project should not treat it as doing so.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit, applying Supreme Court precedent (Feist, Harper & Row); nationally applicable as to Feist.

law.topic: § 301 preempts state claims even over UNCOPYRIGHTABLE facts — Congress intended the underlying events to be in the public domain
law.authority: National Basketball Ass'n v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997), slip op. ¶ 47
law.quote: Adoption of a partial preemption doctrine--preemption of claims based on misappropriation of broadcasts but no preemption of claims based on misappropriation of underlying facts--would expand significantly the reach of state law claims and render the preemption intended by Congress unworkable. It is often difficult or impossible to separate the fixed copyrightable work from the underlying uncopyrightable events or facts. Moreover, Congress, in extending copyright protection only to the broadcasts and not to the underlying events, intended that the latter be in the public domain. Partial preemption turns that intent on its head by allowing state law to vest exclusive rights in material that Congress intended to be in the public domain and to make unlawful conduct that Congress intended to allow.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: "Congress, in extending copyright protection only to the broadcasts and not to the underlying events, intended that the latter be in the public domain" and "to make unlawful conduct that Congress intended to allow." This closes the back door. A rights-holder cannot escape the fact/expression dichotomy by relabelling a copyright claim as a state misappropriation claim — § 301 preempts the relabelled claim too, and the court says in terms that the underlying sporting events were MEANT to be public domain. VERDICTS: (a) PERMITTED, (b) PERMITTED, (c) PERMITTED as against state misappropriation/unfair-competition theories aimed at the facts. The one route this leaves open to a data holder is CONTRACT — a terms-of-use agreement is generally not preempted by § 301 because it adds the extra element of a promise (the opinion cites ProCD v. Zeidenberg approvingly on the subject-matter point, and ProCD is the leading case for contract surviving preemption). That is where the project's real constraint lives, and it is not in this case.
law.jurisdiction: US federal — Second Circuit, 17 U.S.C. § 301.

law.topic: Core holding — First Amendment supersedes the right of publicity for use of real players' names plus their performance data
law.authority: C.B.C. Distribution and Marketing, Inc. v. Major League Baseball Advanced Media, L.P., 505 F.3d 818 (8th Cir. 2007) (Arnold, J.) — official slip opinion, Nos. 06-3357/3358, filed October 16, 2007
law.quote: The Supreme Court has directed that state law rights of publicity must be balanced against first amendment considerations, see Zacchini v. Scripps-Howard Broad., 433 U.S. 562 (1977), and here we conclude that the former must give way to the latter. First, the information used in CBC's fantasy baseball games is all readily available in the public domain, and it would be strange law that a person would not have a first amendment right to use information that is available to everyone. It is true that CBC's use of the information is meant to provide entertainment, but "[s]peech that entertains, like speech that informs, is protected by the First Amendment because '[t]he line between the informing and the entertaining is too elusive for the protection of that basic right.' " ... Because we hold that CBC's first amendment rights in offering its fantasy baseball products supersede the players' rights of publicity, we need not reach CBC's alternative argument that federal copyright law preempts the players' state law rights of publicity.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS (clause relied on): 'the former must give way to the latter' + 'readily available in the public domain' + the entertainment-is-still-speech sentence. HOW OBTAINED: fetched the court's own PDF via curl (ecf.ca8.uscourts.gov, HTTP 200, 40,198 bytes, 13 pages); Justia/FindLaw/openjurist/CourtListener all failed (Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' 403s and a CourtListener API throttle), so this is the slip opinion, not a mirror. Text extracted with pypdf in BOTH default and layout modes; the PDF's justified kerning inserts spurious mid-word spaces that differ between the two modes, so every quote here was machine-checked to appear in both extractions after whitespace normalization — that cross-check is what makes verbatim:true honest. WHAT IT MEANS FOR THE THREE ACTIVITIES: (a) citing one page to prove one fact — PERMITTED as against a right-of-publicity claim; CBC's use was far more commercial and far more central to the product than a trivia card citing a source, and it still won. (b) extracting facts into an own database and citing the source — PERMITTED as against right of publicity; CBC did exactly this (it maintained players' names with performance and biographical data as the substance of a paid product) and the court called that information 'available to everyone.' (c) aggregating at scale into a substituting database — UNCLEAR from this case. The opinion's reasoning contains no scale limit and no substitution analysis, but it also never confronted one; nothing here blesses bulk aggregation, it simply does not speak to it. CRITICAL: all three verdicts are ONLY about state right of publicity. This case decides nothing about copyright, nothing about a site's terms of use, nothing about scraping or trespass to chattels.
law.jurisdiction: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (binding in AR, IA, MN, MO, NE, ND, SD only), applying Missouri right-of-publicity law under Erie; persuasive but not binding everywhere else. Note the panel itself predicted state law: 'When state law is ambiguous, we must "predict how the highest court of that state would resolve the issue."'

law.topic: THE LIMIT MOST OFTEN MISREPORTED — the players DID make out a right-of-publicity claim; CBC won on the constitutional defense, not on the elements
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, Part II.A (8th Cir. 2007)
law.quote: Here, we entertain no doubt that the players' names that CBC used are understood by it and its fantasy baseball subscribers as referring to actual major league baseball players. ... We think that by reasoning that "identity," rather than "mere use of a name," "is a critical element of the right of publicity," the district court did not understand that when a name alone is sufficient to establish identity, the defendant's use of that name satisfies the plaintiff's burden to show that a name was used as a symbol of identity. ... Because we think that it is clear that CBC uses baseball players' identities in its fantasy baseball products for purposes of profit, we believe that their identities are being used for commercial advantage and that the players therefore offered sufficient evidence to make out a cause of action for violation of their rights of publicity under Missouri law.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'the players therefore offered sufficient evidence to make out a cause of action for violation of their rights of publicity under Missouri law' — the Eighth Circuit REVERSED the district court on this point and found for the players on all three Missouri elements (symbol of identity, no consent, commercial advantage). WHAT IT MEANS HERE: do not read C.B.C. as 'names and stats are free.' It holds the opposite at step one. Using a real player's name in a product sold for profit IS a prima facie right-of-publicity violation in Missouri, and 'we use it for purposes of profit' was enough to satisfy commercial advantage — a paid trivia game, a credits economy, or a store would land in the same place. The whole defense is the First Amendment balance in Part II.B, which is a fact-sensitive weighing, not a bright-line rule. Practical consequence for this project: the protection is real but it is a DEFENSE, meaning it is asserted after someone sues, and it depends on the character of the use staying expressive/informational rather than sliding into endorsement or merchandising.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit applying Missouri law (Doe v. TCI Cablevision, 110 S.W.3d 363 (Mo. 2003)); the elements test differs state to state, so this step-one analysis does not transfer cleanly to California, New York, Indiana, or Tennessee

law.topic: Historical records, statistics and past performances are expressly within the protected zone (Gionfriddo adopted)
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, Part II.B (8th Cir. 2007), quoting and adopting Gionfriddo v. Major League Baseball, 94 Cal. App. 4th 400, 411 (2001)
law.quote: Courts have also recognized the public value of information about the game of baseball and its players, referring to baseball as "the national pastime." Cardtoons, 95 F.3d at 972. A California court, in a case where Major League Baseball was itself defending its use of players' names, likenesses, and information against the players' asserted rights of publicity, observed, "Major league baseball is followed by millions of people across this country on a daily basis ... The public has an enduring fascination in the records set by former players and in memorable moments from previous games ... The records and statistics remain of interest to the public because they provide context that allows fans to better appreciate (or deprecate) today's performances." Gionfriddo v. Major League Baseball, 94 Cal. App. 4th 400, 411 (2001). The Court in Gionfriddo concluded that the "recitation and discussion of factual data concerning the athletic performance of [players on Major League Baseball's website] command a substantial public interest, and, therefore, is a form of expression due substantial constitutional protection." Id. We find these views persuasive.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'The records and statistics remain of interest to the public' and 'recitation and discussion of factual data concerning the athletic performance of [players] ... is a form of expression due substantial constitutional protection,' expressly adopted with 'We find these views persuasive.' WHAT IT MEANS HERE: this is the single most on-point passage in American case law for a basketball trivia game. The protected activity the court describes — 'recitation and discussion of factual data concerning the athletic performance' of named athletes, including 'records set by former players' and 'memorable moments from previous games' — is a literal description of a trivia question. It squarely covers the historical/retired-player material, which is the part a project usually worries about most because those players have no current salary offsetting the taking. Note the delicious detail the court flags: in Gionfriddo it was MLB ITSELF asserting this free-expression position against its own former players, so a league arguing the contrary later argues against a position its side has already won on.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit adopting a California Court of Appeal holding; Gionfriddo is itself only California intermediate appellate authority, so the combined weight is persuasive nationally rather than binding

law.topic: An interactive game built on names and playing records is protected SPEECH, not merely a product
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, Part II.B (8th Cir. 2007), citing Interactive Digital Software Ass'n v. St. Louis County, 329 F.3d 954 (8th Cir. 2003)
law.quote: We also find no merit in the argument that CBC's use of players' names and information in its fantasy baseball games is not speech at all. We have held that "the pictures, graphic design, concept art, sounds, music, stories, and narrative present in video games" is speech entitled to first amendment protection. See Interactive Digital Software Ass'n v. St. Louis County, Mo., 329 F.3d 954, 957 (8th Cir. 2003). Similarly, here CBC uses the "names, nicknames, likenesses, signatures, pictures, playing records, and/or biographical data of each player" in an interactive form in connection with its fantasy baseball products. This use is no less expressive than the use that was at issue in Interactive Digital.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'in an interactive form in connection with its fantasy baseball products. This use is no less expressive than the use that was at issue in Interactive Digital.' WHAT IT MEANS HERE: the 'it's a game, not journalism' objection is answered directly and adversely to the rights-holder. The court did not require the product to be commentary, criticism, or news; a commercial, paid, interactive entertainment product using names + playing records qualified as expressive on its own terms. Worth noting exactly which categories the licence enumerated and the court still cleared: 'names, nicknames, likenesses, signatures, pictures, playing records, and/or biographical data.' That list is broader than pure numbers — it includes nicknames and biographical data, both of which trivia leans on heavily. Against right of publicity only; likenesses and pictures carry separate copyright and trademark exposure this case does not touch.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit

law.topic: WHAT THE COURT EXPRESSLY DID NOT DECIDE — copyright preemption was raised and left unresolved
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, end of Part II.B (8th Cir. 2007)
law.quote: Because we hold that CBC's first amendment rights in offering its fantasy baseball products supersede the players' rights of publicity, we need not reach CBC's alternative argument that federal copyright law preempts the players' state law rights of publicity. ... We do not reach the issue of whether Lear is applicable here, though, because we believe that the contested contract terms are unenforceable for a different reason.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the two express 'we need not reach' / 'we do not reach' sentences. WHAT IT MEANS HERE: this row exists to stop the case being over-read. C.B.C. is a right-of-publicity holding and nothing else. It did NOT decide (1) whether copyright preempts publicity claims, (2) whether a statistics compilation is copyrightable or its selection/arrangement protected, (3) whether a website's terms of use can restrict factual extraction, (4) anything about scraping, rate limits, CFAA, or trespass to chattels, (5) anything about trademark or team logos, (6) anything about photographs. For activity (c), aggregating at scale into a substituting database, the copyright question is precisely the one that matters and is precisely the one this court declined to answer. Anyone citing C.B.C. for 'stats are free' is borrowing weight the opinion did not lend. The district court below DID hold that copyright law does not preempt (443 F. Supp. 2d at 1100-03) — i.e. the trial court went AGAINST CBC on that point and the Eighth Circuit simply left it standing unreviewed.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit

law.topic: THE LIVE RISK THE HEADLINE HIDES — a contract can still bind you; CBC escaped its no-use clause only on a warranty breach, and the dissent would have enforced it
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, Part III (majority) and Colloton, J., dissenting (8th Cir. 2007)
law.quote: MAJORITY (Part III): "CBC undertook not to "dispute or attack the title or any rights of Players' Association in and to the Rights and/or the Trademarks or the validity of the license granted," either during or after the expiration of the agreement (the no-challenge provision). CBC also agreed that, upon expiration or termination of the contract, it would "refrain from further use of the Rights and/or the Trademarks or any further reference to them, either directly or indirectly" (the no-use provision). ... For the reasons given above, the Players Association did not have exclusive "right, title and interest" in the use of such information, and it therefore breached a material obligation that it undertook in the contract. CBC is thus relieved of the obligations that it undertook, and the Players Association cannot enforce the contract's no-use and no-challenge provisions against CBC." — DISSENT (Colloton, J.): "I agree with the court’s discussion of the right of publicity in Missouri and the application of the First Amendment in this context. I would resolve the contractual issues differently, however, and I therefore respectfully dissent. ... CBC surely can “agree,” as a matter of good business judgment, to bargain away any uncertain First Amendment rights that it may have in exchange for the certainty of what it considers to be an advantageous contractual arrangement. ... That CBC later decided it did not need a license, and that it preferred instead to litigate the point, does not relieve the company of its contractual obligation."
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the majority's warranty-breach rationale ('it therefore breached a material obligation') versus the dissent's 'bargain away any uncertain First Amendment rights.' WHAT IT MEANS HERE: this is the most operationally important row for this project, and it cuts against us. CBC got out of its no-use clause on a narrow, lucky, sua sponte ground the parties had not even briefed — that MLBPA's section 8(a) warranty of exclusive title was false. That escape hatch does not generalise. Judge Colloton, who AGREED with the entire First Amendment holding, would still have enforced the contract against CBC. Read across to data sourcing: a terms-of-use acceptance, an API agreement, or a licence is a CONTRACT, and the First Amendment holding in Part II does not automatically void it. So the practical rule for the bank is that the constitutional analysis protects us from a publicity claim by a player, but it does NOT protect us from a contract we clicked through on a stats site. Refined verdicts: (a) citing one page — PERMITTED under this case, but a site's own terms are a separate and unaddressed constraint. (b) extracting into an own database — PERMITTED as to publicity, RESTRICTED to whatever we agreed to when we obtained the page. (c) bulk aggregation — the contract exposure is at its worst here, because bulk access is exactly what terms of use single out. Sourcing from pages accepted without any account or clickwrap keeps this row's risk at its lowest.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit; the contract itself was governed by New York law by its own choice-of-law clause ('The agreement provides that its interpretation will be governed by New York law')

law.topic: Why the balance tipped — the specific factors, including the all-players/no-endorsement point
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818, Part II.B (8th Cir. 2007)
law.quote: In addition, the facts in this case barely, if at all, implicate the interests that states typically intend to vindicate by providing rights of publicity to individuals. Economic interests that states seek to promote include the right of an individual to reap the rewards of his or her endeavors and an individual's right to earn a living. ... But major league baseball players are rewarded, and handsomely, too, for their participation in games and can earn additional large sums from endorsements and sponsorship arrangements. Nor is there any danger here that consumers will be misled, because the fantasy baseball games depend on the inclusion of all players and thus cannot create a false impression that some particular player with "star power" is endorsing CBC's products. ... We do not see that any of these interests are especially relevant here, where baseball players are rewarded separately for their labors, and where any emotional harm would most likely be caused by a player's actual performance, in which case media coverage would cause the same harm.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'the fantasy baseball games depend on the inclusion of all players and thus cannot create a false impression that some particular player with "star power" is endorsing CBC's products.' WHAT IT MEANS HERE: this is a checklist, and it is worth designing to. The balance tipped because (i) the athletes were already richly paid for the underlying performance, (ii) the product used ALL players rather than trading on one star's pull, and (iii) no reasonable consumer would infer endorsement. A trivia bank with broad, league-wide coverage sits comfortably inside factor (ii). The design choices that would ERODE this protection are identifiable and avoidable: building a pack around one marquee name, using a player's face or signature as the product's marketing hook, or any framing that implies a player is behind the game. Keeping breadth of coverage and keeping player identity in the informational layer rather than the promotional layer is what keeps the case on our side. Also note factor (i) is weaker for long-retired and pre-modern players, who were NOT 'rewarded, and handsomely' — though the Gionfriddo passage the court adopts speaks directly to former players anyway.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit

WHAT IT MEANS HERE: a judicial opinion is not a data holder, so there is no dump, download, or API tier to report from this source — I am recording the negative explicitly so nobody re-searches it. law.topic: How far the holding travels, and the honest gaps in what I verified today
law.authority: C.B.C. v. MLBAM, 505 F.3d 818 (8th Cir. 2007) — scope assessment
law.quote: Before LOKEN, Chief Judge, ARNOLD and COLLOTON, Circuit Judges. ... Submitted: June 14, 2007  Filed: October 16, 2007 ... For the foregoing reasons, the district court's grant of summary judgment to CBC is affirmed. ... We also review de novo the district court's interpretation of state law, including its interpretation of Missouri law regarding the right of publicity.

WHAT IT MEANS HERE — REACH: this binds federal courts in the Eighth Circuit only (AR, IA, MN, MO, NE, ND, SD), and even there it is an Erie prediction of MISSOURI law, so a suit brought under California or New York or Indiana publicity law is not controlled by it. Elsewhere it is persuasive authority of real weight (it is the most-cited modern athlete-stats case and it drew amici from the NFLPA, NBA Properties, NHL Enterprises, WNBA Enterprises, NASCAR and the PGA Tour on the losing side, which tells you the leagues understood the stakes and lost anyway). Only one judge of three dissented, and on contract grounds alone — the First Amendment holding was unanimous, which strengthens its persuasive pull. law.topic: Browsewrap / assent — the founding case: terms below the fold do not bind a user who never clicked
law.authority: Specht v. Netscape Communications Corp., 306 F.3d 17 (2d Cir. 2002) (Sotomayor, J.) — full text, law.resource.org public-domain reporter scan of F.3d vol. 306
law.quote: [¶ 32] "...a consumer's clicking on a download button does not communicate assent to contractual terms if the offer did not make clear to the consumer that clicking on the download button would signify assent to those terms... California's common law is clear that 'an offeree, regardless of apparent manifestation of his consent, is not bound by inconspicuous contractual provisions of which he is unaware, contained in a document whose contractual nature is not obvious.'" ... [¶ 38] "We are not persuaded that a reasonably prudent offeree in these circumstances would have known of the existence of license terms. Plaintiffs were responding to an offer that did not carry an immediately visible notice of the existence of license terms or require unambiguous manifestation of assent to those terms." ... [¶ 39] "We conclude that in circumstances such as these, where consumers are urged to download free software at the immediate click of a button, a reference to the existence of license terms on a submerged screen is not sufficient to place consumers on inquiry or constructive notice of those terms... Internet users may have, as defendants put it, 'as much time as they need[ ]' to scroll through multiple screens on a webpage, but there is no reason to assume that viewers will scroll down to subsequent screens simply because screens are there." ... [¶ 44] "After reviewing the California common law and other relevant legal authority, we conclude that under the circumstances here, plaintiffs' downloading of SmartDownload did not constitute acceptance of defendants' license terms. Reasonably conspicuous notice of the existence of contract terms and unambiguous manifestation of assent to those terms by consumers are essential if electronic bargaining is to have integrity and credibility. We hold that a reasonably prudent offeree in plaintiffs' position would not have known or learned, prior to acting on the invitation to download, of the reference to SmartDownload's license terms hidden below the 'Download' button on the next screen." ... [¶ 41, contrast, quoting Moore v. Microsoft] "software user was bound by license agreement where terms were prominently displayed on computer screen before software could be installed and where user was required to indicate assent by clicking 'I agree'"
law.what_it_means_here: WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS: everything above is the court's own text, verified by substring match against the fetched file; the following is my reading. ENFORCEABILITY AGAINST A NON-CLICKER: Specht is the origin of the rule that a site cannot bind you by posting terms you were never shown. The operative two-element formula is in ¶ 44 — 'Reasonably conspicuous notice of the existence of contract terms AND unambiguous manifestation of assent.' Both are required. A crawler or a human researcher who lands on a stats page via search, reads it, and leaves has done neither: no conspicuous notice at the point of access, no act the site told them would signify assent. THE THREE ACTIVITIES, judged against the quoted clauses: (a) CITING one page to prove one fact — UNRESTRICTED BY CONTRACT on a pure browsewrap site, because under ¶ 32 no contract formed; whatever restricts this comes from copyright, not the ToU (and under Feist, a historical fact is not copyrightable). (b) EXTRACTING facts into an own database then citing the source — same answer, UNRESTRICTED BY CONTRACT on a pure browsewrap site, for the same clause; but note Specht decides only formation, so if the project ever creates an ACCOUNT or clicks through an 'I agree', ¶ 41's Moore contrast flips this to fully bound. (c) AGGREGATING at scale — UNCLEAR, and Specht does not reach it. Specht is about whether a contract exists, not about the CFAA, trespass to chattels, hot-news, or database-protection theories, none of which need a contract. Do not read a browsewrap failure as a green light for (c). NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE appears in this document — it is a court opinion, not a data holder's terms. WHAT MAKES TERMS MORE ENFORCEABLE, per this case specifically: (1) notice that is 'immediately visible' at the moment of the action, not on the next screen (¶ 38); (2) an offer that 'require[s] unambiguous manifestation of assent' (¶ 38); (3) terms 'prominently displayed... before software could be installed' with a required 'I agree' click (¶ 41). Specht's own negative facts name the failures precisely: terms reachable only by scrolling below the action button, and a free/frictionless transaction where the user has no reason to expect a contract. PRACTICAL CAUTION for this project: Specht's holding is about CONSUMERS in a free-download setting. It is weaker cover for a commercial or systematic user, and ¶ 44's 'circumstances here' language is doing real work.
law.jurisdiction: U.S. federal — Second Circuit; applying California contract law (¶ 33-35). Persuasive, not binding, elsewhere, but universally cited as the leading case.

law.topic: Browsewrap — a conspicuous link on every page, right next to the button, is still not enough without something more
law.authority: Nguyen v. Barnes & Noble Inc., 763 F.3d 1171 (9th Cir. 2014) (Noonan, J.) — official slip opinion PDF, No. 12-56628, filed Aug. 18, 2014
law.quote: "Contracts formed on the Internet come primarily in two flavors: 'clickwrap' (or 'click-through') agreements, in which website users are required to click on an 'I agree' box after being presented with a list of terms and conditions of use; and 'browsewrap' agreements, where a website's terms and conditions of use are generally posted on the website via a hyperlink at the bottom of the screen." ... "Because no affirmative action is required by the website user to agree to the terms of a contract other than his or her use of the website, the determination of the validity of the browsewrap contract depends on whether the user has actual or constructive knowledge of a website's terms and conditions." ... "Were there any evidence in the record that Nguyen had actual notice of the Terms of Use or was required to affirmatively acknowledge the Terms of Use before completing his online purchase, the outcome of this case might be different. Indeed, courts have consistently enforced browsewrap agreements where the user had actual notice of the agreement." ... "But where, as here, there is no evidence that the website user had actual knowledge of the agreement, the validity of the browsewrap agreement turns on whether the website puts a reasonably prudent user on inquiry notice of the terms of the contract." ... "On the other hand, where the website contains an explicit textual notice that continued use will act as a manifestation of the user's intent to be bound, courts have been more amenable to enforcing browsewrap agreements." ... "In short, the conspicuousness and placement of the 'Terms of Use' hyperlink, other notices given to users of the terms of use, and the website's general design all contribute to whether a reasonably prudent user would have inquiry notice of a browsewrap agreement." ... "But the proximity or conspicuousness of the hyperlink alone is not enough to give rise to constructive notice, and Barnes & Noble directs us to no case law that supports this proposition." ... "[W]e therefore hold that where a website makes its terms of use available via a conspicuous hyperlink on every page of the website but otherwise provides no notice to users nor prompts them to take any affirmative action to demonstrate assent, even close proximity of the hyperlink to relevant buttons users must click on—without more—is insufficient to give rise to constructive notice. While failure to read a contract before agreeing to its terms does not relieve a party of its obligations under the contract, Gillman v. Chase Manhattan Bank, N.A., 73 N.Y.2d 1, 11 (1988), the onus must be on website owners to put users on notice of the terms to which they wish to bind consumers. Given the breadth of the range of technological savvy of online purchasers, consumers cannot be expected to ferret out hyperlinks to terms and conditions to which they have no reason to suspect they will be bound." ... [footnote 1] "Indeed, in cases where courts have relied on the proximity of the hyperlink to enforce a browsewrap agreement, the websites at issue have also included something more to capture the user's attention and secure her assent."
law.what_it_means_here: WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS: quotes above are the opinion's own text, verified by substring match against the fetched PDF; two mechanical notes — a running page header ('NGUYEN V. BARNES & NOBLE, INC.12') that the PDF text layer interleaves mid-sentence has been removed, and PDF line breaks are rendered as spaces. Wording is unaltered. The analysis below is mine. ENFORCEABILITY AGAINST A NON-CLICKER: this is the strongest single authority for the proposition that a link-only Terms of Use does not bind a visitor. B&N had a conspicuous 'Terms of Use' link on EVERY page, in blue, and 'directly below the relevant button a user must click on to proceed' — and still lost. The controlling clause is the holding sentence: conspicuous link + close proximity + 'otherwise provides no notice... nor prompts them to take any affirmative action to demonstrate assent' = 'insufficient to give rise to constructive notice.' THE THREE ACTIVITIES: (a) CITING one page — PERMITTED as against the contract, on the clause 'the determination of the validity of the browsewrap contract depends on whether the user has actual or constructive knowledge'; no knowledge, no contract, no restriction. (b) EXTRACTING into an own database and citing the source — PERMITTED as against the contract, on the same clause, WITH ONE LARGE CAVEAT stated in the opinion itself: 'courts have consistently enforced browsewrap agreements where the user had actual notice of the agreement.' The moment this project READS a site's ToU — as it has been doing today — it arguably acquires ACTUAL notice, and Nguyen's own escape hatch closes. That is the single most important practical line in this row: reading the terms can be what binds you to them, even when the site's design would not have. The cases the court cites for that proposition (Register.com; Southwest Airlines v. BoardFirst) are both scraper cases, which is exactly this fact pattern. (c) AGGREGATING at scale — RESTRICTED-to-PROHIBITED in practice, on the same 'actual notice' clause plus the Register.com line of authority: a commercial or automated aggregator that has seen the terms is precisely the party courts have been willing to bind. Note also footnote 2's own framing: courts 'have been willing to enforce terms of use against corporations, but have not been willing to do so against individuals.' WHAT MAKES TERMS MORE ENFORCEABLE, named by this court: (1) requiring the user to 'affirmatively acknowledge the Terms of Use before completing' the transaction; (2) 'an explicit textual notice that continued use will act as a manifestation of the user's intent to be bound' — the court endorses Cairo v. Crossmedia's exact wording, 'By continuing past this page and/or using this site, you agree to abide by the Terms of Use for this site'; (3) an admonition at the point of access tying the action to the terms (the PDC Labs 'STEP 4 of 4: Review terms... and submit order'); (4) proving ACTUAL notice, which the court says would likely have changed the result. It expressly rejects two things as insufficient on their own: proximity, and conspicuousness of the link. NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE in this document (it is an opinion).
law.jurisdiction: U.S. federal — Ninth Circuit; applying New York and California law, which the court treats as materially identical

law.topic: Post-2020, the controlling formulation — the two-part inquiry-notice test, and the specific web-design failures that void terms
law.authority: Berman v. Freedom Financial Network, LLC, 30 F.4th 849 (9th Cir. 2022) (Watford, J.) — official slip opinion PDF, No. 20-16900, filed Apr. 5, 2022
law.quote: "Unless the website operator can show that a consumer has actual knowledge of the agreement, an enforceable contract will be found based on an inquiry notice theory only if: (1) the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to which the consumer will be bound; and (2) the consumer takes some action, such as clicking a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests his or her assent to those terms." ... "First, to be conspicuous in this context, a notice must be displayed in a font size and format such that the court can fairly assume that a reasonably prudent Internet user would have seen it... The text disclosing the existence of the terms and conditions on these websites is the antithesis of conspicuous. It is printed in a tiny gray font considerably smaller than the font used in the surrounding website elements, and indeed in a font so small that it is barely legible to the naked eye." ... "Website users are entitled to assume that important provisions—such as those that disclose the existence of proposed contractual terms—will be prominently displayed, not buried in fine print. Because 'online providers have complete control over the design of their websites,'... 'the onus must be on website owners to put users on notice of the terms to which they wish to bind consumers.'" ... "Second, while it is permissible to disclose terms and conditions through a hyperlink, the fact that a hyperlink is present must be readily apparent. Simply underscoring words or phrases, as in the webpages at issue here, will often be insufficient to alert a reasonably prudent user that a clickable link exists." ... "Customary design elements denoting the existence of a hyperlink include the use of a contrasting font color (typically blue) and the use of all capital letters, both of which can alert a user that the particular text differs from other plain text in that it provides a clickable pathway to another webpage." ... "Unambiguous manifestation of assent. In using the websites, Hernandez and Russell did not take any action that unambiguously manifested their assent to be bound by the terms and conditions. Defendants rely on plaintiffs' act of clicking on the large green 'continue' buttons as manifestation of their assent, but merely clicking on a button on a webpage, viewed in the abstract, does not signify a user's agreement to anything. A user's click of a button can be construed as an unambiguous manifestation of assent only if the user is explicitly advised that the act of clicking will constitute assent to the terms and conditions of an agreement."
law.what_it_means_here: WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS: quotes verified by whitespace-insensitive substring match against the fetched PDF. The PDF text layer inserts stray spaces inside words ('com pel', 'a ssent', 'suff iciently'); those extraction artifacts are normalized above and no word is changed. Analysis below is mine. THIS IS THE OPERATIVE TEST TODAY. Berman is the post-2020 case that matters most, because Nguyen's browsewrap/clickwrap binary stopped describing real websites. Berman replaces it with a two-part test that applies to EVERY online agreement regardless of label, and every later Ninth Circuit case runs through it. DIRECTION OF THE CASE LAW: Berman is not a loosening. It tightened the first prong into a design specification with measurable criteria — font size relative to surrounding elements, colour contrast, whether the hyperlink LOOKS like a hyperlink — and it hardened the second prong into a requirement of explicit advice at the button. THE THREE ACTIVITIES: (a) CITING one page — PERMITTED as against the contract, on prong (2): a visitor who reads a page has taken no 'action, such as clicking a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests... assent'; prong (2) fails outright, so no contract, so no contractual restriction on citing a fact with a link back. (b) EXTRACTING into an own database and citing — PERMITTED as against the contract on the same prong (2) clause, but the very first words of the test are the caveat: 'Unless the website operator can show that a consumer has actual knowledge of the agreement.' Actual knowledge is a separate and independent route to enforceability that the two-part test never reaches. This project has now read several data holders' terms, so the 'no actual knowledge' branch is not safely available to it. (c) AGGREGATING at scale — UNCLEAR under this case and NOT SAFE to infer from it. Berman is a consumer case about arbitration clauses; it says nothing about scraping, and the actual-knowledge carve-out is where a commercial aggregator lands. NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE in this document. WHAT MAKES TERMS MORE ENFORCEABLE — Berman is the most concrete list any of these cases gives, and it reads as a checklist a site can be graded against: (1) notice font size at or above the surrounding page text, not 'tiny gray font'; (2) the hyperlink visually marked as a link — 'a contrasting font color (typically blue)' or 'all capital letters'; underlining ALONE is expressly held insufficient; (3) the notice placed where the page's visual hierarchy leads, not where other elements 'draw the user's attention away'; (4) and decisively, text at the button explicitly stating what the click means — the opinion elsewhere supplies the model wording, 'By clicking the Continue >> button, you agree to the Terms & Conditions.' A site that does all four has terms that will very likely bind; a site that does none of them very likely does not.
law.jurisdiction: U.S. federal — Ninth Circuit; applying California law (the court notes California and New York rules are materially the same)

law.topic: The enforceable side — what a site that WINS looks like, and the court's own advice on the safest design
law.authority: Oberstein v. Live Nation Entertainment, Inc., 60 F.4th 505 (9th Cir. 2023) — official slip opinion PDF, No. 21-56200, filed Feb. 13, 2023
law.quote: "As discussed above, an enforceable agreement may be found where '(1) the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to which the consumer will be bound; and (2) the consumer takes some action, such as clicking a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests his or her assent to those terms.'" ... "Appellees' Terms are not pure clickwrap because they do not, upon some user action, request that users click on a box to confirm agreement before proceeding. Nor are they pure browsewrap, as they are not hidden in links located at the bottom of webpages. Rather, they lie somewhere in between." ... "At three independent stages—when creating an account, signing into an account, and completing a purchase—Ticketmaster and Live Nation webpage users are presented with a confirmation button above which text informs the user that, by clicking on this button, 'you agree to our Terms of Use.' To sign into an account, for example, a user must click the 'Sign in' button, directly above which is language stating: 'By continuing past this page, you agree to the Terms of Use.' Similarly, to place an order, a user must click on the 'Place Order' button, directly above which is language stating: 'By continuing past this page and clicking Place Order, you agree to our Terms of Use.' The 'Terms of Use' hyperlink is written in bright blue font, distinguishing it from the surrounding text." ... "Appellees' notice is conspicuously displayed directly above or below the action button at each of three independent stages that a user must complete before purchasing tickets... And, crucially, the 'Terms of Use' hyperlink is conspicuously distinguished from the surrounding text in bright blue font, making its presence readily apparent." ... "And, in contrast with the noncommittal free trial offered in Sellers, the context of this transaction, requiring a full registration process, reflected the contemplation of 'some sort of continuing relationship' that would have put users on notice for a link to the terms of that continuing relationship." ... "We find it worth emphasizing that while Appellees' Terms meet the reasonably conspicuous standard, this hybrid form of agreement is not without its risks and invites second-guessing... To ensure that an online agreement passes muster, clickwrap is the safest choice." ... "Because the Ticketmaster and Live Nation websites provided reasonably conspicuous notice of the Terms to which Ticket Purchasers unambiguously manifested assent, we hold that the district court did not err in determining that the Terms, including the arbitration provision, were valid and binding."
law.what_it_means_here: WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS: quotes verified by whitespace-insensitive substring match against the fetched PDF, with the same intra-word extraction spaces normalized; no wording changed. (One further mechanical note: the court's rendering of the Place Order banner has internal quote marks around 'Place Order' that I have flattened to avoid nested quoting; the words are unchanged.) Analysis below is mine. WHY THIS ROW MATTERS MOST PRACTICALLY: Berman and Nguyen tell you what a losing site looks like. Oberstein is the ANSWER KEY — an actual site, described in detail, whose terms were held valid and binding. Anything a data holder does that matches this description should be treated as terms that bind. THE THREE ACTIVITIES, for a site built like Ticketmaster: (a), (b) and (c) are all GOVERNED BY THE CONTRACT, on the holding clause 'valid and binding' — whatever that site's ToU says about extraction, reproduction, and automated access applies to you as a matter of contract, and it applies to raw historical facts that copyright would leave free. That is the whole 'contract versus copyright' point, live. (a) CITING one page — still generally permitted, but by the terms' own permission, not by copyright's; check the clause. (b) EXTRACTING into an own database — RESTRICTED, governed entirely by the ToU text. (c) AGGREGATING at scale — typically PROHIBITED by such terms, and here the prohibition is contractually enforceable. THE DIRECTION OF THE CASE LAW, stated plainly: the line has not moved toward users. It has moved toward a design test that sophisticated sites can and do pass. Ticketmaster passed. The practical consequence for this project is that whether a given data source's terms bind is now a per-site factual question about that site's checkout and signup flow, not a general doctrinal answer. WHAT MAKES TERMS MORE ENFORCEABLE — the four features the court credits by name: (1) the notice sits 'directly above or below the action button', inside the flow, not at the page bottom; (2) it uses action-linked wording that states the legal significance of the click — 'By continuing past this page and clicking Place Order, you agree to our Terms of Use'; (3) the hyperlink is in 'bright blue font', visibly a link; (4) it is repeated 'at three independent stages' — account creation, sign-in, and purchase. The court adds a fifth, contextual factor: a 'full registration process' signalling 'some sort of continuing relationship' primes a reasonable user to expect terms, where a 'noncommittal free trial' does not. AND THE COURT'S OWN ADVICE, worth quoting to anyone designing this project's own terms: 'To ensure that an online agreement passes muster, clickwrap is the safest choice.' NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE in this document.
