law.topic: The most recent appellate word — sign-in wrap fails where the button text does not say what the click means
law.authority: Chabolla v. ClassPass Inc., 129 F.4th 1147 (9th Cir. 2025) (Mendoza, J.; Bybee, J., dissenting) — official slip opinion PDF, No. 23-15999, filed Feb. 27, 2025
law.quote: "Like all online contracts, 'a sign-in wrap agreement may be an enforceable contract based on inquiry notice if (1) the website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms to which the consumer will be bound; and (2) the consumer takes some action, such as clicking a button or checking a box, that unambiguously manifests his or her assent to those terms.'" ... "'To be conspicuous, [the] notice must be displayed in a font size and format such that the court can fairly assume that a reasonably prudent Internet user would have seen it.' The 'context of the transaction,' as well as the 'traditional inquiry related to the visuals involved with the notice, such as font size, text placement, and overall screen design,' inform whether a website provides reasonably conspicuous notice of the terms of an agreement... The nature of the service or goods offered and the visual aspects of every page of a multi-page transaction should be considered together." ... "For instance, in Patrick, clicking a 'Place Order' button unambiguously manifested assent because the website explained that 'by submitting an order, the consumer confirms [he] . . . agree[s] to our privacy policy and terms of use.' Similarly in Oberstein, clicking a 'Place Order' button and continuing past webpages unambiguously manifested assent because the website explained that 'by clicking on this button, you agree to our Terms of Use'... In Keebaugh, clicking a 'Play' button unambiguously manifested assent to additional terms because the screen advised that '[b]y tapping Play I agree to the Terms of Service.'... In each of these cases, the website told the user what clicking a button meant. ClassPass's website provides no analogous language providing the user with an option to unambiguously agree to its Terms of Use." ... "Viewed in total, we do not think a reasonably prudent internet user unambiguously manifests assent to the Terms of Use by working her way through ClassPass's multi-page website." ... "IV. CONCLUSION Neither the landing page nor screen 1 provided Chabolla with reasonably conspicuous notice of the Terms of Use. Even if screens 2 and 3 did, at no point did Chabolla unambiguously manifest her assent to the Terms of Use on those screens." ... [Bybee, J., dissenting] "Applying a two-part test we identified in Berman, we have held that '[u]nder California law a sign-in wrap agreement may be enforceable based on inquiry notice,' so long as a 'reasonably prudent Internet user' (1) has 'reasonably conspicuous notice' of the Terms of Use, and (2) unambiguously manifests assent to the Terms of Use... Since Berman, we have upheld these 'hybrid wraps' repeatedly."
law.what_it_means_here: WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS: quotes verified by whitespace-insensitive substring match against the fetched PDF; intra-word extraction spaces normalized, wording unchanged; nested internal quotation marks flattened in two places for readability. Analysis below is mine. WHY THIS IS THE ROW THAT MOVES THE LINE: this is the newest published appellate decision on the question I could actually retrieve, and it cuts AGAINST the site. It is a 2-1 split, and the dissent's own sentence — 'Since Berman, we have upheld these hybrid wraps repeatedly' — is the honest measure of the direction of travel: the run of cases had been going the sites' way (Oberstein 2023, Patrick 2024, Keebaugh 2024), and Chabolla interrupts it. It also isolates the single most decisive design factor in the whole line of cases, in one sentence: 'In each of these cases, the website told the user what clicking a button meant.' ClassPass's failure was not a hidden link — it had a Terms of Use hyperlink on three screens, just above or below the button the user clicked, three times. It lost anyway, because the button said 'Continue' and 'Redeem now' and nothing tied the click to the terms. THE THREE ACTIVITIES: (a) CITING one page — PERMITTED as against the contract wherever prong (2) fails, on the clause 'at no point did Chabolla unambiguously manifest her assent'; a reader who clicks nothing manifests nothing. (b) EXTRACTING into an own database and citing — PERMITTED as against the contract on the same clause, subject to the same actual-knowledge caveat that runs through Berman and Nguyen. (c) AGGREGATING at scale — UNCLEAR; not addressed, and the case is a consumer-subscription dispute about an arbitration clause. NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE in this document. THE HONEST CAVEAT ON THIS ROW, which matters more than usual: it is a split panel decision, ClassPass petitioned for rehearing, and I did NOT verify the outcome of that petition or whether the opinion has since been amended, superseded, or taken en banc — I fetched the February 27, 2025 slip opinion only. Treat it as good law as of that date and check its subsequent history before relying on it. WHAT MAKES TERMS MORE ENFORCEABLE, distilled across all five rows into the practical answer: the strongest form is a clickwrap at an account signup — a separate 'I agree' box, presented with the terms, before access. Short of that, the features courts have actually credited are (1) notice inside the action flow, immediately above or below the button; (2) button-linked wording that states the legal effect of the click ('By clicking X, you agree to the Terms'); (3) a hyperlink that looks like one — blue and/or capitalized, underlining alone is not enough; (4) notice at font size comparable to surrounding text, not fine grey print; (5) repetition at each stage of a multi-step flow; (6) a transactional context — registration, an account, an ongoing relationship — that primes a user to expect terms; and (7) above all, PROVING ACTUAL NOTICE, which sidesteps the entire inquiry-notice test. The corollary for this project is uncomfortable and should be said plainly: the moment we open and read a data holder's Terms of Use, we are much closer to being bound by them than a user who never looked.

law.topic: Van Buren — the holding: what "exceeds authorized access" means under the CFAA
law.authority: Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021) (No. 19-783), slip op. (Barrett, J.), decided June 3, 2021 — official Supreme Court slip opinion PDF
law.quote: Nathan Van Buren, a former police sergeant, ran a license-plate search in a law enforcement computer database in exchange for money. Van Buren's conduct plainly flouted his department's policy, which authorized him to obtain database information only for law enforcement purposes. We must decide whether Van Buren also violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act of 1986 (CFAA), which makes it illegal "to access a computer with authorization and to use such access to obtain or alter information in the computer that the accesser is not entitled so to obtain or alter." He did not. This provision covers those who obtain information from particular areas in the computer—such as files, folders, or databases—to which their computer access does not extend. It does not cover those who, like Van Buren, have improper motives for obtaining information that is otherwise available to them. … In sum, an individual "exceeds authorized access" when he accesses a computer with authorization but then obtains information located in particular areas of the computer—such as files, folders, or databases—that are off limits to him. The parties agree that Van Buren accessed the law enforcement database system with authorization. The only question is whether Van Buren could use the system to retrieve license-plate information. Both sides agree that he could. Van Buren accordingly did not "excee[d] authorized access" to the database, as the CFAA defines that phrase, even though he obtained information from the database for an improper purpose.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: slip op. at 1 (opening holding) and Part IV, at 20. Fetched as PDF, extracted locally with pypdf (WebFetch could not read the binary); the only edits are removal of PDF line-break artifacts (justified-text spacing such as 'wh ether'), so this is the document's own text. WHAT IT SAYS vs WHAT IT MEANS — the quote is the Court; the rest is mine. ACTIVITY VERDICTS, CFAA exposure only: (a) CITING one page to prove one fact = permitted; (b) EXTRACTING facts into our own DB = permitted; (c) AGGREGATING at scale = permitted — all three, on the clause 'It does not cover those who … have improper motives for obtaining information that is otherwise available to them.' Purpose is not the test. What we do with a page we were allowed to load is outside §1030(a)(2). CRITICAL LIMIT: this says nothing about contract. It decides a criminal statute about entry, not about whether a site's terms bind us. Do not read it as permission to scrape.

law.topic: Van Buren — the "gates-up-or-down" reasoning, and footnote 8, which is the reservation everyone forgets
law.authority: Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), slip op. at 13 & n.8 (and n.9) — official Supreme Court slip opinion PDF
law.quote: Van Buren reads the "exceeds authorized access" clause to provide complementary protection for certain information within computers. It does so, Van Buren asserts, by targeting so-called inside hackers—those who access a computer with permission, but then "'exceed' the parameters of authorized access by entering an area of the computer to which [that] authorization does not extend." United States v. Valle, 807 F. 3d 508, 524 (CA2 2015). Van Buren's account of subsection (a)(2) makes sense of the statutory structure because it treats the "without authorization" and "exceeds authorized access" clauses consistently. Under Van Buren's reading, liability under both clauses stems from a gates-up-or-down inquiry—one either can or cannot access a computer system, and one either can or cannot access certain areas within the system.[8] And reading both clauses to adopt a gates-up-or-down approach aligns with the computer-context understanding of access as entry. … [n.8] For present purposes, we need not address whether this inquiry turns only on technological (or "code-based") limitations on access, or instead also looks to limits contained in contracts or policies. Cf. Brief for Orin Kerr as Amicus Curiae 7 (urging adoption of code-based approach).
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the 'gates-up-or-down inquiry' sentence, plus footnote 8 in full. PDF line-break spacing artifacts normalized; no other change. THE POINT OF THIS ROW IS FOOTNOTE 8. The Supreme Court expressly declined to decide whether authorization is fixed by code alone (passwords, IP blocks, logins) or also by contracts and policies (a robots.txt directive, a terms-of-service clause, a cease-and-desist letter). Every confident claim that 'Van Buren means terms of service can't create CFAA liability' is reading past a footnote that says the opposite of settled. ACTIVITY VERDICTS, CFAA only: (a)/(b)/(c) = permitted where no gate is bypassed; UNCLEAR the moment a gate exists, and unclear whether a contractual 'gate' counts at all. OPERATIONAL RULE FOR US: never log in, never defeat a rate limit, block, CAPTCHA or paywall, never use credentials. Those are gates, and the gates-down side of the line is where criminal exposure actually lives.

law.topic: Van Buren — why the Court refused to let terms of service define the crime
law.authority: Van Buren v. United States, 593 U.S. 374 (2021), slip op. at 17–18 (Part III) — official Supreme Court slip opinion PDF
law.quote: To top it all off, the Government's interpretation of the statute would attach criminal penalties to a breathtaking amount of commonplace computer activity. … If the "exceeds authorized access" clause criminalizes every violation of a computer-use policy, then millions of otherwise law-abiding citizens are criminals. Take the workplace. Employers commonly state that computers and electronic devices can be used only for business purposes. So on the Government's reading of the statute, an employee who sends a personal e-mail or reads the news using her work computer has violated the CFAA. Or consider the Internet. Many websites, services, and databases—which provide "information" from "protected computer[s]," §1030(a)(2)(C)—authorize a user's access only upon his agreement to follow specified terms of service. If the "exceeds authorized access" clause encompasses violations of circumstance-based access restrictions on employers' computers, it is difficult to see why it would not also encompass violations of such restrictions on website providers' computers. And indeed, numerous amici explain why the Government's reading of subsection (a)(2) would do just that—criminalize everything from embellishing an online-dating profile to using a pseudonym on Facebook.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the 'breathtaking amount of commonplace computer activity' and 'millions of otherwise law-abiding citizens are criminals' passage, which names terms of service directly. PDF spacing artifacts normalized. This is the passage that does the practical work for a project like ours: the Court treats 'you broke the website's terms of service' as a thing that must NOT by itself be a federal crime. But read what it actually establishes — that a ToS breach is not a CRIME. It is entirely silent on whether a ToS breach is a BREACH. The Court itself calls this reasoning 'extra icing on a cake already frosted' — reinforcement, not the holding. ACTIVITY VERDICTS, CFAA only: (a)/(b)/(c) all permitted; the fact that a site's terms forbid automated collection does not convert our work into a §1030 offence. Contract liability is a separate question this document does not touch.

law.topic: hiQ #1 — Ninth Circuit, Sept 9 2019: public data likely not accessed "without authorization" (THIS DECISION WAS LATER VACATED)
law.authority: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 938 F.3d 985 (9th Cir. Sept. 9, 2019), No. 17-16783 (Berzon, J.; Wallace, J., concurring) — official Ninth Circuit opinion PDF
law.quote: accessing a computer "without authorization" is violated when a person circumvents a computer's generally applicable rules regarding access permissions, such as username and password requirements, to gain access to a computer. It is likely that when a computer network generally permits public access to its data, a user's accessing that publicly available data will not constitute access without authorization under the CFAA. The data hiQ seeks to access is not owned by LinkedIn and has not been demarcated by LinkedIn as private using such an authorization system. HiQ has therefore raised serious questions about whether LinkedIn may invoke the CFAA to preempt hiQ's possibly meritorious tortious interference claim. We note that entities that view themselves as victims of data scraping are not without resort, even if the CFAA does not apply: state law trespass to chattels claims may still be available.

PROCEDURAL POSTURE MATTERS AND IS USUALLY BLURRED: this is the 2019 decision, it reviewed a PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION under a 'serious questions going to the merits' sliding scale — not a merits judgment — and the Supreme Court VACATED it on June 14, 2021 (next row). It is not currently law in its own right; the 2022 opinion on remand reinstated equivalent reasoning. Cite the 2022 opinion, not this one. ACTIVITY VERDICTS as this decision framed them, CFAA only: (a)/(b)/(c) permitted for pages served to anyone with a browser and no login. law.quote: Petition GRANTED. Judgment VACATED and case REMANDED for further consideration in light of Van Buren v. United States, 593 U. S. ___ (2021).

law.topic: hiQ #3 — Ninth Circuit on remand, Apr 18 2022: a public website "has erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place"
law.authority: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180 (9th Cir. Apr. 18, 2022), No. 17-16783, on remand from the Supreme Court (Berzon, J.) — official Ninth Circuit opinion PDF
law.quote: In other words, a user with "authorization" is not subject to "limitations on access," whether those limitations are "code-based" or "contained in contracts or policies." Id. at 1659 n.8. … Van Buren's distinction between computer users who "can or cannot access a computer system," id. at 1658, suggests a baseline in which there are "limitations on access" that prevent some users from accessing the system (i.e., a "gate" exists, and can be either up or down). The Court's "gates-up-or-down inquiry" thus applies to the latter two categories of computers we have identified: if authorization is required and has been given, the gates are up; if authorization is required and has not been given, the gates are down. As we have noted, however, a defining feature of public websites is that their publicly available sections lack limitations on access; instead, those sections are open to anyone with a web browser. In other words, applying the "gates" analogy to a computer hosting publicly available webpages, that computer has erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place.[17] Van Buren therefore reinforces our conclusion that the concept of "without authorization" does not apply to public websites. … [n.17] Of course, even computers and servers hosting public websites may contain areas that require authorization to access. … We AFFIRM the district court's determination that hiQ has established the elements required for a preliminary injunction and remand for further proceedings.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 31 F.4th at 1197–99 and the Conclusion. PDF extracted locally with pypdf; line-break spacing artifacts normalized. THIS is the operative Ninth Circuit decision and the one to cite. Two things to hold at once. First, it is strong for us: a page served to any browser with no login has no gate, so §1030's 'without authorization' does not reach it, and a cease-and-desist letter did not change that on this record. Second, IT IS STILL ONLY A PRELIMINARY INJUNCTION — affirmed on 'serious questions going to the merits' with the balance of hardships tipping sharply, not a merits ruling, and it remands 'for further proceedings' which is exactly where hiQ then lost the contract claim. ACTIVITY VERDICTS, CFAA only, Ninth Circuit: (a) permitted; (b) permitted; (c) permitted — the court draws no line at volume, and its worry about 'information monopolies' cuts our way. Note the panel reads Van Buren n.8 as meaning contract-based limits do not create CFAA authorization gates; that is the Ninth Circuit's reading, not the Supreme Court's holding.

law.topic: hiQ #3, the caveat paragraph — the same court listing every claim the CFAA ruling does NOT dispose of
law.authority: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180, 1201 & n.21 (9th Cir. Apr. 18, 2022) — official Ninth Circuit opinion PDF
law.quote: Entities that view themselves as victims of data scraping are not without resort, even if the CFAA does not apply: state law trespass to chattels claims may still be available.[21] And other causes of action, such as copyright infringement, misappropriation, unjust enrichment, conversion, breach of contract, or breach of privacy, may also lie. See, e.g., Associated Press v. Meltwater U.S. Holdings, Inc., 931 F. Supp. 2d 537, 561 (S.D.N.Y. 2013) (holding that a software company's conduct in scraping and aggregating copyrighted news articles was not protected by fair use). … [n.21] LinkedIn's cease-and-desist letter also asserted a state common law claim of trespass to chattels. Although we do not decide the question, see supra p. 20, it may be that web scraping exceeding the scope of the website owner's consent gives rise to a common law tort claim for trespass to chattels, at least when it causes demonstrable harm.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 31 F.4th at 1201 and n.21. This is the single most important paragraph in the whole hiQ line for a project deciding how to gather data, and it is the one that never survives into the summaries. The court that just ruled FOR the scraper immediately lists six other theories that can still sink one — and cites Meltwater, a case holding that scraping and AGGREGATING copyrighted material was NOT fair use. ACTIVITY VERDICTS on this clause: (a) CITING one page to prove one fact = permitted, nothing here touches it; (b) EXTRACTING facts into our DB = UNCLEAR, exposed to breach of contract and misappropriation depending on the source's terms; (c) AGGREGATING at scale = RESTRICTED — the Meltwater parenthetical is the court signalling that scale plus aggregation is where copyright and misappropriation bite. The FACTS themselves remain uncopyrightable (Feist, not fetched today), but the manner of taking and the volume can create liability independent of the facts' status, which is why this row is marked 'unclear' rather than 'no'.

law.topic: The contract language that did the damage — LinkedIn's anti-scraping clause, quoted by the Ninth Circuit
law.authority: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp., 31 F.4th 1180, 1187 n.6 (9th Cir. Apr. 18, 2022), quoting LinkedIn User Agreement § 8.2 — official Ninth Circuit opinion PDF (same clause reproduced in the Nov. 4 2022 N.D. Cal. order)
law.quote: Section 8.2 of the LinkedIn User Agreement to which hiQ agreed states that users agree not to "[s]crape or copy profiles and information of others through any means (including crawlers, browser plugins and add-ons, and any other technology or manual work)," "[c]opy or use the information, content or data on LinkedIn in connection with a competitive service (as determined by LinkedIn)," "[u]se manual or automated software, devices, scripts robots, other means or processes to access, 'scrape,' 'crawl' or 'spider' the Services or any related data or information," or "[u]se bots or other automated methods to access the Services." HiQ is no longer bound by the User Agreement, as LinkedIn has terminated hiQ's user status.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: footnote 6 of the 2022 Ninth Circuit opinion, reproducing the clause; the N.D. Cal. Nov. 4 2022 order quotes the same bullets ('Scrape or copy profiles and information of others through any means (including crawlers, browser plugins and add-ons, and any other technology or manual work)'). I include the actual contract text because this — not the CFAA — is what hiQ lost on, and because it shows what a fatal clause looks like when you read a source's terms. THREE THINGS TO NOTICE FOR OUR OWN SOURCE REVIEW. First, 'through any means … or manual work' reaches a human copying by hand, not just a bot; a clause drafted this way defeats the 'we did it manually' workaround. Second, 'in connection with a competitive service' is a separate hook that can catch us even where collection is otherwise allowed. Third, and the most useful line in the row: 'HiQ is no longer bound by the User Agreement, as LinkedIn has terminated hiQ's user status' — contract liability attached because hiQ HAD AGREED, i.e. had an account. ACTIVITY VERDICTS: (a) permitted; (b)/(c) prohibited against a source whose terms read like this AND with which we have formed a contract. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE — whether we ever clicked 'I agree' or created an account on a source is a first-order fact about our exposure, and it is cheap to keep straight.

law.topic: SYNTHESIS — what these decisions settled, and the gap they left open, which is the whole practical answer
law.authority: Van Buren, 593 U.S. 374, slip op. at 13 n.8; hiQ, 31 F.4th 1180, 1198, 1201 & n.21 (9th Cir. 2022); hiQ, No. 17-cv-03301-EMC (N.D. Cal. Nov. 4, 2022) — every sentence below is quoted from the documents in the rows above
law.quote: [Van Buren, slip op. at 13 n.8:] For present purposes, we need not address whether this inquiry turns only on technological (or "code-based") limitations on access, or instead also looks to limits contained in contracts or policies. — [hiQ 2022, 31 F.4th at 1198:] applying the "gates" analogy to a computer hosting publicly available webpages, that computer has erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place. — [hiQ 2022, 31 F.4th at 1201:] Entities that view themselves as victims of data scraping are not without resort, even if the CFAA does not apply: state law trespass to chattels claims may still be available. And other causes of action, such as copyright infringement, misappropriation, unjust enrichment, conversion, breach of contract, or breach of privacy, may also lie. — [hiQ, N.D. Cal. Nov. 4, 2022:] In sum, hiQ breached LinkedIn's User Agreement both through its own scraping of LinkedIn's site and using scraped data, and through turkers' creation of false identities on LinkedIn's platform.
law.what_it_means_here: Every sentence in the quote field is lifted from a document in the rows above; only this field is mine. WHAT THEY SETTLED: loading a page that anyone's browser can load, and using what you find for a purpose the owner dislikes, is NOT a federal crime under the CFAA — no gate was passed, and purpose is not the test (Van Buren; hiQ 2022). That is real, and it covers most of what this project does today. WHAT THEY EXPRESSLY DID NOT SETTLE, three distinct holes. (1) Van Buren footnote 8 leaves open whether contracts and policies can themselves be CFAA 'gates'; the Ninth Circuit says no, the Supreme Court has not said. (2) Both hiQ appellate decisions were PRELIMINARY-INJUNCTION rulings on 'serious questions going to the merits' — and the 2019 one was vacated outright — so neither is a merits holding that scraping is lawful. (3) The CFAA question and the CONTRACT question are separate, and hiQ won the first and lost the second in the same case. THE GAP, STATED AS THE PROMPT ASKS: 'not a federal crime' and 'not a breach of contract' are different questions with different answers, and the second is the one that costs money — hiQ paid on the contract, not on the statute. HOW THIS SHOULD SHAPE THE PROJECT. Activity (a), citing one page to prove one fact with a link back, is safe on every authority read today and nothing here disturbs it; it is not scraping, it is reading and attributing, and it is what the bank already does. Activity (b) is where exposure begins, and it turns almost entirely on THE SOURCE'S TERMS AND WHETHER WE HAVE AN ACCOUNT THERE, not on the CFAA. Activity (c) is the one the Ninth Circuit itself flagged, with a fair-use-loss citation attached. The correct next move is therefore not more caselaw — it is reading the actual terms of each source we pull from, and preferring sources with a sanctioned bulk route. NO SANCTIONED BULK ROUTE APPEARS ANYWHERE IN THESE DOCUMENTS: these are court decisions, not data-holder terms, and none of them publishes dumps, a data download, or an API tier. Finding one for our real sources would change the plan more than any prohibition in here does.
law.jurisdiction: United States — Supreme Court, Ninth Circuit, N.D. Cal.

law.topic: Sui generis database right — the core grant, and the definitions of 'extraction' and 're-utilization' (Art 7(1)-(5))
law.authority: Directive 96/9/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 1996 on the legal protection of databases, Chapter III, Article 7 (Object of protection)
law.quote:
Article 7
Object of protection
1. Member States shall provide for a right for the maker of a database which shows that there has been qualitatively and/or quantitatively a substantial investment in either the obtaining, verification or presentation of the contents to prevent extraction and/or re-utilization of the whole or of a substantial part, evaluated qualitatively and/or quantitatively, of the contents of that database.
2. For the purposes of this Chapter:
(a) 'extraction' shall mean the permanent or temporary transfer of all or a substantial part of the contents of a database to another medium by any means or in any form;
(b) 're-utilization' shall mean any form of making available to the public all or a substantial part of the contents of a database by the distribution of copies, by renting, by on-line or other forms of transmission. The first sale of a copy of a database within the Community by the rightholder or with his consent shall exhaust the right to control resale of that copy within the Community;
Public lending is not an act of extraction or re-utilization.
3. The right referred to in paragraph 1 may be transferred, assigned or granted under contractual licence.
4. The right provided for in paragraph 1 shall apply irrespective of the eligibility of that database for protection by copyright or by other rights. Moreover, it shall apply irrespective of eligibility of the contents of that database for protection by copyright or by other rights. Protection of databases under the right provided for in paragraph 1 shall be without prejudice to rights existing in respect of their contents.
5. The repeated and systematic extraction and/or re-utilization of insubstantial parts of the contents of the database implying acts which conflict with a normal exploitation of that database or which unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the maker of the database shall not be permitted.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS FOR THE THREE VERDICTS, all resting on quoted clauses of this Article. (a) CITING one page to prove one card: PERMITTED. Art 7(1) reaches only 'the whole or of a substantial part'; one fact with a link back is neither, and Art 7(2)(b) exhausts nothing we need. (b) EXTRACTING facts into our own database and citing the source: RESTRICTED. Art 7(2)(a) defines extraction as 'the permanent or temporary transfer of all or a substantial part of the contents of a database to another medium BY ANY MEANS OR IN ANY FORM' — hand-typing a box score into questions.js is 'any form', and the fact that we credit the source is legally irrelevant, because nothing in Art 7 contains an attribution defence. This is the single most important thing on this page for us: CITATION DOES NOT CURE EXTRACTION. The only attribution-based carve-out in the whole Directive is Art 9(b), and it is expressly confined to 'illustration for teaching or scientific research... to the extent justified by the NON-COMMERCIAL purpose' — a game with a credit economy does not fit. (c) AGGREGATING at scale: PROHIBITED where the source qualifies. Art 7(5) is the clause that closes the obvious workaround: 'The repeated and systematic extraction and/or re-utilization of INSUBSTANTIAL parts... implying acts which conflict with a normal exploitation of that database' is caught. Our actual working pattern — many small takes from one site over months — is the exact fact pattern Art 7(5) was drafted for. Note also Art 7(4): the right applies 'irrespective of eligibility of the contents... for protection by copyright'. So the familiar US answer ('facts aren't copyrightable, Feist') is simply not responsive in Europe; this is a separate right that sits on top of uncopyrightable facts.
law.jurisdiction: EU / EEA (all Member States; implemented nationally)

law.topic: The limit of the right — facts as such are not protected (Recitals 45 and 46)
law.authority: Directive 96/9/EC, recitals 45 and 46 of the preamble
law.quote:
Whereas the right to prevent unauthorized extraction and/or re-utilization does not in any way constitute an extension of copyright protection to mere facts or data;

Whereas the existence of a right to prevent the unauthorized extraction and/or re-utilization of the whole or a substantial part of works, data or materials from a database should not give rise to the creation of a new right in the works, data or materials themselves;
law.what_it_means_here: This is the clause that keeps the project alive in Europe, and it should be read narrowly. Nobody owns the fact that Robert Horry hit the shot in Game 4 of the 2002 Western Conference Finals. What is owned is a particular COLLECTION of such facts assembled with substantial investment. The practical consequence for how we work: the right attaches to the act of taking from a database, not to the knowledge itself. A fact we already hold, or that we source from a second independent place, or that a person on the team already knew, carries no sui generis encumbrance at all. That makes independent corroboration — which the verify-facts pass already does for accuracy reasons — do double duty as a legal cleanse. It also means the risk is concentrated in exactly one behaviour: systematic taking from a single European-qualifying source. Spreading sourcing across independent origins is not just better research practice, it is the specific thing that dissolves this right.
law.jurisdiction: EU / EEA

law.topic: Lawful users may take insubstantial parts 'for any purposes whatsoever' (Art 8), and the narrow exceptions (Art 9)
law.authority: Directive 96/9/EC, Article 8 (Rights and obligations of lawful users) and Article 9 (Exceptions to the sui generis right)
law.quote:
Article 8
Rights and obligations of lawful users
1. The maker of a database which is made available to the public in whatever manner may not prevent a lawful user of the database from extracting and/or re-utilizing insubstantial parts of its contents, evaluated qualitatively and/or quantitatively, for any purposes whatsoever. Where the lawful user is authorized to extract and/or re-utilize only part of the database, this paragraph shall apply only to that part.
2. A lawful user of a database which is made available to the public in whatever manner may not perform acts which conflict with normal exploitation of the database or unreasonably prejudice the legitimate interests of the maker of the database.

Article 9
Exceptions to the sui generis right
Member States may stipulate that lawful users of a database which is made available to the public in whatever manner may, without the authorization of its maker, extract or re-utilize a substantial part of its contents:
(a) in the case of extraction for private purposes of the contents of a non-electronic database;
(b) in the case of extraction for the purposes of illustration for teaching or scientific research, as long as the source is indicated and to the extent justified by the non-commercial purpose to be achieved;
(c) in the case of extraction and/or re-utilization for the purposes of public security or an administrative or judicial procedure.
law.what_it_means_here: Art 8(1) is the positive permission that covers activity (a) and the honest end of (b): a lawful user — anyone browsing a public site — may extract insubstantial parts 'FOR ANY PURPOSES WHATSOEVER', which explicitly includes commercial purposes. There is no need to argue fair-dealing; the Directive grants it outright. But Art 8(2) is the leash, and it uses the same language as Art 7(5): the user 'may not perform acts which conflict with normal exploitation of the database'. So Art 8 does not scale. It protects the card-by-card habit and withdraws exactly as the habit becomes a harvest. On Art 9: note (b) is the ONLY place in the sui generis regime where indicating the source matters, and it is gated on 'the non-commercial purpose'. This kills the intuition that crediting Basketball-Reference on a card is doing legal work — under EU law it is doing reputational and verification work only. Worth stating plainly in DEEPRESEARCH_KNOWLEDGE.md, because the project's current practice implicitly assumes attribution is a defence.
law.jurisdiction: EU / EEA (Art 9 is optional for Member States — implementation varies)

law.topic: OBTAINING versus CREATING — the holding, and why it decides whether a sports-data holder has any right at all
law.authority: Court of Justice (Grand Chamber), Case C-203/02, The British Horseracing Board Ltd and Others v William Hill Organization Ltd, judgment of 9 November 2004 — operative part 1 and paragraphs 30-33
law.quote:
On those grounds, the Court (Grand Chamber) rules as follows:
1. The expression 'investment in … the obtaining … of the contents' of a database in Article 7(1) of Directive 96/9/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 1996 on the legal protection of databases must be understood to refer to the resources used to seek out existing independent materials and collect them in the database. It does not cover the resources used for the creation of materials which make up the contents of a database.
The expression 'investment in … the … verification … of the contents' of a database in Article 7(1) of Directive 96/9 must be understood to refer to the resources used, with a view to ensuring the reliability of the information contained in that database, to monitor the accuracy of the materials collected when the database was created and during its operation. The resources used for verification during the stage of creation of materials which are subsequently collected in a database do not fall within that definition.
The resources used to draw up a list of horses in a race and to carry out checks in that connection do not constitute investment in the obtaining and verification of the contents of the database in which that list appears.

[para 31] Against that background, the expression 'investment in … the obtaining … of the contents' of a database must, as William Hill and the Belgian, German and Portuguese Governments point out, be understood to refer to the resources used to seek out existing independent materials and collect them in the database, and not to the resources used for the creation as such of independent materials. The purpose of the protection by the sui generis right provided for by the directive is to promote the establishment of storage and processing systems for existing information and not the creation of materials capable of being collected subsequently in a database.
law.what_it_means_here: THIS IS THE ROW THAT CHANGES THE PLAN, AND IT CUTS THE OPPOSITE WAY TO THE INTUITION. The obvious reading — 'sports data is generated by the events themselves, so nobody invested in obtaining it, so no right' — is right about the LEAGUE and wrong about the SITES WE ACTUALLY USE. BHB generated its own race lists; the Court held that spend didn't count and BHB lost. By the same logic the NBA, which generates the box score as a by-product of staging the game, is the party most likely to FAIL the Art 7(1) threshold. But Basketball-Reference, Land of Basketball, a newspaper archive, Transfermarkt — these do not create games. They 'seek out existing independent materials and collect them', which is the Court's own definition of obtaining, word for word. So the distinction HURTS us: it strips the right from the source we scrape least and confers it on the sources we scrape most. Second limb, and it is worse for us: verification investment counts when it is spend 'to monitor the accuracy of the materials collected when the database was created and DURING ITS OPERATION'. A reference site that reconciles disputed historical box scores across decades is accumulating precisely the qualifying investment the Court blessed — and historical basketball statistics are a field where that reconciliation work is real, documented and expensive. VERDICTS: (a) permitted regardless — this row does not touch single-fact citation. (b) restricted, and the restriction is LIVE rather than theoretical for European-qualifying stats compilers, because they clear the obtaining/verification threshold comfortably. (c) prohibited as against such a compiler. The one place this row genuinely helps: raw league-generated outputs (schedules, fixture lists, official results as published by the competition organiser) are weakly protected or unprotected, which argues for preferring official league sources over aggregator sources when a fact is available from both — a sourcing-hierarchy change worth writing into DEEPRESEARCH_KNOWLEDGE.md.
law.jurisdiction: EU (binding interpretation of Directive 96/9/EC); retained as assimilated case law in the UK

law.topic: What counts as a 'substantial part', and the finding that William Hill's actual use was insubstantial
law.authority: Case C-203/02, BHB v William Hill — operative part 3 and paragraphs 74-78
law.quote:
3. The expression 'substantial part, evaluated … quantitatively, of the contents of [a] database' in Article 7 of Directive 96/9 refers to the volume of data extracted from the database and/or re-utilised and must be assessed in relation to the total volume of the contents of the database.
The expression 'substantial part, evaluated qualitatively … of the contents of [a] database' refers to the scale of the investment in the obtaining, verification or presentation of the contents of the subject of the act of extraction and/or re-utilisation, regardless of whether that subject represents a quantitatively substantial part of the general contents of the protected database.
Any part which does not fulfil the definition of a substantial part, evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively, falls within the definition of an insubstantial part of the contents of a database.

[para 74] In that regard, it appears from the order for reference that the materials displayed on William Hill's internet sites, which derive from the BHB database, represent only a very small proportion of the whole of that database, as stated in paragraph 19 of this judgment. It must therefore be held that those materials do not constitute a substantial part, evaluated quantitatively, of the contents of that database.

[para 78] However, it must be observed, first, that the intrinsic value of the data affected by the act of extraction and/or re-utilisation does not constitute a relevant criterion for assessing whether the part in question is substantial, evaluated qualitatively. The fact that the data extracted and re-utilised by William Hill are vital to the organisation of the horse races which BHB
law.what_it_means_here: Two usable measures. QUANTITATIVE substantiality is a ratio against the whole source database — and the denominator here is enormous. Basketball-Reference holds every box score in league history; a few hundred facts is a rounding error against it, and para 74 shows the Court willing to dispose of the quantitative limb on exactly that reasoning. QUALITATIVE substantiality is the sharper edge but also has a helpful floor: para 78 holds that the INTRINSIC VALUE or importance of the data is 'not a relevant criterion'. So 'we only took the famous, interesting facts — the crown jewels' is not, by itself, qualitative substantiality. What matters is the scale of investment in obtaining/verifying THAT PARTICULAR SUBSET. This gives the project a defensible operating rule that is also just good practice: take widely and thinly rather than narrowly and deeply, and never take a source's distinctive curated sets (its leaderboards, its award-share tables, its self-built advanced metrics) wholesale, because those are precisely where a single source's own verification spend is concentrated. Also note the final sentence of operative part 3: anything failing BOTH limbs is insubstantial, and therefore protected by Art 8(1) — subject always to the Art 7(5) cumulative-effect trap in the next row. Confidence is high on the law, medium on any specific application, because substantiality is a fact question a court decides and I have not measured our take against any source's total.
law.jurisdiction: EU (binding interpretation of Directive 96/9/EC); retained in the UK

law.topic: Article 7(5) — the cumulative-effect rule that catches drip-feed extraction
law.authority: Case C-203/02, BHB v William Hill — operative part 4
law.quote: 4. The prohibition laid down by Article 7(5) of Directive 96/9 refers to unauthorised acts of extraction or re-utilisation the cumulative effect of which is to reconstitute and/or make available to the public, without the authorisation of the maker of the database, the whole or a substantial part of the contents of that database and thereby seriously prejudice the investment by the maker.
law.what_it_means_here: This is the clause that separates activity (b) from activity (c), and the Court read it more narrowly than it might have. The test is not 'did you take repeatedly' — it is whether the cumulative effect is 'to RECONSTITUTE and/or make available to the public... the whole or a substantial part' AND 'thereby SERIOUSLY PREJUDICE the investment by the maker'. Both limbs, conjunctive. A question bank is not a reconstitution of a statistics database: it is a derived work of a different shape, it is not queryable as a stats resource, and it does not substitute for the source — a player who wants Horry's 2002 shooting splits still has to go to the source. That is a genuinely strong position for the project as currently scoped. The line we must not cross is the one the wording marks out: the day the project holds something that a European-qualifying source's users could consult INSTEAD OF that source, Art 7(5) engages. Concretely, that argues against ever shipping a bulk player-stat table as a browsable feature, however tempting it is once players.json is rich. FILED-worthy as a scope constraint in DESIGN.md, not merely a research note, because it is a limit on what the product may become rather than on how we gather.
law.jurisdiction: EU (binding interpretation of Directive 96/9/EC); retained in the UK

law.topic: Who can hold the right at all — beneficiaries are EU nationals and EU-established companies only
law.authority: Directive 96/9/EC, Article 11 (Beneficiaries of protection under the sui generis right)
law.quote:
Article 11
Beneficiaries of protection under the sui generis right
1. The right provided for in Article 7 shall apply to database whose makers or rightholders are nationals of a Member State or who have their habitual residence in the territory of the Community.
2. Paragraph 1 shall also apply to companies and firms formed in accordance with the law of a Member State and having their registered office, central administration or principal place of business within the Community; however, where such a company or firm has only its registered office in the territory of the Community, its operations must be genuinely linked on an ongoing basis with the economy of a Member State.
3. Agreements extending the right provided for in Article 7 to databases made in third countries and falling outside the provisions of paragraphs 1 and 2 shall be concluded by the Council acting on a proposal from the Commission. The term of any protection extended to databases by virtue of that procedure shall not exceed that available pursuant to Article 10.
law.what_it_means_here: THE SECOND FINDING THAT CHANGES THE PLAN, and it is the one that most reduces our exposure. The sui generis right is a closed club. A US company — Sports Reference LLC of Philadelphia, which publishes Basketball-Reference — is a national of no Member State, is not formed under the law of one, and has neither registered office nor central administration in the Community. It is therefore NOT A BENEFICIARY of the sui generis right at all, and Art 11(3) makes the only route in a Council agreement extending protection to third countries. I did not find any such agreement covering the United States, and note honestly that I did not search exhaustively for one — but the standing position for thirty years has been that none exists. The practical upshot: for the American sources this project overwhelmingly relies on, the entire EU/UK sui generis analysis in the rows above is MOOT ON THE RIGHTHOLDER SIDE. There is no right for them to assert, whatever we do. Where it does bite is a short and nameable list — EU-established sources (EuroLeague, Spanish/Italian/Greek league sites, Transfermarkt in Germany), and UK-established ones under the parallel UK regime in the rows below (BBC and Guardian archives, Opta/Stats Perform). That converts a vague continent-wide worry into a concrete rule we can actually operate: treat EU/UK-established sources as the restricted tier and cite-only them; US sources are governed by US contract and CFAA analysis instead, which is a different question I was not asked and have not researched here. This is worth a named tier in DEEPRESEARCH_KNOWLEDGE.md's source standard.
law.jurisdiction: EU / EEA — territorial scope of the right

law.topic: Does a US-hosted site readable in Europe get caught? The targeting test
law.authority: Court of Justice (Third Chamber), Case C-173/11, Football Dataco Ltd and Others v Sportradar GmbH and Sportradar AG, judgment of 18 October 2012 — operative part
law.quote:
On those grounds, the Court (Third Chamber) hereby rules:
Article 7 of Directive 96/9/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 1996 on the legal protection of databases must be interpreted as meaning that the sending by one person, by means of a web server located in Member State A, of data previously uploaded by that person from a database protected by the sui generis right under that directive to the computer of another person located in Member State B, at that person's request, for the purpose of storage in that computer's memory and display on its screen, constitutes an act of 're-utilisation' of the data by the person sending it. That act takes place, at least, in Member State B, where there is evidence from which it may be concluded that the act discloses an intention on the part of the person performing the act to target members of the public in Member State B.
law.what_it_means_here: This is the direct answer to 'does any of this reach a US-hosted site that Europeans can read'. Yes, in principle — hosting location does not decide it. Re-utilisation happens where the reader is, and the Court expressly reasoned in terms of a server in one state and a user in another. BUT the operative part attaches a condition that is doing all the work: the act takes place in the reader's state only 'where there is evidence from which it may be concluded that the act discloses an INTENTION... to TARGET members of the public' there. Mere accessibility is not targeting — that is the whole point of the qualifier, and the Court left the assessment to the national court. Ball Knowledge as it stands is English-language, US-sports, hosted on GitHub Pages, with no European localisation, no EUR pricing, no European-language version and no marketing aimed at any Member State. On the face of this test that is accessibility, not targeting. Two things would change the answer and are worth knowing BEFORE they are built rather than after: shipping localised language versions, and taking payment in euros or pounds. Since the economy is already locked to credits rather than real money (DESIGN.md §11), the payment trigger is unlikely to arise — a guardrail chosen for other reasons that happens to hold this door shut too. Confidence high on the rule as quoted; medium on the application, because targeting is a fact-specific judgement for a court and I am assessing our own site.
law.jurisdiction: EU — governs where an act of re-utilisation is located

law.topic: UK post-Brexit — the substantive right is unchanged and still in force
law.authority: The Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/3032), regulations 13 and 16, as currently in force
law.quote:
13.—(1) A property right ('database right') subsists, in accordance with this Part, in a database if there has been a substantial investment in obtaining, verifying or presenting the contents of the database.
(2) For the purposes of paragraph (1) it is immaterial whether or not the database or any of its contents is a copyright work, within the meaning of Part I of the 1988 Act.
(3) This Regulation has effect subject to Regulation 18.

16.—(1) Subject to the provisions of this Part, a person infringes database right in a database if, without the consent of the owner of the right, he extracts or re-utilises all or a substantial part of the contents of the database.
(2) For the purposes of this Part, the repeated and systematic extraction or re-utilisation of insubstantial parts of the contents of a database may amount to the extraction or re-utilisation of a substantial part of those contents.
law.what_it_means_here: PRIMARY SOURCE ON THE POST-BREXIT UK POSITION, retrieved rather than recalled. Brexit did not abolish the UK database right and did not soften it: regs 13 and 16 still carry the same substantive test as Art 7(1) and Art 7(5), in nearly the same words. BHB v William Hill was a UK reference and its interpretation continues to bind as assimilated case law. So all the analysis above — obtaining versus creating, substantiality, cumulative effect — applies unchanged to UK-established sources. Verdicts for the UK are identical to the EU: (a) permitted, (b) restricted, (c) prohibited. What DID change is only who qualifies, in the next row.
law.jurisdiction: United Kingdom

law.topic: UK post-Brexit — the qualification rule narrowed to UK makers, and EU-made databases lost UK protection going forward
law.authority: SI 1997/3032 regulation 18 as amended from 31 December 2020 by The Intellectual Property (Copyright and Related Rights) (Amendment) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019 (SI 2019/605), reg 28(3); and SI 2019/605 reg 38 (saving)
law.quote:
Qualification for database right
18.—(1) Database right does not subsist in a database unless, at the material time, its maker, or if it was made jointly, one or more of its makers, was—
(a) an individual who was a national of [the United Kingdom] or habitually resident within [the United Kingdom],
(b) a body which was incorporated under the law of [any part of the United Kingdom] and which, at that time, satisfied one of the conditions in paragraph (2),
(c) a partnership or other unincorporated body which was formed under the law of [any part of the United Kingdom] and which, at that time, satisfied the condition in paragraph (2)(a) [...]
(2) The conditions mentioned in paragraphs (1)(b) and (c) are—
(a) that the body has its central administration or principal place of business within [the United Kingdom], or
(b) that the body has its registered office within [the United Kingdom] and the body's operations are linked on an ongoing basis with the economy of [the United Kingdom].

[SI 2019/605 reg 38] 38. The amendments made by these Regulations do not apply to any database in which a database right exists under the Copyright and Rights in Databases Regulations 1997 prior to exit day.
law.what_it_means_here: The square brackets are legislation.gov.uk's own markers for text substituted by SI 2019/605 — where they read 'the United Kingdom' the original read 'an EEA state'. That single substitution is the whole post-Brexit change, and it narrows rather than widens: from 31 December 2020 a database qualifies for UK database right only if its maker is a UK national/resident or a UK-established body. An EU-established maker no longer gets a NEW UK right, and reciprocally UK makers no longer get EU rights. Reg 38 is the saving clause and matters for our purposes: databases in which UK database right already existed before exit day keep it on the old EEA-based terms, so EU-made databases built before 2021 remain protected in the UK. Combined with Art 11 in the row above, the net picture for this project is narrow and workable: US sources are outside BOTH regimes entirely; EU sources are protected in the EU and (if pre-2021) in the UK; UK sources are protected in the UK. Nothing here creates any exposure for taking from American basketball-reference sites. Confidence high on the text; I flag that I read the consolidated version on legislation.gov.uk, which carries its own caveat that revised legislation may not be fully up to date, and I did not separately check for amendments after the ones footnoted there.
law.jurisdiction: United Kingdom

law.topic: No sanctioned bulk route found in any of these instruments
law.authority: Directive 96/9/EC (whole text, Chapters I-IV) and SI 1997/3032 — negative finding
law.quote: [No quotable clause — this row records the absence of one. The nearest provisions are Article 7(3), 'The right referred to in paragraph 1 may be transferred, assigned or granted under contractual licence', and Article 9(b), the non-commercial teaching and research exception quoted in an earlier row.]
law.what_it_means_here: Recording this explicitly because the brief asks for a sanctioned bulk route and it would be misleading to leave silence. These instruments are rights-defining, not access-granting: they create no dumps, no statutory API, no compulsory licence, and no bulk tier. The only route the Directive itself offers is Art 7(3) — an ordinary negotiated contractual licence from the maker. So a bulk route, if one exists for any source we care about, will be found in that individual holder's own published terms or developer programme, not in EU or UK law. That is a different research question from the one I was given and I have not investigated it here; flagging it as the obvious next step, because per the brief a sanctioned route would change the plan more than any of the prohibitions above. quote_is_verbatim is false because there is no text to quote for an absence.
law.jurisdiction: EU / EEA and United Kingdom

law.topic: Right of publicity — California statute (the strictest-state baseline, and the one that matters most because most US game companies and most plaintiffs' lawyers reach for it)
law.authority: California Civil Code § 3344 (as amended by Stats. 2025, Ch. 590, Sec. 1 (SB 683), effective January 1, 2026) — fetched from the official California Legislative Information site
law.quote: 3344. (a) (1) Any person who knowingly uses another's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any manner, on or in products, merchandise, or goods, or for purposes of advertising or selling, or soliciting purchases of, products, merchandise, goods, or services, without that person's prior consent, or, in the case of a minor, the prior consent of their parent or legal guardian, shall be liable for any damages sustained by the person or persons injured as a result thereof. In addition, in any action brought under this section, the person who violated the section shall be liable to the injured party or parties in an amount equal to the greater of seven hundred fifty dollars ($750) or the actual damages suffered by them as a result of the unauthorized use, and any profits from the unauthorized use that are attributable to the use and are not taken into account in computing the actual damages. ... Punitive damages may also be awarded to the injured party or parties. The prevailing party in any action under this section shall also be entitled to attorney's fees and costs. ... (d) For purposes of this section, a use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account, or any political campaign, shall not constitute a use for which consent is required under subdivision (a). (e) The use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in a commercial medium shall not constitute a use for which consent is required under subdivision (a) solely because the material containing the use is commercially sponsored or contains paid advertising. Rather it shall be a question of fact whether or not the use of the person's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness was so directly connected with the commercial sponsorship or with the paid advertising as to constitute a use for which consent is required under subdivision (a). ... (g) The remedies provided for in this section are cumulative and shall be in addition to any others provided for by law.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS FOR VERDICTS: subd. (a)(1) is the prohibition; subd. (d) is the news/public affairs/SPORTS ACCOUNT exemption; subd. (e) says commercial sponsorship alone does not convert a protected use into a violation; subd. (g) preserves the parallel common-law claim. (a) CITE ONE PAGE TO PROVE ONE FACT: permitted — a card that says a real player did a real thing is a 'sports broadcast or account' under (d), and (e) forecloses the argument that selling the app alone makes it commercial. (b) EXTRACT FACTS INTO OWN DB AND CITE: permitted — § 3344 reaches uses of a name; it does not reach the act of writing facts down, and (d) covers the output. (c) AGGREGATE AT SCALE: permitted on the same clauses, with one caveat that is real: (d) protects an 'account', and the more the product stops looking like an account of sport and starts looking like merchandise bearing a player's name, the weaker (d) gets. NOTE THE TEETH: § 3344 is strict not because the standard is harsh but because the REMEDY is — statutory minimum $750 PER PLAINTIFF with no proof of harm, disgorgement of profits where the plaintiff need only show gross revenue, punitive damages, and MANDATORY fees to the prevailing party. That fee-shift is what makes a nuisance claim economic against a small developer. PRACTICAL POSTURE: a game played by twenty friends with no revenue has essentially no exposure here — actual damages are zero, profits are zero, and no contingency lawyer takes a $750 case. A published app changes only the economics, not the analysis: the same (d) defence applies, but now there is a revenue number to disgorge and a fee award to chase. The single highest-value control is therefore keeping every card an ACCOUNT (name + verifiable fact + source link) and keeping player names out of anything that reads as marketing — store listings, ads, push notifications, splash art.
law.jurisdiction: California (statutory; applies to conduct/publication reaching California, which for an app store means always)

law.topic: Right of publicity — the California COMMON-LAW claim that survives alongside § 3344, and its elements
law.authority: In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litigation (Keller v. Electronic Arts), 724 F.3d 1268 (9th Cir. 2013), slip op. n.4 — official Ninth Circuit PDF
law.quote: The elements of a right-of-publicity claim under California common law are: "(1) the defendant's use of the plaintiff's identity; (2) the appropriation of plaintiff's name or likeness to defendant's advantage, commercially or otherwise; (3) lack of consent; and (4) resulting injury." Stewart v. Rolling Stone LLC, 105 Cal. Rptr. 3d 98, 111 (internal quotation marks omitted). The same claim under California Civil Code § 3344 requires a plaintiff to prove "all the elements of the common law cause of action" plus "a knowing use by the defendant as well as a direct connection between the alleged use and the commercial purpose."
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: this is the Ninth Circuit stating California's common-law elements. Why it matters separately from § 3344: the common-law claim has NO statutory minimum damages and no fee-shift, but it also has NO subdivision (d) — it has a judge-made 'public interest' defence instead. New Kids (below) holds the two defences run together, so in practice a factual sports account defeats both. (a)/(b)/(c) all permitted on the same reasoning as § 3344. The reason to record this row at all: never plan around § 3344(d) as if it were the only door — a plaintiff will plead both, and if the product ever drifts from 'account' to 'depiction', the common-law claim is the one that survives longest.
law.jurisdiction: California (common law)

law.topic: Right of publicity — New York, the other statute everyone pleads (and unusually, a criminal provision sits behind it)
law.authority: N.Y. Civil Rights Law §§ 50 and 51. Primary host nysenate.gov returned HTTP 403 to curl; text taken from newyork.public.law, which cites nysenate.gov as its source (last modified May 3, 2024) and was independently corroborated by a WebFetch of the nysenate.gov page itself, which returned identical language
law.quote: § 50. A person, firm or corporation that uses for advertising purposes, or for the purposes of trade, the name, portrait, picture, likeness, or voice of any living person without having first obtained the written consent of such person, or if a minor of such minor's parent or guardian, is guilty of a misdemeanor. — § 51. Any person whose name, portrait, picture, likeness or voice is used within this state for advertising purposes or for the purposes of trade without the written consent first obtained as above provided may maintain an equitable action in the supreme court of this state against the person, firm or corporation so using such person's name, portrait, picture, likeness or voice, to prevent and restrain the use thereof; and may also sue and recover damages for any injuries sustained by reason of such use and if the defendant shall have knowingly used such person's name, portrait, picture, likeness or voice in such manner as is forbidden or declared to be unlawful by section fifty of this article, the jury, in its discretion, may award exemplary damages.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the operative trigger is 'for advertising purposes or for the purposes of trade'. New York is strict in FORM — a misdemeanor plus injunctive relief plus exemplary damages — but the statute is narrow in SUBSTANCE: there is no free-standing 'commercial use' prong, and New York courts have long read a newsworthiness/public-interest limit into 'purposes of trade'. Note what is ABSENT from the text I retrieved: unlike California, Ohio, Indiana and Washington, §§ 50-51 contain NO express news/sports/historical exemption on their face — the limit is judge-made. That is a real difference and I am flagging it rather than papering over it. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted, but resting on case law I did not retrieve rather than on quoted statutory text — confidence is lower here than in the four states with an express carve-out. (b) EXTRACT: permitted on the same basis. (c) AGGREGATE: unclear from the statute alone. PRACTICAL: the misdemeanor clause looks alarming and is effectively a dead letter for factual publishing, but § 51's exemplary-damages clause turns on 'knowingly used' — which is one more reason every card should carry its source, since a sourced factual card is evidence of the opposite state of mind.
law.jurisdiction: New York (statutory; § 51 reaches uses 'within this state')

law.topic: Right of publicity — Indiana, the broadest statute in the country (100-year postmortem term, covers gestures and mannerisms, applies regardless of where the personality lives)
law.authority: Indiana Code §§ 32-36-1-1(c), 32-36-1-7, 32-36-1-8(a). The official iga.in.gov page is a JavaScript app and returned an empty shell; § 32-36-1-1 text taken from law.onecle.com (a mirror, snapshot dated May 24, 2006), and independently corroborated word-for-word by the Indiana Supreme Court's own quotation of §§ 32-36-1-1(c)(1)(B), (c)(3), -1-7 and -1-8(a) in Daniels v. FanDuel (2018)
law.quote: Sec. 1. (a) This chapter applies to an act or event that occurs within Indiana, regardless of a personality's domicile, residence, or citizenship. (b) This chapter does not affect rights and privileges recognized under any other law that apply to a news reporting or an entertainment medium. (c) This chapter does not apply to the following: (1) The use of a personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, image, likeness, distinctive appearance, gestures, or mannerisms in any of the following: (A) Literary works, theatrical works, musical compositions, film, radio, or television programs. (B) Material that has political or newsworthy value. (C) Original works of fine art. ... (3) The use of a personality's: (A) name; (B) voice; (C) signature; (D) photograph; (E) image; (F) likeness; (G) distinctive appearance; (H) gestures; or (I) mannerisms; in connection with the broadcast or reporting of an event or a topic of general or public interest. — and, as quoted by the Indiana Supreme Court: "a person may not use an aspect of a personality's right of publicity for a commercial purpose during the personality's lifetime or for one hundred (100) years after the date of the personality's death without having obtained previous written consent." Ind. Code § 32-36-1-8(a).
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: § 32-36-1-8(a) is the prohibition and it is the most aggressive in the US — 100 years postmortem, so every deceased player in the bank from roughly 1926 onward is still inside the term, and § 32-36-1-1(a) applies it 'regardless of a personality's domicile'. But the exemptions in (c)(1)(B) ('material that has political or newsworthy value') and (c)(3) ('broadcast or reporting of an event or a topic of general or public interest') are equally wide, and Daniels v. FanDuel construed the first one BROADLY and in a fantasy-sports context. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted — (c)(1)(B) as construed in Daniels. (b) EXTRACT: permitted — same clause; Daniels involved a defendant that had itself compiled and republished player statistics. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted — Daniels expressly refused to limit (c)(1)(B) to news organisations. PRACTICAL: Indiana is the state a plaintiff's lawyer picks for a historical-player claim because of the 100-year tail, and it is also the state with the most on-point favourable holding. Net: it is not the threat its reputation suggests, PROVIDED the product stays on the facts side. CURRENCY CAVEAT: my source for the statutory text is a 2006 mirror. The 2018 Indiana Supreme Court opinion quotes (c)(1)(B), (c)(3), -1-7 and -1-8(a) identically, so those four are solid; I have NOT verified whether other subsections changed after 2018 (the 2012 amendment adding a criminal-charge exception is noted in Daniels footnote 1).
law.jurisdiction: Indiana (statutory)

law.topic: Right of publicity — Ohio, which is the only state whose statute names HISTORICAL WORKS as an exempt category
law.authority: Ohio Revised Code §§ 2741.02 and 2741.09 — official codes.ohio.gov
law.quote: § 2741.02 (A) Except as otherwise provided in this section, a person shall not use any aspect of an individual's persona for a commercial purpose: (1) During the individual's lifetime; (2) For a period of sixty years after the date of the individual's death... (D)(1) A use of an aspect of an individual's persona in connection with any news, public affairs, sports broadcast, or account does not constitute a use for which consent is required under division (A) of this section. — § 2741.09 (A) This chapter does not apply to any of the following: (1)(a) A literary work, dramatic work, fictional work, historical work, audiovisual work, or musical work regardless of the media in which the work appears or is transmitted, other than an advertisement or commercial announcement not exempt under division (A)(1)(d) of this section; (b) Material that has political or newsworthy value; (c) Original works of fine art... (3) The use of an aspect of an individual's persona in connection with the broadcast or reporting of an event or topic of general or public interest; (4) The use of the persona of an individual solely in the individual's role as a member of the public if the individual is not named or otherwise singled out as an individual... (6) A use of the persona of an individual that is protected by the First Amendment to the United States Constitution as long as the use does not convey or reasonably suggest endorsement by the individual whose persona is at issue.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: § 2741.09(A)(1)(a) exempts a 'historical work... regardless of the media in which the work appears or is transmitted' — the 'regardless of the media' phrase is doing real work, because it means an interactive digital format does not forfeit the exemption. § 2741.09(A)(6) then adds a general First Amendment exemption with an express endorsement proviso, which is the cleanest statutory statement anywhere of the line the reader asked about: protected UNLESS the use 'convey[s] or reasonably suggest[s] endorsement'. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted — (A)(1)(a), (A)(1)(b), (A)(3). (b) EXTRACT: permitted — same. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted — a large historical database is more obviously a 'historical work' than a small one, so scale helps rather than hurts under this clause, which is the opposite of the direction scale cuts in most other analyses. PRACTICAL: Ohio is the best single statutory text to design against, because if the product satisfies § 2741.09(A)(1)(a) + (A)(6) it will almost certainly satisfy California, Indiana and Washington too. Concretely: describe the product to yourself as a historical reference work with a quiz interface, and make sure nothing in it 'reasonably suggest[s] endorsement' — no player-endorsed framing, no 'official', no signature-style marks, no testimonial voice.
law.jurisdiction: Ohio (statutory) — note Ohio is Zacchini's home state, so its legislature wrote against the one Supreme Court right-of-publicity decision

law.topic: Right of publicity — Washington, notably strict on REACH (it purports to protect people regardless of where they lived or died) but with an unusually explicit historical/educational exemption
law.authority: RCW 63.60.020 (definitions) and RCW 63.60.070 (exemptions) — official app.leg.wa.gov
law.quote: RCW 63.60.070 Exemptions from use restrictions — When chapter does not apply. (1) For purposes of RCW 63.60.050, the use of a name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness in connection with matters of cultural, historical, political, religious, educational, newsworthy, or public interest, including, without limitation, comment, criticism, satire, and parody relating thereto, shall not constitute a use for which consent is required under this chapter. A matter exempt from consent under this subsection does not lose such exempt status because it appears in the form of a paid advertisement if it is clear that the principal purpose of the advertisement is to comment on such matter. (2) This chapter does not apply to the use or authorization of use of an individual's or personality's name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness, in any of the following: (a) Single and original works of fine art...; (b) A literary work, theatrical work, musical composition, film, radio, online or television program, magazine article, news story, public affairs report, or sports broadcast or account, or with any political campaign when the use does not inaccurately claim or state an endorsement by the individual or personality; — and from RCW 63.60.020: "Deceased personality" means any individual, regardless of the personality's place of domicile, residence, or citizenship at the time of death or otherwise, whose name, voice, signature, photograph, or likeness had commercial value at the time of his or her death...
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: § 63.60.070(1) is the broadest exemption clause in any US publicity statute — it names 'cultural, historical... educational, newsworthy, or public interest' in a single list, and then says the exemption is not lost merely because the matter appears in a paid advertisement. § 63.60.070(2)(b) separately exempts an 'online... program' and a 'sports broadcast or account' with an express 'does not inaccurately claim or state an endorsement' proviso. Washington earns 'strict' status for its REACH — § 63.60.020 applies to any deceased personality 'regardless of ... domicile, residence, or citizenship... at the time of death or otherwise', which is a long-arm the Ninth Circuit has criticised. (a) permitted, (b) permitted, (c) permitted, all on § 63.60.070(1). PRACTICAL: this is the row that most directly answers 'is a trivia database about dead players safe?' — Washington says yes in terms, using the exact word 'historical', and says a paid placement does not break it so long as the principal purpose is commentary on the matter. The proviso to watch, again, is endorsement.
law.jurisdiction: Washington (statutory, with an express extraterritorial reach)

law.topic: Right of publicity — Tennessee (the ELVIS Act), the newest and in some respects harshest statute; PARTIAL RETRIEVAL, stated as such
law.authority: Ensuring Likeness, Voice, and Image Security Act of 2024, Pub. Ch. 588 (HB 2091 / SB 2096), amending Tenn. Code Ann. §§ 47-25-1101 to -1107 — official enrolled bill PDF from capitol.tn.gov. THE CONSOLIDATED CURRENT TEXT OF § 47-25-1107 COULD NOT BE RETRIEVED: law.justia.com returned HTTP 403, codes.findlaw.com returned HTTP 403, lawserver.com returned an HTTP 307 redirect loop, and a tn.gov PDF attempt failed with curl exit code 000 (connection/timeout). I am NOT filling that gap from memory.
law.quote: SECTION 4. Tennessee Code Annotated, Section 47-25-1103, is amended by deleting subsection (a) and substituting: (a) Every individual has a property right in the use of that individual's name, photograph, voice, or likeness in any medium in any manner. ... SECTION 6. Tennessee Code Annotated, Section 47-25-1105, is amended by deleting subsection (a) and substituting: (a)(1) Any person who knowingly uses or infringes upon the use of an individual's name, photograph, voice, or likeness in any medium, in any manner directed to any person other than such individual, for purposes of advertising products, merchandise, goods, or services, or for purposes of fundraising, solicitation of donations, purchases of products, merchandise, goods, or services, without such individual's prior consent... is liable to a civil action. ... SECTION 10. Tennessee Code Annotated, Section 47-25-1107(a), is amended by deleting "account" and inserting "account, to the extent protected by the First Amendment to the United States Constitution". SECTION 11. Tennessee Code Annotated, Section 47-25-1107(c), is amended by deleting "had knowledge of the unauthorized use" and substituting "had knowledge or reasonably should have known of the unauthorized use". SECTION 13. This act takes effect July 1, 2024, the public welfare requiring it.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS AND ITS LIMITS: SECTION 6 shows the § 47-25-1105(a)(1) liability trigger is 'for purposes of ADVERTISING... or for purposes of fundraising, solicitation of donations, purchases of products' — it is an advertising/solicitation statute, not a general commercial-use statute, which is markedly narrower than California § 3344(a). SECTION 10 is the important one and it cuts BOTH ways: it confirms § 47-25-1107(a) exempts uses 'in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account' (the amendment edits that phrase and so proves its existence), but the 2024 legislature deliberately NARROWED that exemption by appending 'to the extent protected by the First Amendment' — converting a bright-line statutory safe harbour into a constitutional balancing test. SECTION 11 lowers the knowledge standard for intermediaries to 'reasonably should have known'. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted, but now contingent on the First Amendment analysis rather than on the exemption's own terms. (b) EXTRACT: permitted on the same contingent basis. (c) AGGREGATE: unclear — the qualifier is new, untested, and I could not read the consolidated section. WHAT I DID NOT VERIFY: the full current wording of § 47-25-1107(a), (b) and (c). Anyone relying on Tennessee should read the consolidated section before acting. The ELVIS Act's real target is AI voice and likeness cloning (SECTION 3's 'Voice' definition covers simulations; SECTION 6(a)(3) reaches tools whose primary purpose is generating a likeness) — that is a live constraint if the game ever generates player art or audio, and a non-issue for text cards.
law.jurisdiction: Tennessee (statutory)

law.topic: THE CENTRAL CASE FOR THIS PRODUCT — using real players' names plus performance and biographical data, for profit, in an interactive paid product, defeats the right of publicity on First Amendment grounds
