law.authority: C.B.C. Distribution & Marketing, Inc. v. Major League Baseball Advanced Media, L.P., 505 F.3d 818 (8th Cir. 2007) — official Eighth Circuit slip opinion PDF (docket 06-3357, 06-3358)
law.quote: First, the information used in CBC's fantasy baseball games is all readily available in the public domain, and it would be strange law that a person would not have a first amendment right to use information that is available to everyone. It is true that CBC's use of the information is meant to provide entertainment, but "[s]peech that entertains, like speech that informs, is protected by the First Amendment because '[t]he line between the informing and the entertaining is too elusive for the protection of that basic right.'" ... We also find no merit in the argument that CBC's use of players' names and information in its fantasy baseball games is not speech at all. ... Similarly, here CBC uses the "names, nicknames, likenesses, signatures, pictures, playing records, and/or biographical data of each player" in an interactive form in connection with its fantasy baseball products. This use is no less expressive than the use that was at issue in Interactive Digital. ... Nor is there any danger here that consumers will be misled, because the fantasy baseball games depend on the inclusion of all players and thus cannot create a false impression that some particular player with "star power" is endorsing CBC's products. ... Because we hold that CBC's first amendment rights in offering its fantasy baseball products supersede the players' rights of publicity, we need not reach CBC's alternative argument that federal copyright law preempts the players' state law rights of publicity.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the three quoted holdings — (i) a first amendment right to use publicly available information, (ii) entertainment is protected speech and interactivity does not strip protection, (iii) INCLUDING EVERY PLAYER defeats the endorsement inference. Note the court FOUND the prima facie violation first (names were used as symbols of identity, and 'CBC uses baseball players' identities in its fantasy baseball products for purposes of profit') and then held the First Amendment beat it. So the defence is constitutional, not a denial of the elements. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted. (b) EXTRACT INTO OWN DB AND CITE: permitted — CBC ran exactly this, maintaining its own player database after its licence expired. (c) AGGREGATE AT SCALE: permitted, and here scale actively HELPS: the reason no endorsement could be inferred is that the product 'depend[s] on the inclusion of all players'. A comprehensive bank is safer than a curated one built around a few stars. ALSO CRITICAL FOR THIS PROJECT, from Part III: CBC had signed a licence with a no-use and no-challenge clause, kept using the data after it expired, and WON anyway — the Eighth Circuit held those contract terms unenforceable. The lesson is not 'ignore contracts'; it is that an expired or refused licence does not by itself create liability for using public-domain facts. PRACTICAL: for twenty friends this case is overwhelming cover. For a published app it is still the strongest authority available, but note it binds only the Eighth Circuit and rests on a Missouri-law claim.
law.jurisdiction: Eighth Circuit, applying Missouri right-of-publicity law; persuasive elsewhere and expressly followed by the Indiana Supreme Court

law.topic: THE CALIFORNIA ANALOGUE — historical baseball facts, records and statistics about retired players are 'a form of expression due substantial constitutional protection', and charging money does not change that
law.authority: Gionfriddo v. Major League Baseball, 94 Cal. App. 4th 400, 114 Cal. Rptr. 2d 307 (Cal. Ct. App. 2001) — full text via casemine.com (law.justia.com and caselaw.findlaw.com both returned HTTP 403; CourtListener's HTML page returned an empty HTTP 202 and its opinions API requires a token). Key passages independently corroborated by verbatim quotation in the Eighth Circuit's C.B.C. opinion and the Ninth Circuit's Keller opinion, both fetched from official court servers.
law.quote: Major league baseball is followed by millions of people across this country on a daily basis. Likewise, baseball fans have an abiding interest in the history of the game. The public has an enduring fascination in the records set by former players and in memorable moments from previous games. Statistics are kept on every aspect of the game imaginable. Those statistics and the records set throughout baseball's history are the standards by which the public measures the performance of today's players. The records and statistics remain of interest to the public because they provide context that allows fans to better appreciate (or deprecate) today's performances. Thus, the history of professional baseball is integral to the full understanding and enjoyment of the current game and its players. In the uses challenged, Baseball is simply making historical facts available to the public through game programs, Web sites and video clips. The recitation and discussion of factual data concerning the athletic performance of these plaintiffs commands a substantial public interest, and, therefore, is a form of expression due substantial constitutional protection. ... Profit, alone, does not render expression "commercial," however. "'The First Amendment is not limited to those who publish without charge. . . . [An expressive activity] does not lose its constitutional protection because it is undertaken for profit.'" ... The uses challenged in this case are not "commercial speech."
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'making historical facts available to the public through game programs, Web sites and video clips' is held to be protected expression, and 'Profit, alone, does not render expression "commercial"'. This is a California appellate decision applying BOTH the common-law claim and § 3344, so it closes the loop that § 3344(d) alone leaves open. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted. (b) EXTRACT: permitted — the defendant maintained and published exactly such a compilation. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted; the opinion praises comprehensiveness ('Statistics are kept on every aspect of the game imaginable') as part of why the material is of public interest. WHY THIS IS THE MOST QUOTABLE ROW FOR THIS PROJECT: substitute 'basketball' for 'baseball' and this paragraph is a description of Ball Knowledge's premise — that historical records provide the context by which today's players are measured. It is also the answer to the instinctive worry 'but we might charge for it one day': the court says charging does not convert protected expression into commercial speech. Also note the plaintiffs here were RETIRED players whose careers ran 1932-1948 — i.e., exactly the historical-figure cards a knowledge game leans on. Same result under a Black Fives-era card.
law.jurisdiction: California Court of Appeal (binding California authority absent contrary Supreme Court decision; heavily cited nationally)

law.topic: The strictest state's own supreme court applies the newsworthiness exemption to a PAID, GAMIFIED use of player names, pictures and statistics — including for college athletes
law.authority: Daniels v. FanDuel, Inc., 109 N.E.3d 390 (Ind. 2018) (No. 18S-CQ-00134, answering a certified question from the Seventh Circuit) — reporter-paginated PDF hosted by Yale Law School's Information Society Project
law.quote: The plain language of the statute only speaks to the use of a personality's right of publicity in "[m]aterial that has political or newsworthy value." Ind. Code § 32-36-1-1(c)(1)(B). The statute is silent on whether there are any restrictions on who publishes or uses the material. ... Given that the legislature defined and carved out an exception that applies only to news reporting entities, we decline to place a similar restriction on the "newsworthy value" exception at issue here. ... The privilege of enlightening the public is by no means limited to dissemination of news in the sense of current events but extends far beyond to include all types of factual, educational and historical data, or even entertainment and amusement, concerning interesting phases of human activity in general. ... we find that the term "newsworthy" was meant to be construed broadly. ... This information is not stripped of its newsworthy value simply because it is placed behind a paywall or used in the context of a fantasy sports game. On the contrary, fantasy sports operators use factual data combined with a significant, creative component that allows consumers to interact with the data in a unique way. ... At the other end of the newsworthy spectrum, we recognize that the unauthorized use of a personality to advertise or promote a product likely lies outside the scope of what is considered newsworthy. ... We conclude that Indiana's right of publicity statute contains an exception for material with newsworthy value that includes online fantasy sports operators' use of college players' names, pictures, and statistics for online fantasy contests. ... Importantly, however, this finding does not foreclose a court from closely scrutinizing the actions of a particular defendant to ensure no unauthorized endorsements are being made.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: four holdings, each doing separate work. (i) The exemption is NOT limited to news organisations — a game studio gets it. (ii) 'Newsworthy' includes 'all types of factual, educational and historical data, or even entertainment and amusement'. (iii) A PAYWALL does not strip the exemption, and neither does wrapping the data in a game. (iv) The line is drawn at ADVERTISING: using a personality 'to advertise or promote a product' falls outside. (a) permitted, (b) permitted, (c) permitted, all on § 32-36-1-1(c)(1)(B) as construed here. WHY THIS IS THE MOST USEFUL ROW OPERATIONALLY: it is a state supreme court, in the state with the harshest statute, holding that a paid interactive product built on player names, PICTURES and statistics is exempt. And it draws the exact line the reader asked about, in one sentence: content = protected, advertising = not. That maps to a concrete rule for this project — the SAME player name that is fine on a card is a liability in a store screenshot, an ad, or a push notification that says 'new LeBron pack'. Note also the court's closing caveat: it reserved the endorsement question for case-by-case scrutiny, so the exemption is not a licence to imply approval.
law.jurisdiction: Indiana Supreme Court (binding in Indiana; the most authoritative pro-defendant holding on this fact pattern anywhere)

law.topic: THE LIMIT — where a factual product stops being protected: rendered likenesses and avatars. This is the case that would go against the project if it ever draws the players
law.authority: In re NCAA Student-Athlete Name & Likeness Licensing Litigation (Keller v. Electronic Arts Inc.), 724 F.3d 1268 (9th Cir. 2013) — official Ninth Circuit PDF
law.quote: We think that, unlike in Gionfriddo, Montana, and Dora, EA is not publishing or reporting factual data. EA's video game is a means by which users can play their own virtual football games, not a means for obtaining information about real-world football games. Although EA has incorporated certain actual player information into the game (height, weight, etc.), its case is considerably weakened by its decision not to include the athletes' names along with their likenesses and statistical data. EA can hardly be considered to be "reporting" on Keller's career at Arizona State and Nebraska when it is not even using Keller's name in connection with his avatar in the game. Put simply, EA's interactive game is not a publication of facts about college football; it is a game, not a reference source. These state law defenses, therefore, do not apply. [n.12] ... But there is a big difference between a video game like NCAA Football and fantasy baseball products like those at issue in C.B.C. Those products merely "incorporate[d] the names along with performance and biographical data of actual major league baseball players." Id. at 820. NCAA Football, on the other hand, uses virtual likenesses of actual college football players. It is seemingly true that each likeness is generated largely from publicly available data... but finding this fact dispositive would neuter the right of publicity in our digital world. ... Under California's transformative use defense, EA's use of the likenesses of college athletes like Samuel Keller in its video games is not, as a matter of law, protected by the First Amendment. We reject EA's suggestion to import the Rogers test into the right-of-publicity arena, and conclude that state-law defenses for the reporting of information do not protect EA's use.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: footnote 12 states the dividing line explicitly — names + performance and biographical data (C.B.C., protected) versus VIRTUAL LIKENESSES of real people (Keller, not protected). And the body holds that § 3344(d) and the common-law public-interest defence 'protect only the act of publishing or reporting'. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted — this case does not touch it. (b) EXTRACT: permitted — same. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted for facts; PROHIBITED-LEANING for a database of rendered likenesses, per the transformative-use holding. THE WARNING FOR THIS PROJECT, stated plainly because it is the one finding that should change a build decision: the sentence 'it is a game, not a reference source' is the sentence a plaintiff would quote against Ball Knowledge. The defence is that Ball Knowledge IS a reference source with a quiz interface — its entire content is the publication of facts about real games, which is precisely what EA's product was NOT. That defence survives only as long as the product's substance is facts. It weakens the moment the game ships PLAYER PORTRAITS, avatars, or figurine pieces that depict identifiable real people. Per CLAUDE.md the game already sources illustrated art — the medium-honesty rule and this holding point the same way: source or commission GENERIC basketball figures, never recognisable renderings of named real players. Ninth Circuit law governs California, so this is the applicable rule for a US app.
law.jurisdiction: Ninth Circuit, applying California law (companion holding: Hart v. Electronic Arts, 717 F.3d 141 (3d Cir. 2013), same result)

law.topic: The California transformative-use test itself — the standard any depiction of a real player would be measured against
law.authority: Comedy III Productions, Inc. v. Gary Saderup, Inc., 25 Cal. 4th 387, 21 P.3d 797 (Cal. 2001), as quoted verbatim and applied by the Ninth Circuit in Keller (official Ninth Circuit PDF). I did not retrieve the Comedy III opinion directly — scocal.stanford.edu returned HTTP 404 — so this is a first-hand quotation of a second-hand source.
law.quote: The defense is "a balancing test between the First Amendment and the right of publicity based on whether the work in question adds significant creative elements so as to be transformed into something more than a mere celebrity likeness or imitation." Id. at 799. ... First, if "the celebrity likeness is one of the 'raw materials' from which an original work is synthesized," it is more likely to be transformative than if "the depiction or imitation of the celebrity is the very sum and substance of the work in question." Comedy III, 21 P.3d at 809. Second, the work is protected if it is "primarily the defendant's own expression"—as long as that expression is "something other than the likeness of the celebrity." Id. ... Third, to avoid making judgments concerning "the quality of the artistic contribution," a court should conduct an inquiry "more quantitative than qualitative" and ask "whether the literal and imitative or the creative elements predominate in the work." Id. Fourth ... whether "the marketability and economic value of the challenged work derive primarily from the fame of the celebrity depicted." Id. at 810. Lastly, the court indicated that "when an artist's skill and talent is manifestly subordinated to the overall goal of creating a conventional portrait of a celebrity so as to commercially exploit his or her fame," the work is not transformative.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the five Comedy III factors. Note what they measure — a LIKENESS. The test has no purchase on a text card that states a fact, because there is no depiction to be transformative or not. That is the single most useful thing about this row: it tells you the transformative-use minefield is entirely avoidable by not depicting anyone. (a) n/a — no likeness involved. (b) n/a. (c) restricted only insofar as the database contains depictions. PRACTICAL: factor four is the one to design against — 'whether the marketability and economic value of the challenged work derive primarily from the fame of the celebrity depicted'. A trivia game whose value comes from the QUESTIONS and the play, not from owning a picture of a star, sits well clear of it. A card pack sold because it has a famous face on it does not. This is also why the C.B.C. 'include everyone' principle matters commercially as well as legally: breadth of coverage is itself a defence.
law.jurisdiction: California Supreme Court

law.topic: NOMINATIVE FAIR USE — the three-part test, from a case that was itself about a paid reader QUIZ/POLL about real people, and that also disposed of the right-of-publicity claim
law.authority: New Kids on the Block v. News America Publishing, Inc., 971 F.2d 302 (9th Cir. 1992) — full text from law.resource.org (public.resource.org's federal reporter archive; openjurist, findlaw and case.law all returned 403/404)
law.quote: where the defendant uses a trademark to describe the plaintiff's product, rather than its own, we hold that a commercial user is entitled to a nominative fair use defense provided he meets the following three requirements: First, the product or service in question must be one not readily identifiable without use of the trademark; second, only so much of the mark or marks may be used as is reasonably necessary to identify the product or service; and third, the user must do nothing that would, in conjunction with the mark, suggest sponsorship or endorsement by the trademark holder. ... It is no more reasonably possible, however, to refer to the New Kids as an entity than it is to refer to the Chicago Bulls, Volkswagens or the Boston Marathon without using the trademark. ... Both The Star and USA Today reference the New Kids only to the extent necessary to identify them as the subject of the polls; they do not use the New Kids' distinctive logo or anything else that isn't needed to make the announcements intelligible to readers. ... Where, as here, the use does not imply sponsorship or endorsement, the fact that it is carried on for profit and in competition with the trademark holder's business is beside the point. ... The New Kids could not use the trademark laws to prevent the publication of an unauthorized group biography or to censor all parodies or satires which use their name. ... The papers have a complete defense to both claims if they used the New Kids name "in connection with any news, public affairs, or sports broadcast or account" which was true in all material respects. See Cal.Civ.Code § 3344(d); Eastwood v. Superior Ct., 149 Cal.App.3d 409, 421 & 426 (1983) (extending the section 3344(d) defense to common law misappropriation claims)
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the three-part test in ¶21, and the § 3344(d)/Eastwood holding in ¶29. This is the doctrine the prompt asked for and the opinion could hardly be closer to the product: two newspapers ran PAID 900-number POLLS asking readers questions about real famous people, made money doing it, and won on every count. (a) CITE/NAME: permitted. (b) EXTRACT: permitted. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted; ¶26 holds that profit and even direct competition with the rights holder are 'beside the point' where no endorsement is implied. TEAM MARKS — the second prong is the operative constraint and it is concrete: the court notes the papers 'do not use the New Kids' distinctive LOGO or anything else that isn't needed'. Applied here: writing 'Chicago Bulls' on a card is prong-one necessary and prong-two minimal (the opinion literally uses the Bulls as its example). REPRODUCING the Bulls logo, wordmark lettering, or team colourway as chrome is not necessary to identify the team, and fails prong two — which is exactly the kind of thing that turns a defensible reference into a trademark fight. Prong three then bars anything reading as official: no 'official', no league marks in the app icon or store listing, and a visible 'not affiliated with or endorsed by' disclaimer costs nothing and speaks to prong three. Also note ¶29: the § 3344(d) 'sports broadcast or account' defence is a COMPLETE defence to BOTH the statutory and the common-law publicity claim.
law.jurisdiction: Ninth Circuit (the origin of nominative fair use; adopted in varying forms elsewhere, notably modified by the Third Circuit)

law.topic: TRADEMARK / TEAM MARKS — the 2023 Supreme Court decision that narrowed the expressive-work defence, and precisely how far it narrowed it
law.authority: Jack Daniel's Properties, Inc. v. VIP Products LLC, 599 U.S. 140 (2023) — official Supreme Court slip opinion PDF (No. 22-148)
law.quote: Held: 1. When an alleged infringer uses a trademark as a designation of source for the infringer's own goods, the Rogers test does not apply. ... The Second Circuit created the Rogers test for titles of "artistic works" based on its view that such titles have an "expressive element" implicating "First Amendment values" and carry only a "slight risk" of confusing consumers about the "source or content" of the underlying work. 875 F. 2d, at 998–1000. — and, describing the Rogers test itself: When "expressive works" are involved, ... that test requires dismissal of an infringement claim at the outset unless the complainant can show either (1) that the challenged use of a mark "has no artistic relevance to the underlying work" or (2) that it "explicitly misleads as to the source or the content of the work." Id., at 999.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the Held. Jack Daniel's did NOT abolish Rogers v. Grimaldi — it held Rogers unavailable when the mark is used AS A SOURCE DESIGNATOR for the defendant's own goods. (a) NAME A TEAM IN A QUESTION: permitted — that is not source-designating use, so Rogers survives and nominative fair use applies independently. (b) STORE TEAM NAMES IN A DATABASE FIELD: permitted — no use as a mark at all. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted on the same reasoning. THE LINE FOR THIS PROJECT, and it is a bright one: 'Chicago Bulls' inside a question is referential; 'Chicago Bulls' or a team logo on the app icon, the pack artwork, the title screen, or the store listing starts to look like a designation of source for the game itself, and that is exactly the use that loses Rogers and drops you into ordinary likelihood-of-confusion analysis. This is the trademark mirror of the Daniels advertising/content line — same boundary, different body of law, which is a strong signal it is the right boundary to build against.
law.jurisdiction: United States Supreme Court (Lanham Act — trademark, not publicity)

law.topic: THE TRIVIA-SPECIFIC AUTHORITY — a trivia quiz book of 643 questions was held to INFRINGE, and the court explained exactly why a real-world sports trivia game is the opposite case
law.authority: Castle Rock Entertainment, Inc. v. Carol Publishing Group, Inc., 150 F.3d 132 (2d Cir. 1998) (The Seinfeld Aptitude Test) — full text from law.resource.org
law.quote: This case presents two interesting and somewhat novel issues of copyright law. The first is whether The Seinfeld Aptitude Test, a trivia quiz book devoted exclusively to testing its readers' recollection of scenes and events from the fictional television series Seinfeld, takes sufficient protected expression from the original... We conclude that The SAT unlawfully copies from Seinfeld and that its copying does not constitute fair use and thus is an actionable infringement. ... The SAT did not copy from Seinfeld unprotected facts, but, rather, creative expression. Cf. Feist, 499 U.S. at 364 (finding no infringement where defendant produced a multi-county phone directory, in part, by obtaining names and phone numbers from plaintiffs' single-county directory). Unlike the facts in a phone book, which "do not owe their origin to an act of authorship," id. at 347, each "fact" tested by The SAT is in reality fictitious expression created by Seinfeld's authors. The SAT does not quiz such true facts as the identity of the actors in Seinfeld, the number of days it takes to shoot an episode, the biographies of the actors, the location of the Seinfeld set, etc. Rather, The SAT tests whether the reader knows that the character Jerry places a Pez dispenser on Elaine's leg during a piano recital... Because these characters and events spring from the imagination of Seinfeld's authors, The SAT plainly copies copyrightable, creative expression. ... a disclaimer states that "This book has not been approved or licensed by any entity involved in creating or producing Seinfeld."
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the fact/fiction distinction, and specifically the sentence beginning 'The SAT does not quiz such true facts as...'. This is the closest thing in US law to an authority on trivia quizzes as a format, and it is a LOSS — which makes it the most instructive row in the set, because the court volunteered the description of the trivia book that WOULD have been lawful, and that description is Ball Knowledge. A quiz on 'true facts' — who did what, when, biographies, real events — copies nothing protectable. A quiz on invented events inside a copyrighted fictional work copies expression. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted — real-world facts have no author. (b) EXTRACT: permitted. (c) AGGREGATE: permitted for real-world facts; PROHIBITED for the invented contents of a fictional work. RELEVANT LIMIT FOR THIS PROJECT: the safe harbour is 'true facts', so a question drawn from a real game, box score, career or biography is clear. A question drawn from a copyrighted broadcast's COMMENTARY, a documentary's narration, or a film's dramatisation is not automatically clear — the fact is free, the expression around it is not, so write questions from the fact and never from the phrasing. ALSO WORTH COPYING: the SAT's back-cover disclaimer, quoted above, is the template for the one this project should carry. It did not save that book (because the problem was copying, not confusion) but it is the standard device for the endorsement prong.
law.jurisdiction: Second Circuit (copyright, not right of publicity)

law.topic: NEGATIVE FINDING, reported because its absence is load-bearing — there is no US right-of-publicity decision about a trivia or quiz game
law.authority: None located. Searched for right-of-publicity authority specific to trivia games, quiz apps, almanacs or reference works and found none. The nearest analogues are all in this table and none is a trivia game: New Kids (paid reader poll about real people, 9th Cir. 1992), C.B.C. and Daniels (fantasy sports), Gionfriddo (game programmes and websites of historical facts), Castle Rock (a trivia book, decided on copyright not publicity), and Keller (a video game, decided against the defendant on likeness grounds).
law.what_it_means_here: WHY THE ABSENCE IS USEFUL RATHER THAN WORRYING: in a field where sports leagues and players' unions have litigated aggressively against trading cards (Cardtoons), fantasy sports (C.B.C., Daniels, CBS Interactive), video games (Keller, Hart) and photo posters (Montana), the fact that nobody has sued a sports trivia product is itself evidence about perceived merit — the plaintiff-side bar has had thirty years and has gone after every adjacent format. Do not read the absence as an unmapped risk; read it as a format that sits comfortably inside settled doctrine. Two honest caveats on this finding. First, absence of a reported appellate decision is not absence of demand letters, which are invisible. Second, my search was targeted rather than exhaustive, so this is 'none located', not 'none exists'. THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE: because there is no trivia-specific rule, the analysis is entirely borrowed from the fantasy-sports and historical-facts line, which means the project should keep looking like those cases and not like Keller. Concretely, the four things that hold that position are: keep the substance factual and sourced; include everyone rather than curating around stars (C.B.C.); do not depict identifiable real players (Keller); and keep names and team marks out of advertising and out of anything that designates the source of the game (Daniels, Jack Daniel's).
law.jurisdiction: United States (survey)

law.topic: THE FOUNDATION FOR BUILDING YOUR OWN DATABASE — facts are not copyrightable, no matter whose effort collected them
law.authority: Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., 499 U.S. 340 (1991) — full text from law.resource.org's US Reports archive
law.quote: The key to resolving the tension lies in understanding why facts are not copyrightable. The sine qua non of copyright is originality. To qualify for copyright protection, a work must be original to the author. ... Common sense tells us that 100 uncopyrightable facts do not magically change their status when gathered together in one place. ... A compilation is not copyrightable per se, but is copyrightable only if its facts have been "selected, coordinated, or arranged in such a way that the resulting work as a whole constitutes an original work of authorship." § 101. ... Even a compilation that is copyrightable receives only limited protection, for the copyright does not extend to facts contained in the compilation. § 103(b). Lower courts that adopted a "sweat of the brow" or "industrious collection" test which extended a compilation's copyright protection beyond selection and arrangement to the facts themselves—misconstrued the 1909 Act and eschewed the fundamental axiom of copyright law that no one may copyright facts or ideas. ... The raw data are uncopyrightable facts, and the way in which Rural selected, coordinated, and arranged that data is not original.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: '100 uncopyrightable facts do not magically change their status when gathered together in one place', and the express rejection of 'sweat of the brow'. This is the answer to activity (b) and most of activity (c), and it is a Supreme Court answer. (a) CITE ONE FACT: permitted — no copyright interest exists to infringe. (b) EXTRACT FACTS FROM A SOURCE INTO YOUR OWN DATABASE: permitted as a matter of COPYRIGHT — that a stats site spent money compiling a career line does not give it rights in the career line. (c) AGGREGATE AT SCALE: permitted as to the FACTS; the residual limit is 'selection, coordination, or arrangement', meaning you may take the facts but not clone a source's original ORDERING or CURATION (a hand-picked 'top 100' list is a creative selection; a career total is not). TWO IMPORTANT LIMITS, stated so this row is not over-read. First, Feist is copyright only — it says nothing about the right of publicity, nothing about contract, and NOTHING ABOUT A SITE'S TERMS OF SERVICE, which can bind by agreement what copyright leaves free. Second, the practical discipline this implies is one the project already follows: mine facts, restate them in your own words, record the source and dateChecked, and never copy a source's prose or its bespoke arrangement.
law.jurisdiction: United States Supreme Court (copyright)

law.topic: BASKETBALL SPECIFICALLY — scores and statistics taken from NBA broadcasts are uncopyrightable facts, and the NBA lost trying to stop their redistribution
law.authority: National Basketball Association v. Motorola, Inc., 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997) — full text from law.resource.org
law.quote: Although the broadcasts are protected under copyright law, the district court correctly held that Motorola and STATS did not infringe NBA's copyright because they reproduced only facts from the broadcasts, not the expression or description of the game that constitutes the broadcast. The "fact/expression dichotomy" is a bedrock principle of copyright law that "limits severely the scope of protection in fact-based works." ... "'No author may copyright facts or ideas. The copyright is limited to those aspects of the work—termed 'expression'—that display the stamp of the author's originality.'" ... We agree with the district court that the "[d]efendants provide purely factual information which any patron of an NBA game could acquire from the arena without any involvement from the director, cameramen, or others who contribute to the originality of a broadcast." ... Because the SportsTrax device and AOL site reproduce only factual information culled from the broadcasts and none of the copyrightable expression of the games, appellants did not infringe the copyright of the broadcasts.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: 'they reproduced only facts from the broadcasts, not the expression', and 'purely factual information which any patron of an NBA game could acquire from the arena'. This is the sport-specific application of Feist and it is BASKETBALL, against the NBA itself. (a) permitted, (b) permitted — the defendants literally employed people to watch games and key the facts into a commercial database, which is activity (b) in its purest form and it was lawful, (c) permitted for the facts. THE ONE RESIDUAL RISK THIS CASE FLAGS: the Second Circuit went on to hold the NBA's state-law 'hot news' misappropriation claim mostly preempted, but left a narrow surviving hot-news tort for TIME-SENSITIVE, free-ride-on-the-plaintiff's-costs, direct-competition situations. That doctrine has essentially no application to a historical trivia bank — the facts on the cards are years or decades old and compete with nobody's live product — but it would matter if the game ever ingested live scores in real time. WORTH RECORDING FOR THE PROJECT SEPARATELY: the underlying GAMES are not copyrightable, only the BROADCASTS are. So a question about what happened in a game is free; copying a broadcaster's footage, call, or graphics is not.
law.jurisdiction: Second Circuit (copyright and New York misappropriation)

law.topic: THE SANCTIONED ROUTE, since one exists and the prompt rightly prizes finding it — NBPA group licensing for NBA player names and likenesses, and why it is almost certainly the wrong door for this project
law.authority: National Basketball Players Inc. d/b/a THINK450, Digital & Gaming Licensing Application — Prospective Licensee Information Form (official NBPA licensing application PDF). Under the NBA CBA the NBPA, not the league, controls group licensing of player names, numbers and images in groups of three or more.
law.quote: Thank you for your interest in becoming a licensee of National Basketball Players Inc. d/b/a THINK450 ("THINK450" or "we" or "our"). ... THE APPLICATION IS NOT AND WILL NOT BE DEEMED AN OFFER TO CONTRACT OR A SOLICITATION BY THINK450. UNLESS YOU HAVE RECEIVED THINK450's EXPRESS WRITTEN CONSENT, YOUR PRODUCT AND/OR PRODUCT SUGGESTIONS HAVE NOT BEEN APPROVED AND YOU MAY NOT USE, DISTRIBUTE, EXECUTE, PROMOTE, MARKET, ADVERTISE, EXHIBIT, OR OTHERWISE EXPLOIT ANY RIGHTS MAINTAINED BY THINK450. THINK450 regularly receives numerous licensing suggestions. You acknowledge that other parties (including, without limitation, THINK450 employees) may submit, make public, may have already submitted or made public, product suggestions that are indistinguishable from those included in your submission. THINK450 reserves the right to license such products. You acknowledge that you will not be entitled to any compensation derived from such products or product suggestions. ... 3. FINANCIAL INFORMATION & CREDIT REFERENCES Please include (i) letter(s) from your bank(s) and at least two credit references; (ii) copies of your company's audited financial statements and corporate tax returns for the last three (3) years, and (iii) copies of any bank covenants related to your company's debt securitization.
law.what_it_means_here: BASIS: the application's own terms. This is a genuine, official, bulk route to NBA player names and likenesses, and naming it is more useful than any prohibition — so here it is, with an honest read of what it costs. (a)/(b)/(c) would all become expressly PERMITTED under a THINK450 licence, for active NBA players. THREE REASONS IT IS PROBABLY NOT THE MOVE, stated with the arithmetic visible. First, the ENTRY BAR is corporate: three years of audited financials, corporate tax returns, bank letters and two credit references. A solo project cannot produce those, so this door is effectively shut today regardless of merit. Second, the IDEA-SUBMISSION CLAUSE is adverse — you acknowledge THINK450 may already have or may later license an indistinguishable product and you get nothing. Applying therefore has a real downside and no guaranteed upside. Third and most important, THE PROJECT DOES NOT NEED IT. Everything above — C.B.C., Gionfriddo, Daniels, § 3344(d), Ohio § 2741.09(A)(1)(a), RCW 63.60.070(1) — says names plus factual performance data need no licence. A licence buys you LIKENESSES and official association, which are exactly the two things Keller says to avoid and Jack Daniel's says complicate the trademark position. COVERAGE GAP WORTH NOTING: THINK450 covers active NBA players only. Retired players, WNBA, college and historical figures sit under different bodies entirely, so a licence would not even solve the whole bank. RECOMMENDATION: do not apply. Revisit only if the product ever wants official player IMAGES or league branding, which is a different product.
law.jurisdiction: Contractual / licensing (United States)

verdict.biggest_legal_risk:
CONTRACT, not copyright — specifically Sports Reference LLC's Web Site Terms of Use § 5, now read with actual notice, which is the only document in the set whose prohibitions describe both this project's METHOD and its OUTPUT.

Two clauses, in SRL's own words: (i) you may not "use any material or Content from the Site, including without limitation any statistics or data, (i) to create any database, archive, or other data store that competes with or constitutes a material substitute for the services or data stores offered on the Site"; and (ii) you may not "copy or use any material or Content from the Site... for purposes of training, fine-tuning, PROMPTING, or INSTRUCTING artificial intelligence models or technologies in any manner, including without limitation for purposes of (i) generating answers, text, scores, statistics..."

Why this is the biggest and not merely the loudest, kept separate from what the documents say — this is my reading:

1. It survives every copyright answer. Feist, NBA v. Motorola and SRL's own "facts cannot be copyrighted" concession all establish that the DATA is free. None of them touch a promise. hiQ is the proof case: it won the CFAA question at the Ninth Circuit ("that computer has erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place") and then LOST on breach of the User Agreement in the same litigation — "In sum, hiQ breached LinkedIn's User Agreement both through its own scraping of LinkedIn's site and using scraped data." Not a crime, still a breach, and the breach is what cost money.

2. The cheapest defence has already been spent. Nguyen: "courts have consistently enforced browsewrap agreements where the user had actual notice of the agreement." Berman's two-part inquiry-notice test opens with "Unless the website operator can show that a consumer has actual knowledge of the agreement." SR's terms are pure browsewrap with no clickwrap and no account, which is the weakest possible formation posture — but this project has now READ them, in this run, in full. Reading the terms is arguably what binds you to them when the site's own design would not have.

3. The AI clause has no track record in either direction. It is a product of one of SRL's two most recent revisions (page history: 2004, 2008, 2011, 2015, 2020, last updated May 19 2023). Every scraper in the "nobody has ever been enforced against" evidence — jaebradley 2016, swar 2018, vishaalagartha — predates it. So the comfort the enforcement record provides does not extend to this clause. Its plain words cover pasting a b-ref page into a model to have it write or check a card, which is the default way an AI-built question bank gets made.

4. The magnitude is real even without litigation. § 22: "If SRL does take any legal action against you as a result of your violation of the Agreement, SRL will be entitled to recover from you, and you agree to pay, all reasonable attorneys' fees and costs of such action." § 17 reserves termination "for any reason whatever or no reason."

The mitigations the documents themselves supply, which is why this is manageable rather than fatal: § 20 routes disputes through written notice, a 10-business-day exchange, 60 days of negotiation and mediation before either side may litigate — the contract itself points at a letter and a conversation first. Guiding principle (1) of § 5 expressly welcomes "sharing, using, modifying, repackaging, or publishing data found on individual SRL webpages... whether for commercial or non-commercial purposes," conditioned on credit. And sharing.html, the SHARE-widget page, is the most permissive thing SRL publishes anywhere: "You are free to use this data anywhere, we would just ask that you include the citation." A hand-read, per-card, credit-carrying trivia bank sits inside principle (1) and inside the SHARE route. A crawler, a mirror, or a model fed b-ref HTML does not.
verdict.most_likely_to_actually_bite:
BEING BLOCKED — and specifically, being blocked SILENTLY, mid-run, from infrastructure you chose for convenience. This is the only risk in the entire set with a documented hit rate of essentially 100%, it has already happened twice inside this very research session, and it costs hours rather than money.

The evidence, dated and first-hand:

- Sports Reference runs Cloudflare behavioural bot filtering, and BASKETBALL is on the permanently-filtered list. Sean Forman, Oct 7 2022: "we get scraped. A LOT... We've gotten a number of emails around this this week as people who have been scraping us have found themselves blocked." Baseball and pro football got filtering switched off seasonally; soccer, basketball, hockey and the college sites did not.
- The published ceiling is 20 requests/minute on basketball-reference (10 on FBref/Stathead), "regardless of bot type and construction and pages accessed" — no user-agent or path raises it — and violation puts your session "in jail for up to a day." robots.txt independently says Crawl-delay: 3, which is the same number. Two documents agreeing is a real limit.
- In this run, WebFetch got HTTP 403 from sports-reference.com on the first attempt at data_use.html and bot-traffic.html. Both needed a curl retry.
- The NBA blocks datacenter IP ranges wholesale. Two requests to stats.nba.com/stats/* from this machine hung to FULL TIMEOUT with zero bytes and no HTTP status (curl exit 28) — once bare, once with the complete canonical header set including x-nba-stats-origin and x-nba-stats-token — while a control request to stats.nba.com/ returned HTTP 200 at 447,702 bytes in the same minute. The swar/nba_api issue record shows this unbroken from 2018 to 2026 (#5, #124, #176, #320 still open since Dec 2022, #389, #498 on EC2, #633 open, #650 "I want to know how long I should wait between requests to avoid IP bans," opened Mar 2026 and still unanswered).
- Wikimedia deployed hard per-user rate limits in 2026: 10 req/min unidentified, 200 with a compliant User-Agent, 3 concurrent connections max, and "if you don't supply a User-Agent header, or you supply an empty or generic one, your request will fail with an HTTP 403 error." The UA policy names curl and Python-urllib specifically, and separately says "Do not copy a browser's user agent for your bot" — which is exactly what this session did.

Why this bites harder than its size suggests: THE FAILURES ARE DISHONEST. nba_api issue #678, opened May 2026 and still open, is titled "nba_api.live silently swallows 403s and raises a misleading JSONDecodeError." A block does not arrive as "you are blocked." It arrives as a hang, a malformed-JSON exception, or an hour of debugging your own parser. That is why the same issue gets reopened every few months by someone who thinks the service is down. For a project whose CLAUDE.md already warns about asserting things you did not measure, a source that lies about why it failed is a specific, named hazard.

Second most likely, and the only legally-shaped thing on this list with a working enforcement channel: A TAKEDOWN OF A PUBLISHED BULK EXPORT. Kaggle demonstrably acts on copyright complaints — Retraction Watch, 29 July 2026, documents Kaggle pulling a dataset for infringement — and GitHub honours DMCA. The mechanism exists and functions; it simply has never been aimed at an NBA or Basketball-Reference derivative. If this project ever ships a big derived stats table as a public artifact, it moves from the category nobody has ever bothered with into the category where a form letter already works.

Third: A WRONG CARD. Not legal at all, but it is what actually damages the product. Wikidata is CC0, which licenses the data and warrants nothing about it; Wikimedia's own dumps page says "Your use of this material is AT YOUR OWN RISK." The free backbone is a legally clean INDEX, not a citable authority.
verdict.theoretically_true_never_enforced:
These clauses are real, quoted verbatim from live documents, and there is no public record of any of them ever being used against anyone reusing basketball facts. Ranked by how scary they read versus how inert they are.

1. THE COMPETING-DATABASE CLAUSE (SR ToU § 5(i)). Bars using SR data "to create any database, archive, or other data store that competes with or constitutes a material substitute for the services or data stores offered on the Site." Against it: four separate searches for a cease-and-desist, lawsuit, DMCA notice, PyPI removal or GitHub takedown by Sports Reference LLC returned NOTHING — no case, no docket, no Lumen entry. Meanwhile jaebradley/basketball_reference_web_scraper (552 stars, MIT, public since ~2016, README: "hopefully they don't get too pissed off at me for creating this") is unarchived, 4,492 PyPI downloads last month; vishaalagartha/basketball_reference_scraper (289 stars) documents the rate limiter rather than fearing it; Kaggle hosts datasets whose URL slug is literally "nba-data-from-basketball-reference." SRL's entire demonstrated enforcement toolkit is Cloudflare and a 24-hour timeout.

2. NBA ToU § 6 / WNBA § LINKS — THE DEEP-LINK BAN. "All links to Services from a Permissible Site must be to the Services' home page or to the homepage of a particular team — links to internal pages within the Services (e.g., a player page, a photo gallery, or a feature article)... are not permitted." This is a 1990s-vintage clause that essentially the entire internet, including Google, violates continuously, and no enforcement of it against anyone was found. It still matters — it tells you the NBA is a bad citation source by design — but nobody has ever been made to answer for a deep link.

3. NBA ToU § 9(vii) / WNBA (vii) — THE COMPREHENSIVE-DATABASE CLAUSE. Bars use "in connection with any website, product, or service that features a database (in any medium or format) of comprehensive, regularly updated statistics." Written for exactly this activity. Yet swar/nba_api — 3.7k stars, 722 forks, 236,010 PyPI downloads in the last 30 days, named after the league, public since 2018 — has never been touched. Its own README does not even claim a licence; it just links the ToU. Kaggle's wyattowalsh/basketball "NBA Database", built on the same endpoints, is live. Zero letters, zero suits, zero takedowns across roughly a quarter-million monthly installs over a decade.

4. WNBA § INJUNCTIVE RELIEF. The user pre-consents that a violation "may result in irreparable injury" and that the League "may obtain injunctions." Frightening drafting; zero enforcement actions of any kind by the WNBA against any data reuser surfaced. Confidence low-to-moderate on that absence, because the WNBA is a small surface that generates little coverage either way — but pbpstats scrapes WNBA play-by-play in the open and is unmolested.

5. THE EU/UK SUI GENERIS DATABASE RIGHT. The most alarming doctrine in the whole set on paper — it protects uncopyrightable facts, Art 7(5) catches "repeated and systematic extraction of insubstantial parts," and attribution is NOT a defence. And it is MOOT for this project's actual sources. Art 11 limits beneficiaries to EU nationals and EU-established bodies; Sports Reference LLC is a Philadelphia company, so it is not a beneficiary at all, and Art 11(3) makes the only route in a Council agreement extending protection to third countries, of which none was found. UK reg 18 was narrowed post-Brexit to UK makers. Football Dataco v Sportradar makes location turn on TARGETING, not accessibility, and an English-language US-sports site on GitHub Pages with no EUR pricing is accessibility. The whole continent's analysis collapses to: don't bulk-pull EuroLeague, Transfermarkt, or a BBC/Guardian archive.

6. THE CFAA. Van Buren settled that purpose is not the test — "It does not cover those who... have improper motives for obtaining information that is otherwise available to them" — and hiQ (2022) that a public page has "erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place." Loading a page anyone's browser can load is not a federal crime. Never a realistic exposure here, and Van Buren footnote 8's reservation only bites if you defeat a gate, which the do-not-do list forecloses.

7. HOT-NEWS MISAPPROPRIATION. Survives preemption only in a narrow INS-shaped form requiring five conjunctive elements, of which (ii) is "the information is time-sensitive." The court found data delayed two to three minutes from a LIVE GAME still time-sensitive. A 1987 rebounding title is the opposite pole. Dormant unless the project ever ships live scores.

8. RIGHT OF PUBLICITY, INCLUDING INDIANA'S 100-YEAR POSTMORTEM TERM. Every historical player from ~1926 on is inside Indiana's term, and Washington's statute reaches deceased personalities "regardless of... domicile, residence, or citizenship at the time of death." And Indiana's own Supreme Court, in Daniels v. FanDuel, held a paid gamified use of college players' "names, pictures, and statistics" exempt as newsworthy, refusing to limit the exemption to news organisations, and holding that a paywall does not strip it. Ohio names "historical work" as exempt outright; Washington names "historical" and "educational"; California § 3344(d) exempts a "sports... account." NO US right-of-publicity decision about a trivia or quiz game was located — in a field where the plaintiffs' bar has litigated trading cards, fantasy sports, video games and posters for thirty years. That absence reads as a format sitting comfortably inside settled doctrine, not as unmapped territory.
verdict.safest_construction:
SOURCE TIERS — the single most useful change, and it is a sourcing-hierarchy change, not a legal one.

TIER 1, BULK-SAFE, CARRIES THE SPINE. Wikidata structured data (CC0), taken from the weekly JSON dump at dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/ or via SPARQL at query.wikidata.org/sparql — never by crawling wikidata.org. Wikipedia article dumps for facts (not prose). Wikimedia Analytics datasets (CC0). Use for: canonical names, birth dates and places, height, position, teams-played-for with start/end dates, draft year, Hall of Fame membership, franchise histories, and — the highest-value item — the EXTERNAL ID CROSSWALK (NBA.com player id, Basketball-Reference slug), which is the cheapest legal way to join our records to every restricted source without ever fetching one.

TIER 2, CITATION-ONLY, ONE FACT AT A TIME, BY HAND, WITH A LINK. Basketball-Reference and the sports-reference family. Their own data_use page concedes "copyright law is clear that facts cannot be copyrighted, so you are free to reuse facts found on this site," and sharing.html says "You are free to use this data anywhere, we would just ask that you include the citation." Both permissions attach to FACTS and to the manual route; every prohibition on those pages attaches to the verb "scrape." So the project must be able to say honestly that it did not scrape — and the way to be able to say that is to actually not scrape.

TIER 3, DO NOT SOURCE FROM AT ALL WHERE ANY ALTERNATIVE EXISTS. nba.com, stats.nba.com, wnba.com, stats.wnba.com. Three independent reasons, each sufficient: § 9(ii) confines use to "legitimate news reporting or private, non-commercial purposes" and a published game is neither; § 6 / § LINKS forbids the deep link that makes a citation checkable, naming "a player page" as the example; and www.nba.com/robots.txt carries a blanket "Disallow: /" for anthropic-ai, ClaudeBot and Claude-Web with no Allow exceptions, while granting GPTBot and Google-Extended a carve-out list. A fact proved against Basketball-Reference carries none of that. A fact proved against nba.com carries all of it.

TIER 4, EU/UK-ESTABLISHED SOURCES — CITE ONLY, NEVER SYSTEMATICALLY. EuroLeague, Spanish/Italian/Greek league sites, Transfermarkt, BBC and Guardian archives, Opta/Stats Perform. These are the only holders in the entire survey who can assert the sui generis database right, because Art 11 limits beneficiaries to EU nationals and EU-established bodies. Name this tier explicitly in DEEPRESEARCH_KNOWLEDGE.md so the distinction survives the next session.

THE ROUTE THE HOLDER ACTUALLY BUILT, AND NOBODY USES. Every stats table on basketball-reference.com carries a SHARE link in its header that lets you delete rows and columns down to what you want and export HTML, iframe or pre-formatted text WITH AN SR CITATION ATTACHED AT THE BOTTOM. It is first-party, free, unmetered, and its terms are the most permissive language SRL publishes anywhere. It requires JavaScript and a human, which is the point — it is extraction by the exact method SRL built for the purpose, so none of the scraping prohibitions attach. For a project that needs discrete facts rather than a mirror, this is a better fit than the $5,000 custom-dataset route and it exists today. Practical shape: when a card needs a table-derived fact, a human opens the page, clicks SHARE, exports the trimmed table, and the export's own citation string becomes the card's provenance.

ATTRIBUTION — WHAT TO CARRY AND WHERE.
- On every card, in the card: source name + the exact URL that proves the fact + dateChecked. This already exists and already satisfies SR ToU § 5 principle (2), "explicitly credit SRL as the source of the data to the maximum extent possible," and CC BY-SA's first attribution option, "hyperlink... to the page or pages that you are reusing."
- One app-level SOURCES page listing every holder credited by name, with "Data from Wikidata" (their own suggested wording) even though CC0 requires nothing.
- A disclaimer on that page and in the store listing, modelled on the one Castle Rock quotes: not approved, licensed, or endorsed by the NBA, the WNBA, any team, or any player. This does no copyright work but speaks directly to New Kids prong three, Ohio § 2741.09(A)(6)'s endorsement proviso, and Daniels' reserved endorsement scrutiny.
- Never treat attribution as a legal cure for extraction. Under EU law only Art 9(b) makes source-indication matter, and it is gated on "the non-commercial purpose." Under the NBA/WNBA terms attribution is a condition ON TOP OF the non-commercial limit, not a substitute for it.

WRITING DISCIPLINE, WHICH IS WHERE MOST OF THE PROTECTION ACTUALLY LIVES.
- Store the DATUM, never the sentence. Feist: others may copy the underlying facts "but not the precise words used to present them." Castle Rock is the one trivia-format case and it was a LOSS turning entirely on copied expression — the court volunteered the description of the lawful trivia book, and it is this project: one that quizzes "such true facts as the identity of the actors... the biographies."
- Never let a scraper's default verbatim-capture behaviour put source prose on disk. This is the failure mode, because verbatim is the easy implementation.
- Normalise into our own schema. Volume is not the copyright risk; STRUCTURE is. Ten thousand facts is no worse than ten, but reproducing a source's ordering, tiers, groupings or leaderboard cuts imports their protectable selection.
- Keep the pack-design and selection rationale written down. Feist protects "selection, coordination, and arrangement" where there is a "creative spark," and a documented curatorial rationale is the evidence of it. This is the project's own strongest asset and it costs nothing.

COVERAGE AS A LEGAL ASSET. C.B.C. defeated the endorsement inference because the product "depend[s] on the inclusion of all players." Breadth is a defence. This aligns exactly with the MINE IT DRY rule already in CLAUDE.md — the messy wide pile is not just better research, it is the safer construction.

RATE AND IDENTITY DISCIPLINE, AS CODE NOT VIBES. A single fetch helper, used everywhere, that: honours 3 seconds between requests to any sports-reference host (their Crawl-delay, and the same 20/min as bot-traffic.html); caps Wikimedia at 3 concurrent connections with a real UA of the form BallKnowledge/1.0 (https://<site>; <email>); refuses any URL matching */gamelog/, */splits/, */on-off/, */lineups/, */shooting/ or /play-index/; refuses any nba.com or wnba.com host outright; and never presents a copied browser UA. Per CLAUDE.md's own rule that scripts run and reminders do not, this belongs in tools/ with a test, not in a doc.

STAY ACCOUNT-FREE ON RESTRICTED SOURCES. No Stathead subscription, no NBA account, no clickwrap accepted under the project's identity. hiQ's contract liability attached because it had agreed; the Ninth Circuit noted "HiQ is no longer bound by the User Agreement, as LinkedIn has terminated hiQ's user status." Whether we ever clicked "I agree" on a source is a first-order fact about exposure and it is cheap to keep straight — record it per source in TABLES.md or the source registry.

IF SOMETHING GOES WRONG, THE REMEDY IS A CONVERSATION. SR ToU § 20 requires written notice, a 10-business-day exchange, 60 days of negotiation and then mediation before either side litigates, and the blog says "if you are blocked by our servers, the blocks reset after 24 hours, so with some more polite settings on your bot you may be able to try again the next day." A block is a correction. If a letter ever arrives, the answer is a paragraph explaining that the bank is a few thousand hand-written questions with a link back on every one, that it is not a substitute for basketball-reference.com, and an offer to remove anything they name.
verdict.openly_licensed_backbone:
YES — AND IT IS WIKIDATA UNDER CC0. This is the strongest single finding in the run and it changes the plan more than any prohibition in it.

WHAT IT IS, in the holder's own words. Wikidata:Copyright, which is the whole of the policy page: "All structured data from the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespaces is available under the Creative Commons CC0 License; text in the other namespaces is available under the Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike License." dumps.wikimedia.org/legal.html says the same: "Copyrights of structured data in the main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema namespaces are waived using the Creative Commons Zero (CC0) public domain dedication."

ATTRIBUTION IS REQUESTED, NOT REQUIRED — and this is the exact sentence, from Wikidata:Data access: "We offer the data in Wikidata freely and with no requirement for attribution under CC-0. In return, we would greatly appreciate it if, in your project, you mention Wikidata as the origin of your data." They even supply the wording: "Powered by Wikidata", "Data from Wikidata", "Source: Wikidata". Put one on the sources page. It costs nothing and it is the only thing they ask for.

NO VOLUME CAP, NO NON-COMMERCIAL LIMIT, NO SHARE-ALIKE, NO ANTI-SUBSTITUTION CLAUSE. Bulk is the INTENDED use: "Use a dump when your result set is likely to be very large. You'll also find a dump important when setting up your own query service." The Wikimedia Robot policy's first rule is literally "Consider if dumps are more efficient than live requests."

THE THREE ROUTES, all free, no account, no key:
1. Wikidata JSON entity dumps, weekly, at https://dumps.wikimedia.org/wikidatawiki/entities/ — described by Wikidata itself as "the recommended dump format." Canonical RDF and smaller "truthy" RDF at the same location; 24-hour incremental add/change dumps at dumps.wikimedia.org/other/incr/wikidatawiki/.
2. SPARQL at https://query.wikidata.org/sparql, GET or POST, programmatic use expressly sanctioned. Honour 429 + Retry-After. You may self-host an instance "and query it as much as you like."
3. Per-entity Linked Data (Special:EntityData/Q42.ttl, ?flavor=dump) for one-off checks.

WHAT IT CAN CARRY. The spine of players.json: canonical and alternate names, birth date and place, height, position, teams-played-for with start/end dates, draft year and pick, awards and Hall of Fame membership, franchise histories, season links — and the external-id properties (NBA.com id, Basketball-Reference id, sports-reference slug), which are the cheapest legal way to join our records to every restricted source without fetching a single page from one.

WHAT IT CANNOT CARRY, said plainly so this is not over-read:
- STAT LINES A CARD TURNS ON. CC0 licenses the data and warrants nothing about it. For a quiz where a wrong card is the product defect, Wikidata is a legally free INDEX, not a citable authority. Its own statements carry references to third-party sources; those references are what a card should be proved against under the existing source tiers.
- MEDIA. Wikidata:Licensing says nothing whatsoever about images. The CC0 dedication reaches the P18 STATEMENT saying "this item's image is File:X.jpg" — not the pixels. Every file lives on Commons under its own per-file licence and must be cleared individually. I did not fetch the Commons licensing policy in this run.
- NON-COPYRIGHT RIGHTS. CC0 is a copyright waiver by a contributor and cannot waive what the contributor never held: publicity/personality rights and trademarks are untouched. Every NBA team mark reachable through Wikidata is still a trademark.
- NAMESPACE EDGE. Talk, Help and project-page PROSE is CC BY-SA, not CC0. The two lists disagree — the body of Wikidata:Licensing says "main, property and lexeme," the footer and Wikidata:Copyright say "main, Property, Lexeme, and EntitySchema." Take the footer version; the body predates the EntitySchema namespace. Irrelevant to us, we touch main only.

THE SECOND OPEN LAYER: WIKIPEDIA. Article text is CC BY-SA 4.0 + GFDL, but the FACTS are free of even that, because WMF ToU § 7 severs the one right that could otherwise reach a fact compilation: "Where you own Sui Generis Database Rights covered by CC BY-SA 4.0, you waive these rights. As an example, this means facts you contribute to the projects may be reused freely without attribution." That single sentence disposes of the database-right theory every other holder in the survey leans on. The condition is a writing discipline, not a negotiation: facts in, our sentences out. Copy Wikipedia's PROSE and CC BY-SA § 3(b) would put a bulk export of our own bank under BY-SA.

THIRD LAYER, FREE AT USEFUL SIZE: WIKIMEDIA ENTERPRISE. Free account, no credit card — On-demand API up to 50,000 requests/month, Snapshot API 30 requests/month with up to 1,500 chunks, Structured Contents included, every response carrying machine-readable licence metadata, which is exactly the field a per-card provenance system wants. Its API License Agreement § 3.2 pushes the CONTENT question back to the free licences: "the terms of this Agreement shall not apply to any Content."

THE HONEST HOLE, AND IT IS BIG. The prompt named four candidate backbones. THIS RUN ONLY ESTABLISHED ONE. Government archives, out-of-copyright newspapers, and official league record books were NOT RESEARCHED — no row in either set touches them, and I will not characterise them from memory. That is the highest-value next search in the whole project, because a pre-1930 newspaper archive would carry the Black Fives and early-league material where Wikidata is thinnest and where no commercial holder has a claim at all. Filed as an open question, not answered here.

RECOMMENDED DIVISION OF LABOUR: Wikidata dump/SPARQL for the spine and the ID crosswalk (CC0, zero obligations, no rate ceiling once downloaded); Wikipedia dumps for facts to seed questions, never for prose; Basketball-Reference read one page at a time, by hand or via the SHARE widget, to PROVE the specific claim a card asserts, with the URL on the card; NBA/WNBA properties avoided entirely.
do_not_do: Do not fetch anything from nba.com, stats.nba.com or any NBA-family host under a Claude or Anthropic-identified agent. www.nba.com/robots.txt carries 'User-agent: anthropic-ai / Disallow: /', 'User-agent: ClaudeBot / Disallow: /' and 'User-agent: Claude-Web / Disallow: /', all with no Allow exceptions, while GPTBot and Google-Extended get an explicit carve-out list including /players and /player/*profile$. Knowingly crawling under a named denial is the single worst-looking act available in this whole set, and it is not a close call.

Do not spoof a browser User-Agent to get past a block anywhere. Wikimedia's UA policy names it: 'Do not copy a browser's user agent for your bot, as bot-like behavior with a browser's user agent will be assumed malicious.' Sports Reference's blocking is Cloudflare behavioural filtering built specifically to catch rotated IPs and spoofed agents. Evasion turns an operational failure into evidence of intent, and it is the one thing that would make a polite letter into an unfriendly one.

Do not mirror basketball-reference season pages, league tables or career logs wholesale into any public table, JSON export, or browsable feature of the game. This is verbatim the fact pattern of ToU § 5: 'to create any database, archive, or other data store that competes with or constitutes a material substitute for the services or data stores offered on the Site.' The clause is a substitution test, not a volume test — a few thousand discrete cards with links back is not a substitute for basketball-reference.com; a copy of their season tables is. That distinction is the project's entire defence and it only works if it stays true.

Do not fetch */gamelog/, */splits/, */on-off/, */lineups/ or */shooting/ paths on basketball-reference, or /play-index/*.cgi?*. robots.txt disallows all of them for 'User-agent: *', even though the parent /players/ and /leagues/ pages are wide open. A fact sourced from a gamelog URL is on the wrong side of the file while the same fact from the player page is not.

Do not paste a Sports Reference page into a model to have it write, check or grade a card. ToU § 5 bars using Content 'for purposes of training, fine-tuning, prompting, or instructing artificial intelligence models or technologies in any manner, including without limitation for purposes of (i) generating answers, text, scores, statistics.' On the document's own words that describes the default workflow of an AI-built question bank. Read the number off the page, write the card by hand, cite the URL.

Do not source WNBA facts from wnba.com or stats.wnba.com when Basketball-Reference or contemporaneous reporting has the same fact. The WNBA's § NBA STATISTICS (ii) limits use to 'legitimate news reporting or private, non-commercial purposes' — a published, publicly playable game fails on 'private' regardless of whether money changes hands, so the credits-not-cash guardrail in DESIGN.md § 11 does not rescue it. Do not let stats.wnba.com's wide-open two-line robots.txt talk the project into a bulk pull; fetching is unrestricted there and USE is heavily restricted, and it is use we need.

Do not deep-link an nba.com or wnba.com internal page as a card's proof link. Both documents name the exact thing: 'links to internal pages within the Services (e.g., a player page, a photo gallery, or a feature article) other than to the home page of a League's team are not permitted.' If an NBA-family page must ever be credited, credit it as a word link to the homepage and prove the fact somewhere else.

Do not create an account, accept a clickwrap, or take a Stathead subscription under the project's identity and then feed the bank from it. hiQ won the CFAA question and lost on breach of the User Agreement in the same case; the contract bound because hiQ had agreed, and the Ninth Circuit noted hiQ was 'no longer bound by the User Agreement' once its user status was terminated. Staying account-free on every restricted source preserves the cheapest defence available. Record per-source whether we ever clicked 'I agree'.

Do not apply to the NBA Developer Portal. Its landing page says 'The NBA Developer Portal is only available for NBA Teams and Official NBA Business Partners, please do not reach out without the proper affiliation.' It is free but affiliation-gated — no budget buys this door. Recorded so no future session spends an afternoon rediscovering it.

Do not apply for a THINK450 / NBPA group licence at this stage. It demands three years of audited financial statements, corporate tax returns, bank letters and two credit references, and its idea-submission clause makes you acknowledge that indistinguishable products may already be licensed and 'you will not be entitled to any compensation.' It also only covers active NBA players, so it would not even solve the historical, WNBA or college halves of the bank — and every authority read says names plus factual performance data need no licence at all.

Do not ship illustrated portraits, avatars, or figurine pieces that depict identifiable real players. Keller is the case that goes against this project if that ever happens: 'EA's interactive game is not a publication of facts about college football; it is a game, not a reference source.' The whole defence is that Ball Knowledge IS a reference source with a quiz interface, and that survives only while the substance is facts and no likeness is rendered. Per the medium-honesty rule, source or commission GENERIC basketball figures.

Do not put player names, team names or league marks in the app icon, store listing, pack artwork, splash screen, push notifications or any advertising. Daniels draws the line exactly there — 'the unauthorized use of a personality to advertise or promote a product likely lies outside the scope of what is considered newsworthy' — and Jack Daniel's removes the Rogers defence when a mark is used as a designation of source for your own goods. The SAME name that is safe inside a question is a liability in a screenshot that sells the game.

Do not build packs around one marquee name. C.B.C.'s no-endorsement finding rested on the product depending 'on the inclusion of all players'; a curated star pack is precisely the thing that could 'create a false impression that some particular player with star power is endorsing' the game. Breadth of coverage is a legal asset, which happens to be the same thing MINE IT DRY already asks for.

Do not store or ship any source's sentences. Feist: others may copy the underlying facts 'but not the precise words used to present them.' Castle Rock is the only trivia-format case and it was a loss decided entirely on copied expression — the court itself described the lawful version: a quiz on 'such true facts as the identity of the actors... the biographies.' Verbatim capture is the default behaviour of every scraper, so this has to be enforced in the pipeline, not remembered.

Do not publish a bulk export of the bank that contains lifted Wikipedia prose. CC BY-SA § 3(b) would put the whole export under a BY-SA licence. Keeping the question text original is what keeps the project's own licensing free — a build discipline, not a negotiation.

Do not run any verification fetcher against stats.nba.com from CI, a cloud runner, GitHub Actions or this sandbox, and do not treat the failures as flaky. Cloud IP ranges are blocked wholesale; two requests from this machine hung to full timeout with zero bytes and no HTTP status while the HTML site answered 200 in the same minute. Assume BROKEN BY DEFAULT and budget accordingly, rather than writing retry logic against a silent drop.

Do not quote the 'nobody has ever been sued' finding as permission, in a commit message, a doc, or a conversation with Aaron. Absence of a public enforcement record measures RISK, not RIGHTS, and it says nothing about SR's AI-prompting clause, which is newer than every repository in that record and has no track record in either direction.

Do not exceed the published ceilings, ever, and do not test where they actually sit. 20 requests/minute on any sports-reference.com site (10 on FBref and Stathead), 3-second crawl delay, 'regardless of bot type and construction and pages accessed'; 3 concurrent connections and a descriptive contactable User-Agent on Wikimedia; and never crawl Wikipedia or Wikidata live when a dump exists — their own Robot policy's first rule says to prefer the dump.

Do not ship a browsable bulk player-stat table as a game feature, however rich players.json gets. That is the moment a trivia bank becomes something a source's users could consult INSTEAD OF the source, which is the trigger for both SR's material-substitute clause and EU Art 7(5)'s 'reconstitute... the whole or a substantial part'. This is a limit on what the product may BECOME and belongs in DESIGN.md, not in a research note.

Do not copy any source's curated selections — top-100 lists, 'greatest games', award-share tables, bespoke advanced metrics, editorial rankings. Feist leaves 'selection, coordination, and arrangement' protectable even where the facts are free, and BHB makes qualitative substantiality turn on where a compiler's own verification investment is concentrated. Exhaustive chronological tables are the weakly-protected part; the hand-built lists are the strong part. Normalise into our own schema and never mirror their ordering.
