open_questions: THE BIGGEST HOLE, AND IT IS THE ONE THE BRIEF ASKED ABOUT: government archives, out-of-copyright newspapers, and official league record books were NOT RESEARCHED AT ALL in this run. Not one row touches them. The only openly-licensed backbone actually established is Wikimedia/Wikidata. A pre-1930 newspaper archive is where the Black Fives and early-league material lives, it is exactly where Wikidata is thinnest, and no commercial holder has any claim over it. This is the highest-value next search in the project and it should be run as its own brief.

Does SR ToU § 5's AI clause reach a HUMAN who reads a page and then writes a card in their own words? The clause bars 'copy or use any material or Content from the Site... for purposes of training, fine-tuning, prompting, or instructing artificial intelligence models.' If no model ever sees the page, arguably nothing is being used to prompt anything. If a model drafts the card from a human-typed fact, arguably still nothing. If a model reads the page, plainly yes. Nobody has litigated it and the clause is newer than every scraper in the enforcement record, so there is no track record in either direction. This is the single question with the most bearing on how the mine-questions pass should be built.

Does Sportradar's trial tier permit DURABLE STORAGE of historical NBA/WNBA facts in a question bank, or only transient use? developer.sportradar.com was never opened. This is the only route in the entire survey where a rights holder affirmatively sells NBA and WNBA data to third parties at a documented tier, and it is the most promising answer to the WNBA coverage problem, which is the thinnest side of the bank. A search result described entry pricing as 'low thousands per month' and the reading agent expressly refused to assert it.

What did the hiQ v. LinkedIn consent judgment actually say? Unretrievable. Secondary sources report stipulated liability for trespass to chattels AND misappropriation plus destruction of derived data — if true, the case most often cited as proving scraping is lawful ended with the scraper conceding two of the very torts the Ninth Circuit had flagged. That materially changes how much comfort the hiQ line provides.

Is C.B.C. still good law in 2026? No Supreme Court docket was fetched, so its certiorari posture is unchecked, and no survey of later circuits was run. It is the central favourable authority for this whole product and its subsequent history is simply unverified. The same applies to Chabolla v. ClassPass, retrieved as a Feb 2025 slip opinion with a pending rehearing petition whose outcome was never checked.

Does New York's judge-made newsworthiness limit on 'purposes of trade' in Civil Rights Law §§ 50-51 cover a paid trivia game? Unlike California, Ohio, Indiana and Washington, the NY statute has NO express news, sports, historical or educational carve-out on its face — the limit is entirely case law, and no NY case law was retrieved. NY also carries a misdemeanor provision and exemplary damages for 'knowing' use.

Is Tennessee's § 47-25-1107 sports-account exemption still in a usable form? The 2024 ELVIS Act amendment appended 'to the extent protected by the First Amendment' to it, converting a bright-line statutory safe harbour into an untested constitutional balancing test, and the consolidated current text could not be retrieved from four sources. Also unverified: whether Indiana's statute changed after 2018 outside the four subsections the Indiana Supreme Court quoted in Daniels — the text used came from a 2006 mirror.

Is there any Council agreement under Directive Art 11(3) extending sui generis database protection to US-made databases? The reading agent searched non-exhaustively and found none, and the thirty-year standing position is that none exists. The entire 'US sources are outside the EU database right' conclusion rests on that negative.

Is the project 'commercial' for the purposes of NBA § 9(v) / WNBA (v) given a credits-only, no-real-money economy? The clauses turn on 'commercial product or service' — but § 9(ii) independently requires the use be for 'legitimate news reporting or PRIVATE, non-commercial purposes', and a publicly playable game appears to fail on 'private' whether or not it is commercial. The DESIGN.md § 11 guardrail may therefore buy nothing here. Not settled from the text alone.

Would Sports Reference grant permission if simply ASKED, and what does asking cost? Nobody has asked. The $5,000 floor is for CUSTOM DATASETS ('requests for data for custom downloads'), which is a completely different request from 'may we cite you on a few thousand trivia cards with a link back.' The Feedback Form is the stated channel. Worth noting the risk of asking: a refusal on the record is worse than silence, and SRL's own admission that 'in some cases, we cannot even give you explicit permission to reuse en masse' means they may be contractually unable to say yes even if willing.

Which rate limit does SR's server ACTUALLY enforce? bot-traffic.html (updated May 2024) says 20 requests/minute and jail 'up to a day'; the 429 page (copyright line still 2000-2023) says 'more than thirty pages in less than a minute' in its reasons and 'in jail for an hour' in its policy; the Oct 2022 blog says 'the blocks reset after 24 hours'. Three documents, three numbers. Nobody tested it, deliberately — tripping a rate limiter to learn its value is the one research method this exercise exists to avoid.

Is Wikidata's basketball coverage actually deep enough to carry the spine? No coverage measurement was made against players.json at all. The recommendation to use it as the backbone rests on what the LICENCE permits, not on what the data contains. Before committing to it, count: how many players in the bank have a Q-id, how many carry a Basketball-Reference slug as an external id, and how complete the teams-played-for statements are for pre-1980 players.

Do Wikimedia Commons per-file licences clear any usable player imagery? The Commons licensing policy was never fetched. All that is established is a negative — Wikidata's CC0 covers the STATEMENT naming an image file, never the pixels. Given the art pipeline this project already runs, this is worth its own read.

Can the basketball-reference SHARE widget be driven without a browser, and is its citation string stable enough to store as a card's provenance? The page says 'javascript required', which makes it a browser action rather than a curl — so the practical question is whether it fits a workflow at all, or whether it is a nice permission that nobody will ever use. Untested.

What is Kaggle's real takedown rate for sports-stats derivatives? Kaggle could not be read at all — curl hit a Google reCAPTCHA challenge on both the site and its internal datasets endpoint, and WebFetch returned only page titles. Only dataset titles, URL slugs and live-ness were confirmed; licence fields, provenance text and download counts were never seen. The one thing established is that the takedown channel FUNCTIONS (Retraction Watch, 29 July 2026, Kaggle removing a dataset for copyright infringement) and simply has not been pointed at these.

Does nba.com actually enforce its robots.txt denial of Anthropic agents, or is it declaratory? Never tested — no request was made presenting a ClaudeBot UA string, and guessing was refused. Two adjacent facts: robots.txt and the ToU both returned HTTP 200 to a spoofed Chrome UA from this host, and www.nba.com/stats returned 200 at 447,702 bytes, so the HTML front end is not IP-blocking this address. Whatever blocking exists on the stats API is happening somewhere else.

What is in vishaalagartha/basketball_reference_scraper issue #110 ('Getting Status Code 403 On All Requests', opened 2025-08-05, still open)? Body unread — the session's GitHub proxy is scoped to aselkridge/ball-knowledge and returned 'GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this session' for both the API and the HTML. Title, date and state only. Same limitation applies to the swar/nba_api issue bodies quoted second-hand through WebFetch summarisation rather than byte-verified.

Do the Black Fives Foundation, the Naismith Hall of Fame, the NCAA, USA Basketball, or any international federation publish terms that would open or close a route for the historical and college material? None were read. BLACKFIVES-OUTREACH.md is already a pending action in this repo and its shape — a written permission request to a rights holder — is exactly the shape the WNBA and NBA terms both name as the only door ('the Operator's express prior consent', 'the written permission of the Operator').

Does the project's own compilation copyright in the bank's selection and arrangement actually hold, and is it worth documenting deliberately? Feist says selection and arrangement are protectable where there is a 'creative spark', and a documented curatorial rationale is the evidence of it — but nobody has assessed whether the pack design currently reads as curated or as merely exhaustive. The parts that are exhaustive (a roster table) inherit Rural's weakness; the parts that are chosen for playability, difficulty spread and era balance do not. Unmeasured.

What is the actual legal status of the ~1,500 facts already in the bank, source by source? No audit of the existing citations against these tiers has been run. Before any of this becomes policy, someone should count: how many current cards cite an nba.com or wnba.com URL (Tier 3, the ones with the deep-link and non-commercial problems), how many cite a b-ref gamelog or splits path (robots-disallowed), and how many could be re-proved against a Tier 1 or Tier 2 source instead. That count is cheap, it is a script, and it turns this whole memo into a work item.
verdict.prose:
This is not legal advice. It is a record of what 94 documents say, read on 7 August 2026, with the eight I could not reach named at the end and the guesses left out.

Three findings change how the bank should be built.

**The facts are free, and the people who own the pages say so.** Sports Reference writes it on its own site: "copyright law is clear that facts cannot be copyrighted, so you are free to reuse facts found on this site." The Supreme Court said the same thing in Feist — "100 uncopyrightable facts do not magically change their status when gathered together in one place" — and the Second Circuit said it about basketball specifically, against the NBA, in 1997, in a case where a company paid people to watch games and type the stats into a commercial database. That was held lawful. So the question was never whether you may know that Robert Horry hit the shot. It is how you got the page, and what you agreed to on the way in.

**The real exposure is contract and connectivity, not copyright.** hiQ v. LinkedIn is the whole lesson in one case: hiQ won the criminal-statute question (a public webpage "has erected no gates to lift or lower in the first place") and then lost on breach of LinkedIn's user agreement. Not a crime, still a breach, and the breach is what cost money. A site's terms can forbid what copyright leaves free. Two things follow. First, never create an account or click "I agree" on a source you then mine — hiQ was bound because it had agreed. Second, and this is uncomfortable: reading a site's terms is itself part of what binds you to them. Courts have "consistently enforced browsewrap agreements where the user had actual notice." This project has now read them all. That is not a disaster, but the cheapest defence is spent, and the honest posture from here is compliance rather than deniability.

**There is a genuinely free backbone and it is Wikidata.** Every fact in Wikidata's main namespace is CC0 — public domain, no attribution required, no volume cap, no share-alike, no non-commercial limit. They publish complete weekly dumps and invite you to run your own copy. In their words: "We offer the data in Wikidata freely and with no requirement for attribution." Use it for the spine — names, birth dates, teams, draft years, awards, and above all the ID crosswalk that links our records to Basketball-Reference and NBA.com without ever fetching a page from either. What it cannot do is prove a stat line. CC0 licenses the data and warrants nothing about it, so Wikidata is a legally clean index, not a citable authority.

Put those together and the shape is: **Wikidata carries the bulk, Basketball-Reference proves single cards one page at a time with a link back, and nba.com and wnba.com are avoided entirely.** The NBA is worth avoiding for three independent reasons — its terms limit use to news reporting or private purposes, it forbids linking to the exact player page that would prove your fact, and its robots.txt bars Claude's crawlers from the entire site with no exceptions while granting other AI crawlers a carve-out list. That last one is not a legal argument; it is a refusal, in writing, and ignoring it would be the worst-looking thing this project could do.

On risk, honestly: **the thing that will actually happen is getting blocked.** It already happened twice in this research run. Sports Reference runs Cloudflare filtering with basketball on the always-on list, caps you at twenty requests a minute, and jails you for a day. The NBA blocks cloud IP ranges wholesale — requests from this machine hung to full timeout with zero bytes. Worse, the failures lie: one library's bug report is titled "silently swallows 403s and raises a misleading JSONDecodeError." You will lose hours to what looks like your own broken parser.

**The thing that has never happened is anyone being sued.** Across roughly a quarter-million monthly installs of scraper libraries named after these sites, running publicly for a decade, with datasets on Kaggle whose URLs literally say "from-basketball-reference," the total recorded legal enforcement by Sports Reference, the NBA and the WNBA is zero. Everything either holder has actually done was done by a load balancer. That is a measurement of risk, not permission — and it says nothing about SR's newer clause forbidding use of their content for "prompting" AI models, which describes how an AI-built question bank works and has no track record at all.

Two practical notes. Basketball-Reference built a SHARE button above every table that exports the data with a citation attached, and says "You are free to use this data anywhere." That is the sanctioned route, it is free, and nobody uses it. And write every question in your own words: the one trivia case in the record was lost on copied sentences, not on copied facts.
